title: An Extended Dataset of Educational Quality Across Countries (1970–2023)
weight_fields_interpretation: This paper constructs a cross-country panel dataset (country-year observations) by harmonizing and imputing test-score series and then deriving educational quality indexes for age cohorts. The only explicit weighting described is for the working-age educational quality index (ages 15–64), where population weights are used to aggregate cohort-specific normalized test scores into Q (15–19, 20–24, …, 60–64). The manuscript does not report the use of ILSA-style sampling/survey weights for student-level inference, and the ML imputation step (LASSO) is described as a standard supervised learning procedure with a train/validation split and cross-validation rather than complex-survey estimation. Therefore, analysts should treat the dataset as harmonized/constructed panel data with population-weighted aggregation for Q, not as a survey microdata file requiring student replicate-weight variance estimation.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The study is a dataset construction/harmonization paper that imputes missing country-year test-score observations using linear interpolation/extrapolation and a supervised LASSO prediction model, rather than estimating or analyzing ILSA Plausible Values (PV) for student achievement outcomes. Because the dependent variables are constructed harmonized scores (Tscore_INT/Tscore_ML) and derived indexes (Tscore1519_INT/Tscore1519_ML, Q_INT/Q_ML) at the country-year level, PV-specific combining rules are not applicable. Missingness is addressed via interpolation and ML-based prediction, but the paper does not frame this as a PV-multiple-imputation workflow with a standard PV handling category, so PV handling is set to not_applicable and missing-data handling is not_reported in the PV/missing-data schema.
outcome_summary: This paper does not estimate educational achievement effects on student-level outcomes; instead, it constructs an extended cross-country educational quality dataset from 1970–2023 by harmonizing mathematics and science test scores from TIMSS and PISA (plus earlier IEA/IAEP studies) onto the TIMSS 1995 metric (mean 500, SD 100). It anchors PISA to the TIMSS scale using equi-percentile linking and then averages mathematics and science to form a single harmonized achievement measure. Missing country-year observations (581 out of 1212; 48%) are filled using two approaches: linear interpolation/extrapolation (Tscore_INT) and a supervised LASSO regression imputation (Tscore_ML) trained on 80% of the data with 20% validation and grid search with tenfold cross-validation to minimize RMSE. The LASSO model reports RMSE of 17.5 and R² of 0.912 (and an out-of-sample RMSE of 15.7 and R² of 0.905), and the two imputation methods show high agreement (correlation 0.967). The working-age educational quality index Q is then computed using population-weighted aggregation across age cohorts with an assumed return parameter derived from wage-return estimates.
null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is intentionally sparse for ML/predictive findings because the manuscript is primarily a dataset construction and harmonization study (a data paper) rather than an empirical predictive modeling paper with a clearly defined student-level target variable and reported predictive performance for a specified outcome. As a result, there are no distinct target variables for which the schema requires StructuredFinding rows, and confounders/predictors are not extracted as conceptual controls because the LASSO is used for imputing missing harmonized scores rather than for causal or policy-relevant prediction of an educational outcome.
sample_filtering_criteria: The dataset covers 101 countries and 12 assessment years (1970, 1980, 1984, 1990, 1995, 1999, 2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019, 2023), forming 1212 potential country-year observations (101×12). Observed harmonized test-score inputs come from 631 original observed data points across TIMSS (1995–2023; 323), PISA (2000–2022; 245), and earlier IEA/IAEP studies (1970–1991; 63). The analytic panel is balanced via imputation of 581 missing country-year observations (48%) using (i) linear interpolation/extrapolation within each country and (ii) LASSO regression predictions using 501 fully observed World Bank economic/education indicators (from an initial pool of 3442). Countries are excluded if they lack nationally representative samples (explicitly noting China and India) or if key World Bank indicators are missing, which are required for panel construction and imputation.
effect_size: Best model: LASSO (see outcome_summary for metrics)

It anchors PISA to the TIMSS scale using equi-percentile linking and then averages mathematics and science to form a single harmonized achievement measure. Missing country-year observations (581 out of 1212; 48%) are filled using two approaches: linear interpolation/extrapolation (Tscore_INT) and a supervised LASSO regression imputation (Tscore_ML) trained on 80% of the data with 20% validation and grid search with tenfold cross-validation to minimize RMSE. The LASSO model reports RMSE of 17.5 and R² of 0.912 (and an out-of-sample RMSE of 15.7 and R² of 0.905), and the two imputation methods show high agreement (correlation 0.967). title: Investigating the Performance of Artificial Neural Networks in Predicting Affective Responses
journal: Journal of Measurement and Evaluation in Education and Psychology
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for the Lebanese sample (5614 participants initially) and then restricts the analytic dataset to 4631 cases after deleting observations with missing or extreme values to satisfy CFA/ANN assumptions. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA complex survey weights or any replicate-weight procedure, and it does not name any weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or software that would automatically apply them. Because the predictive component is an ANN trained on questionnaire Likert responses, the authors appear to have proceeded without explicit survey-weighted estimation; this means results may not be fully representative of the target population under PISA’s sampling design. No grade/school-type filtering is described beyond the missing/extreme-value deletion, and the ANN inputs are the six remaining Awacom items used to predict two held-out items.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are affective/intercultural communicative awareness Likert items (Awacom items ST218Q01HA–ST218Q07HA) rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. The study instead predicts item responses directly (scaled to 0–1 and then mapped back to ordinal categories), so PV generation/combining is not part of the analysis pipeline. Missing data handling is reported as listwise deletion (cases with missing and extreme values were deleted), so the missing-data strategy is documented.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 Lebanese student questionnaire data and focuses on the Awacom affective latent trait (intercultural communicative awareness). After deleting cases with missing and extreme values, the authors train feed-forward artificial neural networks to predict two held-out Awacom items (Item3 and Item7) from the other six items, scaling ordinal responses to 0–1 for ANN training and then mapping back to ordinal categories. For Item3, the best model (Model1) achieved RMSE around .619 (all) and produced moderate agreement with actual responses (match ratio .63; Kappa .42), with CFA-based validity/reliability showing improved factor loadings and reliability despite weaker fit indices. For Item7, the best model (ModelB) had RMSE around .708 (all) and lower agreement (match ratio .58; Kappa .37), but predicted subsets still improved variance explained, loadings, and reliability. Limitations include listwise deletion for missing/extreme values, no reported use of PISA sampling/replicate weights, and the fact that predictive overlap does not imply causal relationships.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 Lebanese sample data. Started with 5614 Lebanese students who participated in PISA 2018, then deleted cases with missing data and extreme values to meet assumptions for CFA (SEM) and ANN modeling; the final analytic sample contained 4631 students. No additional grade, school-type, or subgroup restrictions are described beyond this missing/extreme-value deletion.
effect_size: Best ANN model (Model1) selected by RMSE closeness across all/train/test: RMSE All=.619, Train=.618, Test=.623. Similarity between predicted vs actual Item3: Match ratio=.63; marginal homogeneity test p>.05; Kappa=.42 (moderate). Construct validity/reliability: for predicted subset RMSEA=.106, CFI=.965, TLI=.948, R-square=.983, Loading=.992, Alpha=.903 (vs actual subset RMSEA=.081, CFI=.972, TLI=.959, R-square=.613, Loading=.783, Alpha=.891).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 (Lebanon) Awacom item the study leveraged Item1, Item2, Item4, Item5, and Item6 responses to predict Item3 responses, finding that predicted and actual Item3 responses overlapped at a moderate level (Kappa=.42; match ratio=.63) while CFA fit indices were only partially weakened. This indicates that ANN-based response prediction within the same affective latent construct can preserve measurement structure and slightly improve reliability, suggesting potential for data augmentation or missing-item recovery in intercultural awareness scales, though the study does not establish causal effects and uses listwise deletion for missing/extreme values.
confounders: Item1 intercultural awareness; Item2 intercultural awareness; Item4 intercultural awareness; Item5 intercultural awareness; Item6 intercultural awareness; Item7 intercultural awareness

title: Combining Clickstream Analyses and Graph-Modeled Data Clustering for Identifying Common Response Processes
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIAAC 2012 PSTRE interactive task process data (item U01a) and constructs action-pattern similarity graphs from time-stamped action sequences. The analytic sample is restricted to examinees with a correct response and further reduced to a randomly chosen subset (N=225) because solving the cluster-editing ILP for the full set was computationally infeasible. The manuscript does not report applying PIAAC complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures; therefore, population-representativeness of the discovered response-process cliques cannot be assumed. Weighting is not discussed as part of the clustering/ILP workflow, which focuses on graph structure derived from observed action sequences and action-level times.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper uses PSTRE plausible values (PV) to relate discovered response-process cliques to external performance, but it does not describe a PV-combining rule (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or the exact PV aggregation strategy used in the reported summaries. Missing-data handling is also not documented for the PVs or for the process-log variables used to build action patterns, which is a reporting gap because PV-based analyses in ILSA typically require explicit handling of missingness and PV replication/combining.
outcome_summary: The paper proposes an exploratory two-step workflow for identifying common response processes in interactive tasks: (1) compute similarity between examinees’ time-stamped action patterns using an LCS-based measure that can be made sensitive or less sensitive to action-level timing, and (2) apply cluster edge deletion (a cluster-editing/ILP graph clustering method) to obtain homogeneous cliques representing dominant and idiosyncratic response processes. The empirical illustration uses PIAAC 2012 PSTRE process data for the US sample, focusing on item U01a and a correct-response subset (N=225) due to computational constraints. Incorporating action-level times increased edge deletions and produced substantially more cliques (e.g., 30 vs 73 vs 140 depending on similarity sensitivity), indicating greater differentiation of response processes. When relating cliques to PSTRE plausible values, action-only dominant processes were not predictive of proficiency, whereas timing-informed cliques supported differentiation within strategies; age showed related patterns. Limitations include the exploratory nature, lack of reported survey-weight usage, and no single supervised predictive performance metric.
null_fields_interpretation: This is an exploratory process-data clustering paper rather than a supervised predictive ML study: it does not train a predictive model with accuracy/AUC/RMSE metrics. Consequently, ml_techniques are left empty (no supervised learner is evaluated), and the main outputs are graph-clustering results (edge deletions, clique counts, and descriptive PV differentiation).
sample_filtering_criteria: Uses the PIAAC 2012 US sample process data for a single PSTRE item (U01a). The analysis includes only examinees with a correct response (678 correct in total) and then restricts to a randomly chosen subset of N=225 (about one third) because the ILP-based cluster edge deletion could not be solved for the full correct sample within a reasonable time (<3 days). The item’s initial 'start' action is dropped (time-to-action would be zero by definition), and non-essential actions are aggregated into higher-level action categories, yielding 36 aggregated actions for constructing action sequences and action-level times.
effect_size: Not reported (graph-based clustering outputs: number of edges deleted and number of cliques; no predictive accuracy metric). Action-based similarity: 15,385 edges with 60.57% deleted; modified time-related similarity: 4,577 edges with 70.48% deleted; original similarity: 1,006 edges with 73.06% deleted. Edited graphs yield 30, 73, and 140 cliques (action-based, modified, original).
primary_finding: Using PIAAC 2012 PSTRE (US) Item U01a process data, the study leveraged Age and PSTRE plausible values as external covariates to interpret the discovered dominant response processes, finding that incorporating action-level times into the action-pattern similarity substantially increased edge deletions and produced more, smaller, and more differentiated cliques than action-only similarity. This indicates that fine-grained timing information can improve the granularity and interpretability of response-process typologies for interactive assessment design, though the clustering is exploratory and not a supervised predictive model.
confounders: Age; PSTRE plausible values

title: An exploratory analysis of the latent structure of process data via action sequence autoencoders
authors: Xueying Tang; Zhi Wang; Jingchen Liu; Zhiliang Ying
journal: British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIAAC 2012 PSTRE process-log data (14 items) and constructs an analytic dataset at the respondent–item level with both action sequences and final outcomes. The manuscript does not report applying PIAAC sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures, nor does it name any weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or variance estimation approach. Because the analysis relies on neural-network-based feature extraction (autoencoders) followed by generalized linear/logistic/linear models, the paper does not describe any complex-survey design correction; this is a potential limitation for population-representativeness and standard error calibration. The main preprocessing described is (i) converting polytomous outcomes to binary (fully corrected=1, otherwise=0) and (ii) simplifying process data into action-sequence representations with variable lengths handled by the autoencoder architecture.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in the case study are derived from process logs (binary item outcomes created from fully corrected responses) and from PIAAC literacy/numeracy scores used as continuous outcomes; the paper does not describe whether these scores are PV-based achievement estimates or alternative scaled scores. The manuscript also does not report a missing-data strategy (e.g., how respondents/items with incomplete process sequences or missing background variables were handled), beyond reporting counts of respondents who answered 7 vs 14 items. Given the absence of explicit documentation, the missing-data handling is treated as a reporting gap that prevents assessing bias from nonresponse or item noncompletion.
outcome_summary: This paper proposes an action-sequence autoencoder to extract fixed-length latent features from PIAAC 2012 PSTRE process logs, where each respondent–item interaction is represented as a variable-length sequence of categorical actions. The authors train the autoencoder (using LSTM or GRU recurrent units) with validation-based early stopping, then apply principal component analysis to obtain interpretable feature dimensions. In simulations, the extracted features preserve information and recover latent group structure with high reconstruction and classification accuracy (e.g., group accuracy near 1.00 in scenario I). In the PIAAC case study (14 PSTRE items; 11,464 respondents’ response processes), derived variables—including binary item outcomes—are reconstructed with prediction accuracy >0.80 for all 93 derived variables and >0.975 for 35 variables. For competency and background variables, process-feature models improve out-of-sample R2 for literacy and numeracy and increase gender prediction accuracy from 0.55 (baseline) to up to 0.63, with age OSR2 about doubling versus baseline. Limitations include lack of reported complex-survey weighting and missing-data handling, and the study is predictive rather than causal.
ml_all_techniques: Autoencoder, LSTM, GRU, Logistic Regression, Linear Regression
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIAAC 2012 PSTRE process-log data for 14 PSTRE items. The analytic dataset includes 11,464 respondents’ response processes across the 14 items; 7,620 respondents answered 7 items and 3,645 respondents answered all 14 items. For each respondent–item pair, both the action sequence and the final response outcome were recorded. Final outcomes that were originally polytomous were simplified into binary outcomes: fully corrected responses labeled 1 and all others labeled 0. For feature extraction and downstream prediction, the paper further restricts to derived variables/actions/pairs that meet frequency thresholds in simulations (rare actions/pairs appearing fewer than 0.05n times excluded) and uses training/validation/test splits within the available respondent–item data.
effect_size: Derived-variable reconstruction: prediction accuracy > 0.80 for all 93 derived variables; 75/93 variables accuracy > 0.90; 35 variables accuracy > 0.975. Cross-item outcome prediction: process-model improves prediction accuracy over baseline model for many item pairs (exact aggregate metric not reported).
primary_finding: Using PIAAC 2012 PSTRE process data (14 items) the study leveraged autoencoder-derived process features—especially attentiveness-related and sequence-length-related features—to predict binary item outcomes and other derived process indicators, finding that process features reconstruct derived variables with high accuracy (all >0.80; 75 >0.90; 35 >0.975). This indicates that response-process information can substantially improve the prediction of item correctness beyond using final outcomes alone, suggesting that assessment analytics and scoring models could incorporate process-derived latent features to better diagnose performance and error patterns, though the paper does not report survey-weighted inference or a missing-data strategy.
confounders: Sequence length (log); Attentiveness feature; Gender; Age; Literacy score; Numeracy score

title: Improving the Precision of Ability Estimates Using Time-On-Task Variables: Insights From the PISA 2012 Computer-Based Assessment of Mathematics
authors: Reis Costa; D. Reis Costa; M. B. (not specified in provided text); J. T. (not specified in provided text); B. A. (not specified in provided text)
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics log-file data for 10 released items and combines them with the corresponding item-response data to estimate latent proficiency. The analytic sample is restricted to students with valid final scores and complete timing information, and additionally excludes countries where log-file data were unavailable for two analyzed items (Chile). The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or replicate weights; therefore, it is unclear whether complex survey design features were incorporated via weight variables in estimation. The authors instead rely on model-based estimation (Mplus) with full information maximum likelihood (FIML) under a missing-at-random assumption for missing responses within the modeling framework.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because the study estimates latent proficiency directly via an IRT-style graded response model and reports EAP reliability and standard errors, rather than using PISA achievement plausible values. Missing responses are handled using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in Mplus under a missing-at-random (MAR) assumption, which is not a standard PV-multiple-imputation workflow; the schema maps this to multiple_imputation for missing-data handling. The paper provides sufficient detail on the MAR/FIML approach, but it does not explicitly describe any PV-based combining rules because PVs are not the target representation in this analysis.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics log-file data for 10 released digital math items, estimating latent proficiency using three hierarchical measurement models: M1 (response accuracy only), M2 (response accuracy plus response times via a simple-structure speed factor), and M3 (adds cross-loadings linking response times directly to proficiency). Across 31 participating countries/economies (18,970 students after exclusions), the baseline GRM fit was acceptable (SRMR=0.036; RMSEA=0.050). Measurement precision improved when response times were included: EAP reliability increased from 0.73 (M1) to 0.77 (M2) and 0.80 (M3), while average standard errors decreased from 0.51 to 0.49 and 0.45. Country-level mean proficiency estimates were largely stable across models, but correlations between ability estimates differed, especially between M1 and M3. The paper uses FIML under MAR for missing responses and does not report survey-weighted estimation, so results reflect measurement-model assumptions rather than causal effects.
null_fields_interpretation: No machine-learning algorithms were trained or evaluated; the paper compares statistical measurement models (hierarchical IRT-style models estimated in Mplus) to study changes in measurement precision and invariance. Therefore, ml_techniques.primary is left null and all_techniques is empty, consistent with the study’s focus on psychometric measurement modeling rather than predictive ML.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics log-file data for 10 released and valid items (cluster-based administration) and excluded Chile because log-file data were unavailable for two analyzed items (I20Q1 and I20Q3). Further excluded students with invalid information, including those who did not receive final scores or had incomplete timing information. The remaining analytic sample comprises 18,970 students across 31 countries/economies, with country-level sample sizes reported in Table 1 for the full computer-based mathematics clusters (41 items) and for the subsample with valid log-file data (10 items).
effect_size: Model fit: GRM SRMR=0.036; RMSEA=0.050. EAP reliability: M1=0.73, M2=0.77, M3=0.80. Average SE: M1=0.51, M2=0.49, M3=0.45. Reported precision gains: many countries show increases in EAP reliability at or above 0.05 for M2 vs M1; additional gains for M3 vs M2 generally 0.02–0.03.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2012 Computer-Based Mathematics the study leveraged response accuracy, time-on-task (response times), and country-level heterogeneity to estimate student ability precision, finding that adding response-time information increased EAP reliability and reduced average standard errors versus response-accuracy-only modeling. This indicates that incorporating time-on-task variables into the measurement model can improve the precision of operational proficiency estimates, though the study is measurement-model based (not causal) and does not report survey-weighted estimation.
confounders: Response accuracy (graded responses); Time-on-task (response times); Country/economy

title: The potential of international large-scale assessments for meta-analyses in education
authors: Ronny Scherer; Tobias Nilsen; Felix Scherer
weight_fields_interpretation: This article is a methodological review of how meta-analysts can include international large-scale assessment (ILSA) data in education meta-analyses; it does not estimate student-level outcomes from an ILSA micro-dataset. Consequently, there is no analytic sample drawn from PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS/ICILS microdata for which student or replicate weights would be applied. The paper instead discusses, at a conceptual level, that correct effect-size extraction from ILSA primary studies requires accounting for complex survey design features (e.g., multistage clustering, sampling weights, variance estimation via replicate/jackknife methods, and plausible value-based achievement estimation). For practitioners implementing the recommended approaches, the weighting and variance-estimation steps should follow the ILSA technical documentation and the effect-size computation guidance cited in the review (e.g., Rutkowski et al., 2010; Rust, 2014).
handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a methodological review (and systematic review of existing meta-analyses) rather than an empirical analysis predicting student outcomes from ILSA microdata. Therefore, plausible values (PVs) and missing-data handling strategies are not implemented or reported as part of the study’s own estimation pipeline. The paper discusses PV-based achievement estimation and complex survey design considerations as requirements for future meta-analytic implementations, but it does not execute those computations on a new PV-based dataset.
outcome_summary: This methodological review synthesizes principles and practices for integrating international large-scale assessment (ILSA) data into education meta-analyses, focusing on two substantive contexts: gender differences and socioeconomic status (SES) gaps in student achievement. It proposes an analytic framework with four effect-size inclusion approaches: separate meta-analyses, indirect inclusion via Bayesian meta-analysis, one-stage direct inclusion, and two-stage direct inclusion. Across the systematic review of existing meta-analyses, the authors report that ILSA data were not eligible for all meta-analyses and that inclusion was limited, with only one gender meta-analysis explicitly addressing dependence structures via multilevel meta-analysis. The paper emphasizes that correct effect-size extraction from ILSA requires accounting for complex survey design (weights, clustering, variance estimation) and plausible-value achievement estimation, and that meta-analytic data structures can introduce secondary clustering that may require multilevel meta-analysis or robust variance estimation. Limitations include that the framework’s performance is not evaluated via simulations or large-scale meta-analytic benchmarking.
null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical ML study and does not train or evaluate predictive models on ILSA microdata. It is a methodological and systematic review of how ILSA data have been included in prior meta-analyses, so there is no student-level target variable, no analytic sample of students, and no PV/missing-data handling implemented by the authors’ own estimation pipeline.
sample_filtering_criteria: Systematic review of meta-analyses: searched ERIC and PsycINFO (plus hand-searching key journals and PsyArXiv), screened meta-analyses published in English between 1995 and 2020, required full-text availability, and applied topic- and eligibility-based inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., correlational/observational relations for gender/SES vs achievement; excluded effectiveness/intervention meta-analyses; excluded outcomes not assessed in ILSAs; excluded non-ILSA-eligible samples such as primary-school-only or medically selected groups).

title: Automated Scoring of Constructed-Response Items Using Artificial Neural Networks in International Large-scale Assessment
authors: Ji Yoon Jung; L. Tyack; M. v. Davier
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 constructed-response items (US English responses) and creates an analytic dataset by splitting responses into training (80%) and validation (20%) sets using simple holdout validation. The paper describes three training-data weighting/filtering approaches based on agreement between human rater scores and IRT-based expected scores (unweighted all data; weighted all data with a 2:1 match:mismatch ratio; and match-data unweighted). However, it does not report applying TIMSS sampling/survey weights (e.g., student weights or replicate weights) in the ANN training or evaluation. Because the models are supervised ANNs trained on text-derived features, the manuscript does not indicate any complex-survey weighting variables were used; the only “weighting” discussed is IRT-based reweighting of training instances for quality control.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are dichotomous item scores (correct vs incorrect) for four TIMSS constructed-response items, derived from human rater scoring and IRT-based expected scores (MAP thresholding). TIMSS plausible values are typically generated for cognitive achievement scales, but this study does not model PV-based achievement outcomes; instead it performs automated classification of item-level correctness. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data strategy for student responses (e.g., how missing text responses or missing fields were handled), so the missing-data handling is not reported.
outcome_summary: The study evaluates ANN-based automated scoring for four TIMSS 2019 constructed-response items using US English responses, comparing automated predictions to professional human rater scores. Using a feed-forward neural network trained on bag-of-words text features, the average agreement between human and automated scores was very high across items (average Pearson r=0.91). For the easier items (SE71054, SE71077), agreement was consistently high (r≈0.93–0.94), with the best result for SE71077 when training on responses where human and IRT-expected scores matched (r=0.96). For the more difficult items (ME72209, SE62005), agreement remained strong but more variable (r≈0.85–0.92), with IRT-based weighting improving SE62005 (r=0.87). The paper reports holdout validation (20%) and 5-fold CV within training, but it does not report a missing-data strategy and does not apply TIMSS sampling weights; the only “weighting” is IRT-based reweighting/filtering for training quality control.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used four released TIMSS 2019 constructed-response items and analyzed student responses collected from the United States (US English responses). Each item is dichotomously scored (full credit for correct, no credit for incorrect). For model training, responses were split into training (80%) and validation (20%) sets via simple holdout, preserving class distribution within each item. Three training-data variants were created: (1) all data unweighted (raw human scores), (2) all data weighted using IRT-based expected scores with a 2:1 match:mismatch ratio (match defined as human score equals IRT-expected score), and (3) match data unweighted (only responses where human and IRT-expected scores matched).
effect_size: ANN agreement with human scores (Pearson r): all data unweighted r=0.93; all data weighted r=0.92; match data unweighted r=0.93. Average across approaches for this item: ~0.93.
primary_finding: Using TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS constructed-response item SE71054 the study leveraged human rater scoring and IRT-expected scoring (used to weight/filter training instances) to predict item correctness with an ANN, finding that automated scores matched human scores very closely (r≈0.93) and that IRT-based weighting/filtering did not materially change performance. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.
confounders: Human rater score; IRT-expected score (MAP); Item difficulty level

title: Research engagement in the Progress in International Reading Literacy Study: A systematic review
authors: Jamie Stiff; Jenny Lenkeit; Therese Hopfenbeck; Heather Kayton; Joshua McGrane
weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a systematic review of PIRLS-related peer-reviewed journal articles rather than an analysis of PIRLS microdata. As such, there is no student-level sampling frame, no plausible-value (PV) scaling step, and no application of PIRLS/TIMSS/OECD complex survey weights (e.g., student or replicate weights). The review’s “sample” consists of bibliographic records identified through database searches (ERIC, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, Zetoc) and then screened using inclusion/exclusion criteria (English-language, peer-reviewed journal, PIRLS as a main data source/topic). Therefore, weighting variables and replicate-weight variance estimation are not applicable to the review’s descriptive counts and qualitative synthesis.
handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a systematic review that does not estimate student-level PIRLS achievement scores or any PV-based outcomes. The dependent information is bibliographic and thematic coding of included studies (e.g., article nature, cycle focus, topic categories), so PV handling is not part of the methodology. Missing-data handling for PVs is therefore not applicable to the review’s design, and the paper does not report a PV/missing-data strategy because no PV-based modeling is conducted.
outcome_summary: This systematic review synthesizes 221 PIRLS-related peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2004 and 2022, building on a prior database of 113 articles (2004–2015) and adding 108 newly identified articles (2015–2022). The review’s descriptive results show an overall increase in research engagement with PIRLS, particularly after the 2011 cycle, and a shift toward secondary data analyses rather than critiques or policy/impact studies. Across the included literature, most articles focus on overall reading performance rather than specific reading purposes or comprehension processes, and only a small number address subscales such as literary vs. informational purposes or the four comprehension processes. Qualitatively, the review highlights recurring themes: teacher characteristics and instruction practices, socioeconomic predictors of reading outcomes, and critiques of PIRLS scaling/IRT practices (e.g., measurement invariance and DIF). Because this is not an empirical ML study, there are no predictive metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) and no PV-based modeling; the main contribution is mapping how PIRLS data are used in the research community and where gaps remain.
null_fields_interpretation: This record is a systematic review rather than an empirical study using PIRLS microdata. Consequently, there is no student-level analytic sample, no country-level per-country N table for the review itself, no PV handling or missing-data strategy for achievement modeling, and no ML training/evaluation pipeline. The extraction therefore leaves ML and weighting fields empty/null by design, while still capturing the review’s bibliographic search and screening methodology.
sample_filtering_criteria: The review constructed a bibliographic database starting from Lenkeit et al. (2004–2015; 113 articles). It searched five digital databases (ERIC, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, Zetoc) for PIRLS-related terms in all fields, restricting the date range to January 2015–May 2022 to reduce overlap. authors: Susu Zhang; Zhi Wang; Jitong Qi; Jingchen Liu; Zhiliang Ying

outcome_summary: This paper proposes a process-incorporated latent trait scoring method that refines IRT-based ability estimates using features extracted from students’ problem-solving action sequences. The empirical evaluation uses OECD PIAAC 2012 PSTRE process data for respondents in five countries/regions who completed all 14 PSTRE items; the authors exclude omissions and split the 14 items into scoring (Bs) and reference (Br) sets to evaluate reliability via split-half agreement. Across scoring-set lengths from 2 to 7 items, the process-incorporated estimator achieved consistently lower MSE against the reference-set latent estimate and higher Kendall’s τ rank agreement than response-only scoring; notably, with 2 items it matched the response-only performance of using about 5 items, and with 4+ items it matched or exceeded response-only scoring using all 7 items. The method uses regression-based conditional expectations (with ridge regression for the first conditional expectation) and relies on feature extraction via multidimensional scaling of action sequences. Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weight usage, reliance on split-half reference estimates rather than true θ, and the fact that the paper’s theoretical guarantees depend on regularity assumptions about local independence and monotonicity.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used OECD PIAAC 2012 PSTRE process data for respondents assigned to PSTRE for both blocks. Each PSTRE block contained 7 items (14 total across both blocks). title: Using convolutional neural networks to automatically score eight TIMSS 2019 graphical response items
authors: Lillian Tyack; Lale Khorramdel; Matthias von Davier
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical response items (eight items across Grade 4 and Grade 8) with student responses collected from participating countries. The analytic sample is constructed per item by taking screenshot-based image responses, converting them to greyscale, resizing to fixed pixel dimensions, and mapping human rater scores to integer labels (incorrect/partial/full). The paper does not report applying TIMSS complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures; instead, it trains CNN classifiers using keras and evaluates performance via hold-out splits and five-fold cross-validation. Because the modeling is ML-based image classification and the manuscript does not describe weight-aware estimation, the analysis is treated as unweighted, and results should be interpreted as validation of scoring agreement rather than population-representative achievement estimation.

outcome_summary: This study evaluates whether convolutional neural networks can automatically score TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical constructed-response items by matching human rater classifications. The authors selected eight items (five Grade 4 and three Grade 8; one Grade 8 item, ME62300, is trichotomous) and pre-processed student screenshots into fixed-size greyscale images for CNN training. Performance was assessed using hold-out validation and five-fold cross-validation, reporting exact-match accuracy, loss, and F1-scores to account for class imbalance. For the seven dichotomous items, best CNNs achieved very high agreement (average accuracy about 99.37%–99.92% and F1 between 0.9948 and 0.9992). For the trichotomous item ME62300, accuracy was 97.99% with F1 = 0.9766, and performance dropped on responses that were incorrectly human-scored (accuracy 88.81%). sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical response items: identified all graphical response items in TIMSS 2019, excluded the “Building” PSI item already modeled by von Davier et al. effect_size: Best CNNs: average accuracy 99.37%–99.92% across seven dichotomous items; F1-scores between 0.9948 and 0.9992; losses reported as low (e.g., 0.0063–0.0298 average loss across items in Table 8).
primary_finding: Using TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 4 graphical response item the study leveraged convolutional neural networks to classify each student image into the same score categories as human raters, finding that the CNNs achieved near-perfect agreement (≈99% accuracy and F1 ≥ 0.9948) for dichotomous items. title: USING A MACHINE LEARNING APPROACH TO EXPLORE NON-COGNITIVE FACTORS AFFECTING READING, MATHEMATICS, AND SCIENCE LITERACY IN CHINA AND THE UNITED STATES

title: Exploration of Variables Predicting Sense of School Belonging Using the Machine Learning Method—Group Mnet
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for Korean students and constructs a modeling dataset by merging four questionnaires (student background, ICT familiarity, educational career, and parent). The authors explicitly removed weighting variables (e.g., W_FSTURWT) during preprocessing, along with identification and administration variables, and then restricted the plausible values by retaining only the first PV per subject while deleting the other PVs. They further removed variables with ≥30% missingness and near-zero variance variables, and then applied k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) imputation to handle remaining missingness. Because the manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (and the weighting variable was removed), the ML models are treated as unweighted analyses; this may affect generalizability and uncertainty estimates under the clustered sampling design.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 Korean student data to predict students’ sense of school belonging measured by ST034 (4-point Likert; Cronbach’s alpha = .80). After preprocessing (removing identification/administration/weighting variables, retaining only the first PV per subject, deleting variables with ≥30% missingness and near-zero variance, and using k-NN imputation for remaining missingness), the authors fit Group Mnet, a penalized regression method designed for grouped dummy-coded predictors and multicollinearity. Model performance was assessed via repeated random train/test splits (70/30) with 10-fold CV on training to select the penalty, repeated 100 times; test RMSE was stable at a mean of 0.39 (SD=0.009). Across runs, Mnet selected on average 74.55 variables (≈14.8% of 504), and 32 variables were selected in ≥75 iterations, spanning student, parent, peer/teacher, ICT, and learning/physical activity domains. Limitations include unweighted ML estimation (PISA weights removed/not applied) and the fact that penalized selection counts identify predictive contribution rather than statistical significance or causality.
sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample is Korean students participating in PISA 2015 (n=5581; most are 10th graders). The authors began with 927 student and parent variables after merging four questionnaires, removed irrelevant variables including identification (e.g., CNTSTUID), weighting (e.g., W_FSTURWT), and administration (e.g., ADMINMODE), and retained only the first plausible value (PV1) for each subject while deleting other PVs. They then deleted variables with ≥30% missingness (68 variables), removed near-zero variance variables (65 variables), removed derived variables (56 variables such as ANXTEST and MOTIVA) and instead included individual items, yielding 504 variables. For missingness in the remaining predictors, they used k-NN imputation after listwise deletion would have retained only ~8.13% of observations (454/5581).
effect_size: Group Mnet — test RMSE stable across 100 iterations: range 0.36–0.41, mean 0.39 (SD=0.009). Average selected variables per run: 74.55 (SD=22.14) out of 504; ~14.8% selected per run.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 (KOR) the study leveraged student gender, home ICT resources, perceived school climate threats, teacher treatment, and life satisfaction to predict students’ sense of school belonging (ST034), finding that predictors spanning background, school climate, peer/teacher relationships, parental involvement, motivation/anxiety, ICT attitudes, and learning/physical activities contributed to prediction with stable test RMSE (≈0.39). title: The limits of inference: reassessing causality in international assessments
authors: David Rutkowski; Leslie Rutkowski; Greg Thompson; Yusuf Canbolat
weight_fields_interpretation: This article is a conceptual and methodological critique of causal inference claims using international large-scale assessment (ILSA) data, not an empirical analysis of ILSA microdata. As such, it does not define an analytic sample from PIRLS/PISA/TIMSS microdata, does not report any sampling or replicate-weighting scheme, and does not specify weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT, TOTWGT) for estimation. The discussion instead focuses on design assumptions in randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental approaches (e.g., potential outcomes framework, SUTVA, parallel trends) and how ILSA features (cross-country heterogeneity, standardization, country-level treatment measures, and limited longitudinal linkage) constrain causal validity. Therefore, there are no weight-based data preparation steps to apply for model estimation in this paper.
handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not conduct an empirical ILSA-based estimation with a cognitive achievement dependent variable; instead, it reviews and critiques causal inference approaches and discusses limitations of quasi-experimental designs when applied to ILSA data. Because there is no PV-based outcome modeling (and no reported PV estimation pipeline), plausible values handling is not applicable. Missing-data handling is also not reported because the paper is not fitting statistical models to an ILSA dataset with item nonresponse or PV generation.
outcome_summary: This article does not estimate predictive or causal effects using ILSA microdata; instead, it reassesses the validity of causal claims made with ILSA data. It contrasts randomized controlled trials with quasi-experimental designs grounded in the potential outcomes framework, emphasizing that quasi-experimental identification relies on strong, often untestable assumptions. Using illustrative examples, it argues that ILSA-specific features—cross-country heterogeneity, assessment standardization, limited ability to define exogenous treatments, and frequent reliance on country-level treatment measures—undermine key causal conditions such as equivalence of groups in expectation (parallel trends) and the stability/no-hidden-variation assumptions. The paper concludes with a framework for critically evaluating quasi-experimental designs using ILSAs and recommends caution in translating statistical associations into policy-relevant causal interpretations.
null_fields_interpretation: The extraction yields null sample and ML fields because the manuscript is a conceptual/methodological review and critique rather than an empirical study with an analytic dataset, model training, or reported performance metrics. It discusses causal inference frameworks and evaluates the plausibility of causal assumptions in prior quasi-experimental studies that use ILSA data, so there is no student-level PV handling, missing-data strategy, or weighting scheme to extract.
sample_filtering_criteria: No analytic sample is constructed from ILSA microdata. The paper synthesizes and critiques prior studies (including examples using PIRLS and other quasi-experimental designs) rather than estimating models on a newly defined student-level dataset.

title: Evaluating uncertainty: the impact of the sampling and assessment design on statistical inference in the context of ILSA
authors: Diego Cortes; D. Hastedt; S. Martin
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 data and explicitly relies on PIRLS-provided estimation weights that combine inclusion probabilities and nonresponse adjustments (school-level and within-school nonresponse factors). For sampling variance, the paper describes the Jackknife Repeated Replications (JRR) approach used in PIRLS, which approximates the sampling distribution of the estimator under the complex stratified multistage design. The authors’ design-effect calculations therefore require both the base sampling weights and the JRR replicate structure to reflect clustering (students within classes within schools) and stratification. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name in the excerpt, but it states that PIRLS weights and JRR are used as the basis for quantifying sampling-design uncertainty.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are central to the assessment-design uncertainty in PIRLS: the paper uses the random multiple imputation framework (Rubin) where measurement variance is derived from variability across plausible-value replications. However, the excerpt does not specify a concrete missing-data handling rule for any additional missingness beyond the by-design item missingness (e.g., item nonresponse or student nonresponse), so the missing-data handling for those cases is not documented here. This is a reporting gap for secondary-analysis users who need to know how any non-PV missingness was treated.
outcome_summary: This paper is a design-effect and uncertainty quantification study rather than a predictive modeling paper. Using PIRLS 2016 reading achievement data for grade four, it decomposes total uncertainty into sampling variance (complex stratified multistage sampling with clustering) and assessment variance (matrix sampling of items and plausible-values measurement). For sampling variance, it relies on PIRLS’ Jackknife Repeated Replications (JRR) to approximate the sampling distribution of estimators under the complex design. For assessment variance, it uses the random multiple imputation framework underlying plausible values, treating variability across plausible-value replications as measurement variance. Across 57 participating populations, the authors find that when estimating the mean achievement, the sampling design effect is often larger than the assessment design effect, but this is context dependent (e.g., assessment design effects exceed sampling effects in Macao and Malta). For other parameters—benchmark exceedance/probabilities and an OLS regression coefficient—the relative dominance of sampling vs assessment design effects attenuates and becomes less predictable, implying that credible inference requires accounting for both sources of design-based uncertainty.

Consequently, there are no ML algorithms, no predictive target variable, and no model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) to extract; the main empirical outputs are design-effect comparisons and confidence-interval implications. title: Interpretable Machine Learning Models for PISA Results in Mathematics
authors: Ismael Gómez-Talal; Luis Bote-Curiel; José Luis Rojo-Álvarez
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the OECD PISA 2022 microdata for Spain and applies a preprocessing pipeline that first removes rows with excessive missingness (students with nine or more missing values across columns are excluded). The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the ML training/evaluation stage, and it does not name any weight variables. Because the analysis is based on standard ML classifiers (e.g., SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) and the paper focuses on predictive discrimination and SHAP interpretability, the weighting strategy is not documented; readers should treat the results as model-based patterns rather than fully design-weighted population estimates.

The analytic dataset was then used to create a three-category mathematics proficiency target (Low/Medium/High) and to train binary classifiers for three pairwise scenarios (Low vs High, Medium vs High, Low vs Medium).

primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data for Spain, the study leveraged grade repetition, digital devices with screens, extra mathematics classes, number of books at home, and gender to predict mathematics proficiency (Low vs High), finding that the stacking meta-model outperformed individual classifiers with an AUC of 0.9766. This indicates that targeting grade repeaters and optimizing home learning resources (digital access and books) alongside structured extra mathematics support may improve the identification and support of students at risk of low mathematics achievement, though the results are predictive and SHAP-based interpretability does not establish causality.

title: A graphically based machine learning approach to predict secondary schools performance in Tunisia
authors: Sonia Rebai; Fatma Ben Yahia; Hedi Essid
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 school and student data for Tunisia, but the analytic unit is the school (105 public secondary schools after excluding private schools and removing observations with missing data). The paper does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/school weights) or any replicate-weight procedure; instead, it estimates school-level directional distance function inefficiency scores and then fits regression trees and random forests in R. Because the ML stage (RT/RF) is described without any survey-weight integration, the analysis appears to treat the school sample as an unweighted dataset. Analysts should therefore interpret results as descriptive/predictive associations for the observed Tunisian school sample rather than fully population-representative estimates.
outcome_summary: The paper analyzes Tunisian public secondary schools using PISA 2012 school and student data, with the analytic unit being 105 schools (private schools excluded and missing observations removed). In stage 1, it computes a school-level inefficiency score via a directional distance function (DDF) implemented with DEA, using weekly learning time in mathematics/science/language as inputs, school-average PISA standardized scores (mathematics, reading, science) as desirable outputs, and principal-reported dropout proportion as the undesirable output; PISA plausible values are handled by averaging at the school level. In stage 2, it fits regression trees and random forests in R to model inefficiency as a function of six school-level covariates (school size, class size, rural location, proportion of girls, competition, parental pressure). RF variable importance indicates the largest contributions come from proportion of girls and school size (≈47.8% and 46.5%), while RT reveals non-linear interaction thresholds (e.g., class size and gender composition ranges). The study also runs OLS and Tobit as robustness checks, but these linear models mainly identify competition and location as significant at 5%, highlighting that linear approaches miss non-linear interactions; however, survey weights are not reported and the ML models are not framed as causal estimators.
sample_filtering_criteria: Extracted PISA 2012 school and student data for Tunisia; restricted to public secondary schools by eliminating 153 private schools. Removed all observations with missing data, resulting in a final sample of 105 secondary schools for the school year 2011–2012. The first-stage DEA/DDF uses school-level inputs (weekly learning time in mathematics, science, language) and outputs (school averages of PISA standardized scores in mathematics, reading, science) plus a bad output (principal-reported dropout proportion). The second-stage ML uses six school-level covariates (school size, class size, rural location dummy, proportion of girls, competition dummy, parental pressure dummy).
effect_size: Regression tree (RT): graphical splits and mean inefficiency by node; Random Forest (RF): variable importance ranges (Pressure 8.492%, Competition 10.499%, Location 10.913%, Class size 21.022%, School size 46.517%, % Girls 47.773%). Linear robustness checks: OLS and Tobit reported significance at 5% for Competition and School location (coefficients shown in Tables 6–7).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2012 (Tunisia) school-level the study leveraged school size, class size, proportion of girls, competition, and parental pressure to predict school inefficiency (a DDF/DEA-derived measure combining PISA achievement and dropout). It found that inefficiency is strongly and non-linearly associated with school size and the proportion of girls, with RF importance ranking % girls and school size as the top contributors (≈48% each), while competition and parental pressure show conditional effects through interactions captured by the regression tree. This indicates that Tunisian secondary-school improvement policies should prioritize organizational levers (school/class size and gender composition) and tailor interventions to interaction patterns rather than assuming linear, one-factor-at-a-time relationships, though the study’s ML stage does not report survey-weighted inference and causality cannot be inferred from predictive importance.
confounders: School size; Class size; School location (rural); Proportion of girls; Competition (dummy); Parental pressure

title: Rethinking TIMSS quality assurance: utilizing neural network models with regression‑based bias mitigation strategies for validating country‑level math and science achievement scores
authors: Henry Isaiah Braun; Matthias von Davier; Jihang Chen
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS microdata from the 2011, 2015, and 2019 administrations and constructs country-level mean predictions by first predicting student-level scores and then aggregating to country means. The manuscript describes TIMSS as using probability samples and discusses TIMSS quality control and paradata, but it does not report applying TIMSS sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation in the neural-network/regression pipeline. Because the core models are feedforward neural networks followed by regression-based bias mitigation, the paper does not specify any weight-aware estimation approach, suggesting an unweighted (or at least not weight-documented) analysis. The analytic sample is restricted by design pairing rules (e.g., Grade 4 from one administration with Grade 8 from the next) and by the set of countries contributing to each component analysis (Table 1), rather than by an explicit missing-data or weight-based filtering rule.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that TIMSS cognitive achievement scores are derived using latent regression analysis and that plausible values are available for each student, but it does not document how plausible values were combined when training the neural networks and when aggregating to country-level means. It also does not report a missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case restriction or imputation) for the background variables used as inputs. Given the absence of explicit PV-combining and missing-data documentation, this represents a reporting gap that limits reproducibility and may affect uncertainty quantification.
outcome_summary: The paper proposes a TIMSS quality-assurance enhancement that uses supervised neural networks plus regression-based bias mitigation to predict country-level Grade 8 mean achievement from background/context variables, then flags countries with unusually large positive residuals for follow-up. It applies two related methods: Method 1 predicts 8th-grade outcomes using the prior administration’s Grade 4 context (same cohort linkage), while Method 2 predicts 8th-grade outcomes using the prior administration’s Grade 8 outcomes (different cohorts). For 2015 Grade 8 mathematics (29 countries in both pairs), residual distributions were approximately symmetric with medians of −0.2 (IQR 7.7) and 0.6 (IQR 7.6), and only 5 countries per pair exceeded the 80th percentile. For 2015 Grade 8 science (22 countries), medians were 0.0 (IQR 7.5) and 0.1 (IQR 7.8) with 4 upper-tail countries per pair. The composite indicator’s overlap with TIMSS-documented sample-quality/population-definition issues was modest, and the manuscript does not report how plausible values and missing data were handled, limiting uncertainty quantification and reproducibility.
sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses TIMSS administrations 2011, 2015, and 2019 and constructs four component analyses for Method 1 (RQ1): Grade 4 from one administration paired with Grade 8 from the succeeding administration, separately for mathematics and science. Method 1 residuals are computed by predicting Grade 8 student scores using Grade 4 background/context inputs (with the grade indicator modified) and then aggregating to country-level mean predictions; residuals are then formed as observed country means minus predicted country means. Method 2 (RQ2) uses Grade 8 data from one administration to predict Grade 8 outcomes in the succeeding administration (different cohorts). For each component analysis, the set of contributing countries is restricted to those participating in both administrations in the relevant pair (Table 1 reports 34/25/29/22 countries for the four components). Background variables are restricted to those common across the paired administrations and recoded to harmonize response formats (e.g., one-hot encoding for ordinal/numeric categories and recoding of Likert items).
countries_formatted: ARE; ITA; NZL; KWT; CHL; IRN; IRL; TUR; QAT; HKG; USA; ZAF; AUS; MYS; GEO; KAZ; BHR; JOR; LBN; MAR; SWE; SAU; RUS; ESP; KEN; QAT; TWN; GBR; CAN; NOR; KOR; EGY
effect_size: Residual screening: countries with positive residuals above the 80th percentile (no RMSE/accuracy reported). For 2015 Grade 8 Math (29 countries in both pairs): Method 1 (2011–2015) median residual −0.2, IQR 7.7; Method 2 (2015–2019) median residual 0.6, IQR 7.6; 5 countries above 80th percentile in each pair (2011–2015: Dubai, Italy, New Zealand, Kuwait, Chile; 2015–2019: Iran, Ireland, Chile, Italy, Turkey).
primary_finding: Using TIMSS 2011→2015 and 2015→2019 Grade 8 Mathematics the study leveraged country indicator and student background/context variables (e.g., books at home, gender, school belonging, and math self-confidence) to predict country-level mean math achievement and compute residuals for screening. It found that residual distributions were generally well-behaved and that only a small set of countries fell into the upper tail (above the 80th percentile), suggesting the composite residual indicator can flag potentially unusual outcomes without producing widespread false alarms. This indicates that neural-network-based prediction with regression-based bias mitigation could strengthen TIMSS quality assurance by providing an additional, model-based screening signal for follow-up investigations, though the paper does not establish causal validity or provide uncertainty metrics for the screening threshold.

title: Evaluating AI-generated vs. human-written reading comprehension passages: an expert SWOT analysis and comparative study for an educational large-scale assessment
weight_fields_interpretation: The study used an online blinded review questionnaire (LimeSurvey) with a snowball-recruited sample of N=89 reviewers who evaluated a small set of six reading comprehension texts (four GPT-4 generated and two human-written). The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme; participants were not drawn via a probability sample of students or schools from ÉpStan. Because the analysis is based on human ratings and group comparisons (e.g., MANOVA/Tukey HSD) rather than ILSA achievement PV estimation, there is no PV-based weighting requirement. Consequently, no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is specified, and the results should be interpreted as evidence about perceived text quality rather than population-representative estimates.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not analyze ILSA-style cognitive achievement outcomes with Plausible Values; instead, it uses Likert-scale human judgments of text quality dimensions and a subjective discernibility judgment (human vs AI). Missing-data handling is not described for the questionnaire items; the only explicit attrition information is that 72 of 161 enrolled participants did not complete the survey, leaving N=89. This means the paper provides limited transparency on how partially missing item responses (if any) were treated within the completed cases.
outcome_summary: This mixed-methods study evaluated GPT-4’s usefulness for generating German reading comprehension passages aligned with Luxembourg’s ÉpStan context, focusing on Grade 5 narrative and informative genres. In a qualitative focus group (N=6 SMEs), experts developed a Text Analysis Cognitive Model (TACM) and SWOT-informed constraints for text generation. In a quantitative blinded review, N=89 participants rated six texts on five Likert-scale quality dimensions (readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, adequacy) and judged whether each text appeared human-written or AI-generated. Results showed ceiling-level quality (all means >4) and genre-dependent prompt effects: one-shot prompting performed best for informative texts, while human-written texts were superior for narratives in engagement/coherence/adequacy; correctness did not differ significantly across narrative conditions. Authorship discernibility was weak (no condition >50% correct; many undecided), implying that AI-generated texts can be human-like, but human oversight and governance are required. Limitations include small stimulus set (four AI texts) and lack of reported missing-item handling for the questionnaire.
sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were recruited via snowball sampling and completed a three-week online blinded review. The analytic sample comprised only those who completed the questionnaire (N=89) after excluding non-completers (72 of 161). Reviewers evaluated six German reading comprehension texts (two human-written and four GPT-4 generated) presented in randomized order; the manuscript does not report additional exclusions based on demographics or language proficiency beyond the general assumption that the sample could evaluate German texts in the Luxembourgish primary context.
effect_size: MANOVA (Pillai’s Trace) for narrative: V=0.169, F(10, 522)=4.82, p<0.001; MANOVA for informative: V=0.077, F(10, 522)=2.093, p=0.023. Narrative post-hoc: significant differences in readability, engagement, coherence, adequacy; correctness showed no significant differences. Informative post-hoc: significant differences in readability (human vs one-shot), AI one-shot vs zero-shot (readability, coherence, adequacy). Descriptives: all mean dimension scores >4 on 5-point Likert; Cronbach’s alpha per dimension ~0.71–0.89; ceiling effects reported.
primary_finding: Using ÉpStan-aligned German Grade 5 reading comprehension texts the study compared human-written versus GPT-4 texts under zero-shot and one-shot prompting and evaluated five human-rated quality dimensions, finding that overall text quality was similarly high and that prompt type mattered by genre (one-shot better for informative texts; human-written better for narratives). This indicates that generative AI can support reading-text development in large-scale assessment contexts, but prompt strategy and genre-specific oversight are necessary to preserve engagement and coherence.

title: Principal component analysis on the covariance matrix for data reduction in large‑scale assessments
authors: Paul A. Jewsbury; Matthew S. Johnson
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses NAEP 2022 data within an IRT-latent regression framework with plausible values (PV) for proficiency estimation, and it applies a data-reduction step to contextual predictors (PCA on correlation vs covariance matrices). The paper does not report the use of NAEP complex survey sampling weights (e.g., student/school weights) or replicate-weight procedures; instead, it focuses on how PCA-COR vs PCA-COV changes the latent regression predictor set and thus PV-based group mean/variance estimation. In the simulation, the authors treat a real NAEP dataset as a population and draw with replacement samples, which is not the same as NAEP’s operational complex sampling design. Therefore, readers should not assume population-representative weighted estimation unless the operational NAEP weighting variables are explicitly applied in the analysis code (not described in the provided text).
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper describes plausible values as multiple imputations drawn from an approximation to the conditional posterior distribution and states that PV-based estimators follow Rubin’s rules, but it does not explicitly document how missing contextual or item-response data were handled in the empirical NAEP 2022 analysis beyond NAEP’s standard contrast-coding and SWEEP operator steps. In the simulation, item responses are generated with missing completely at random (MCAR), but the paper does not provide a corresponding explicit missing-data handling procedure for the empirical NAEP analysis (e.g., whether missingness indicators are used, whether cases are excluded, or whether any imputation is performed beyond PV generation). This is a reporting gap for missing-data handling at the empirical-data stage.
outcome_summary: This paper proposes PCA on the covariance matrix (PCA-COV) as a data-reduction method for contextual variables used in NAEP-style IRT-latent regression models that generate plausible values (PVs). In a simulation study built from NAEP 2019 Grade 8 mathematics contextual-variable structure (with low test reliability for a subset), PCA-COV substantially reduces estimation bias and mean squared error for PV-based group means and dramatically improves MSE for PV-based group variances relative to the conventional PCA-COR approach that uses a correlation matrix. The authors also evaluate a hybrid variant that directly includes main reporting constructs (gender, race/ethnicity, English learner status, disability status, and FRPL-based SES) before applying PCA-COV to remaining contextual variance. In the empirical NAEP 2022 Grade 8 reading and mathematics comparison, the transition to PCA-COV-H shows small differences in subgroup means (<0.5 points) and largely preserves trend significance versus 2019, with only one borderline case (ELL in mathematics) changing from barely significant to non-significant. Limitations include lack of explicit documentation of missing-data handling for the empirical NAEP analysis beyond PV generation and NAEP’s contrast-coding/SWEEP steps, and the fact that the method is methodological rather than ML predictive modeling.
null_fields_interpretation: This is a methodological paper focused on statistical data reduction for NAEP-style PV generation and latent regression, not on training predictive ML models. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms to extract (ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty and primary is null), and the main results are reported as estimation bias/MSE improvements and trend-comparability checks rather than ML accuracy/AUC metrics. The paper’s empirical component uses NAEP 2022 operational procedures (IRT-latent regression with PVs) and compares PCA-COR vs PCA-COV-H, so the extraction emphasizes assessment methodology and estimation quality outcomes rather than ML model performance.
sample_filtering_criteria: Empirical case study uses NAEP 2022 reading and mathematics grade 8 data and follows operational NAEP procedures: contextual variables are converted to contrast-coded dummy variables, then a SWEEP operator removes variables with near-perfect multicollinearity or near-zero variance. For the real-data comparison, the IRT-latent regression is fit separately for each state sample, generating PVs for students within each state and combining PVs across states. The PCA-COR procedure applies PCA to the correlation matrix of remaining dummy variables with a minimum number of components explaining 80% variance, capped by a predictor-to-sample-size ratio threshold (capped at 8). The PCA-COV-Hybrid procedure directly includes five main constructs (gender, race/ethnicity, English learner status, disability status, and FRPL-based socioeconomic status) as predictors, regresses remaining contextual variables on these main constructs, then applies PCA to the covariance matrix of residuals and selects components explaining 90% of residual variance.
effect_size: Real-data comparison: differences in composite means between COR and COV-H are <0.5 points for all categories; trend significance vs 2019 is the same in all but one test (ELL in mathematics: p=0.049 COR vs p=0.070 COV-H).
primary_finding: Using NAEP 2022 Grade 8 Reading the study leveraged a hybrid PCA-COV approach that directly includes main constructs (gender, race/ethnicity, English learner status, disability status, and FRPL-based SES) while applying PCA-COV to the remaining contextual variables to predict PV-based group mean estimates, finding that primary trend inferences were largely unaffected when transitioning from PCA-COR to PCA-COV-H. This indicates that NAEP can broaden contextual reporting scope and improve estimation robustness without materially changing headline trend conclusions, though one borderline ELL mathematics trend test changed significance.
confounders: Gender (main construct); Race/ethnicity (main construct); English learner status; Disability status; FRPL eligibility (SES)

title: Technology factors related to the differences in paper and online reading scores in PIRLS 2016
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 paper reading and ePIRLS 2016 electronic reading data from the same grade 4 students in seven European countries, restricting the analytic sample to students who participated in both modes (Ireland removed due to low overlap). PIRLS/ePIRLS employ a complex multistage cluster sampling design (schools sampled with PPS, intact classrooms sampled within schools) and multiple-matrix booklets/tasks, so the authors compute standard errors using the PV-specific procedures. For the student-and-school models, they apply student total weights after merging school characteristics to students; for the teacher model they apply teacher total weights. Because the dependent variable is derived from plausible values (differences between corresponding PVs across modes), analyses are repeated across the five PVs and combined using both sampling weights and replicate weights via the R package RALSA.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper describes the plausible values (PVs) generation and the required PV-repeated estimation with sampling and replicate weights, but it does not explicitly report a separate missing-data strategy for questionnaire variables (e.g., listwise/pairwise deletion or imputation rules). Given that PIRLS/ePIRLS contextual scales are constructed by the IEA study center and the analysis is conducted through RALSA, the authors likely rely on the IDB’s prepared variables and PV framework; however, the manuscript does not document the exact missingness handling for the ICT/background predictors. This is a reporting gap because missingness in predictors can affect regression coefficients and their standard errors.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2016 paper reading and ePIRLS 2016 electronic reading for grade 4 students in six European countries (Ireland excluded due to low overlap), using the difference between corresponding plausible values (PVs) across modes as the outcome. Because PIRLS/ePIRLS use complex sampling and PVs, the authors repeat computations across five PVs and aggregate standard errors using sampling and replicate weights via RALSA. They fit ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions (multilevel modeling deemed unsuitable due to low between-school variance) and report country-specific R-squared/adjusted R-squared and F-statistics rather than ML performance metrics. Results show statistically significant but small coefficients in a subset of countries: access and use of technology (especially in Italy and Portugal) and student self-efficacy (Portugal and Slovenia) relate to mode differences, while classroom teacher variables show no significant relationships. The study is cross-sectional and does not provide a documented missing-data strategy for predictors beyond the PV framework, so causal claims about technology effects cannot be inferred.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIRLS 2016 (paper) and ePIRLS 2016 (electronic) for grade 4 students in European countries that took both modes with the same sample; retained only students who participated in both modes (paper and ePIRLS sessions). Ireland was removed because the overlap between PIRLS and ePIRLS samples was only 53.7% (below the study’s quality threshold). The remaining countries’ overlap was high (average 86.6%, with Denmark as low as 71.4% and Portugal as high as 98.2%), and analyses were conducted at the population level using PV-based score differences rather than individual-level comparisons.
countries_formatted: DNK; ITA; NOR; PRT; SVN; SWE
effect_size: OLS regression with PV-difference outcomes; model fit reported as country-specific R-squared/adjusted R-squared and F-statistics (e.g., Model 1 R-squared ranges ~0.00–0.02; Model 2 R-squared ranges ~0.01–0.03). No ML metrics (accuracy/AUC/RMSE) reported.
primary_finding: Using PIRLS 2016/ePIRLS 2016 Grade 4 reading-for-information the study leveraged device use in and out school, computer self-efficacy, home resources for learning, home digital device access, and computers-to-students ratio to explain the mode difference between electronic and paper reading PVs, finding limited and country-specific associations (notably device use and self-efficacy in Portugal; home digital access in Italy; computers-to-students ratio and digital-resource-shortage instruction effects in Denmark/Italy; and home resources for learning predicting differences in several countries). This indicates that technology-related inequalities and school ICT capacity may shape whether electronic reading outperforms paper, but effects are small and not consistent across all European contexts.
