title: Working with missing data in large-scale assessments
weight_fields_interpretation: The tutorial’s applied example uses Belgian PISA 2018 student and school datasets and fits two-level random-intercept multilevel models. In the imputation and analysis workflow, the authors explicitly incorporate complex survey weights at both levels by specifying student weights (w_fstuwt) and school-level weights (w_schgrnrabwt) in the rblimp/Blimp imputation model and again in the WeMix model-fitting stage. The weights are treated as covariates/inputs to the imputation model (congenial imputation) and are also used in the substantive multilevel model with robust standard errors. Replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is not described in the excerpt, so replicate-weight usage cannot be confirmed from the provided text.
outcome_summary: This article is a software tutorial focused on missing-data handling in large-scale assessments, using an applied example with Belgian PISA 2018 mathematics. The authors demonstrate how to impute missing predictors in a multilevel (students nested in schools) and weighted setting while accounting for plausible values (10 mathematics PVs). They compare three analytic conditions: the original dataset with 90% complete cases, a reduced dataset with 82% complete cases created by additional missingness in ESCS, and a multiply imputed dataset created via Blimp/rblimp with 20 imputations per plausible value (200 total imputed datasets). Rather than reporting predictive accuracy, they evaluate how fixed-effect estimates and random-effects components (including ICC) change across conditions, finding that multiply imputation yields results closest to the 90% complete baseline and alters between-school variance when compared with the 82% complete case. The tutorial emphasizes that listwise deletion can bias estimates when missingness is not MCAR and that congenial imputation should reflect the substantive model structure, including weights and plausible values.
sample_filtering_criteria: The applied tutorial example uses the Belgian PISA 2018 student and school datasets (merged, reduced dataset). The analytic focus is on predicting student mathematics abilities using 10 mathematics plausible values (pv1math–pv10math) and a multilevel structure with students nested in schools (cntschid). To demonstrate missing-data handling, the authors create an additional missingness scenario by selecting a variable with minimal missingness (escs, 2% missing) and then removing an additional 10% of escs values such that missingness is related to the first mathematics plausible value (missing at random). They then fit models on the original dataset (90% complete), the additional-missing dataset (82% complete), and the final multiply imputed datasets (200 multiply imputed datasets across 10 plausible values).
effect_size: Fixed-effect estimates compared across three conditions: 90% complete data (results C), 82% complete data (results B), and multiply imputed datasets (results A) using 200 multiply imputed datasets (20 imputations per plausible value across 10 plausible values). No predictive accuracy metrics reported; differences assessed via coefficient similarity and random-effects ICCs.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics (Belgium) the study leveraged Gender, ESCS, immigration status, student behavior hindering learning, and lack of teaching staff to model math achievement from plausible values, finding that results from the multiply imputed analysis (A) were closest to the 90% complete analysis (C), while the 82% complete analysis (B) showed larger discrepancies, especially for level-2 coefficients and the intercept. This indicates that multiple imputation in a multilevel, weighted plausible-values setting can reduce bias introduced by listwise deletion/complete-case reductions, supporting more transparent and less error-prone missing-data practice in LSA analyses.

title: The relationship between personal‑collaborative motivation profiles and students’ performance in collaborative problem solving
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 CPS assessment data from four mainland China regions (B-S-J-G) and includes both student and school questionnaire responses. After restricting to the CPS assessment sample, the authors deleted missing observations by variable because the missing rate for all variables was below 5% (maximum SOIAICT at 2.53%), yielding a final analytic sample of 9398 students from 264 schools. To address unequal probability of selection and nonresponse bias, they applied the student-level sampling weight W_FSTUWT and also used a school-level sampling weight W_FSCHWT. The analysis then proceeds with person-centred LPA and multilevel modeling; the manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty estimation is described through the modeling framework rather than explicit replicate procedures.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 collaborative problem solving (CPS) for 9398 Chinese students from 264 schools in four mainland regions (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Guangdong). It uses latent profile analysis (LPA) to identify four personal–collaborative motivation profiles based on instrumental motivation, achievement motivation, enjoy cooperation, and value cooperation, and then compares psychological attributes and CPS behaviors using log-derived timing and action counts. For CPS achievement, the dependent variable is PV-based CPS performance (10 plausible values scaled to mean 500, SD 100), estimated in a multilevel linear model with Rubin’s rules for PV imputation. The results show the achievement-oriented collaborator profile performs best and the instrument-oriented nonteam player profile performs worst, with ESCS and gender also significantly associated with CPS achievement. Limitations include the absence of ML predictive-model evaluation metrics (the paper uses LPA/HLM rather than supervised ML) and the correlational nature of profile membership, so causality cannot be inferred.
null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper uses person-centred modeling (LPA) and multilevel regression with PVs, it does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive algorithms (no supervised ML learners such as Random Forest/XGBoost/SVM are reported). Therefore, ml_techniques.primary is left null and all_techniques is empty, while the empirical results are captured as profile-based associations with PV-based CPS achievement and log-derived CPS behaviors.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 CPS assessment data for four mainland China regions (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Guangdong; B-S-J-G). Included students with CPS assessment participation and corresponding student/school questionnaire data; deleted missing observations by variable (overall missing rate <5%, max SOIAICT 2.53%) and retained the final analytic sample of 9398 students from 264 schools.
effect_size: Not reported as ML metrics (multilevel linear model coefficients and significance reported; PVs estimated using Rubin’s rules).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 CPS the study leveraged motivation-profile membership (derived from instrumental/achievement motivation and enjoy/value cooperation) together with student and school covariates such as ESCS to model CPS achievement (plausible values). It found that students in the achievement-oriented collaborator profile scored highest, while the instrument-oriented nonteam player profile scored lowest, with positive dummy coefficients for the other three profiles relative to the instrument-oriented nonteam player baseline. This indicates that strengthening achievement motivation alongside valuing collaboration may be more effective for improving CPS achievement than focusing on instrumental engagement alone, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

title: A Theoretical Framework for a Mathematical Cognitive Model for Adaptive Learning Systems
authors: S. Sun; X. Wang; T. Xu
weight_fields_interpretation: This paper does not use an ILSA/PISA/TIMSS micro-dataset for achievement scoring; instead, it constructs a mathematical cognitive model using expert questionnaires, interviews, and student verbal reports. Because the study is based on expert calibration (52 experts) and a small validation activity (one fourth-grade student), there is no complex survey sampling frame and no student-level sampling weights to apply. The ISM procedure uses expert judgments to build a structural self-interaction matrix (SSIM) and then derives adjacency/reachability matrices; these steps are not population-representative estimation. Therefore, standard ILSA weight variables (e.g., student sampling weights or BRR/jackknife replicate weights) are not applicable to the reported model-construction workflow.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the study does not estimate cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA assessment; it develops and validates a theoretical cognitive attribute model using interpretive structural modeling (ISM) and expert/student judgments. The paper also does not report a missing-data strategy because the core inputs are expert questionnaire responses and qualitative/verbal-report validation rather than a PV-based scoring dataset with item nonresponse handled via PV procedures.
outcome_summary: This paper proposes a theoretical framework for constructing a mathematical cognitive model intended for cognitive diagnostic assessment and adaptive learning systems. Using TIMSS’s cognitive framework as a starting point, the authors list 16 cognitive attributes (S1–S16) and apply interpretive structural modeling (ISM) to derive hierarchical relationships among attributes via expert judgments. title: Digital gender gaps in Students’ knowledge, attitudes and skills: an integrative data analysis across 32 Countries
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICILS 2013 and ICILS 2018 grade-8 student microdata under a stratified two-stage cluster sampling design (schools sampled with PPS, then 20 students sampled within schools). In stage 1, the authors estimate multigroup SEMs with complex sampling survey characteristics, explicitly incorporating sampling weights and jackknife/balanced repeated replication procedures, and they also incorporate plausible values for the digital skills outcomes. Missing data are handled via multiple imputation within each country and plausible-value-specific complete datasets, with parameter pooling using Rubin’s rules. In stage 2, the authors meta-analyze the resulting country-level direct and indirect effects using random- and mixed-effects models; the weighting logic is therefore embedded in the primary (country) effect-size generation rather than in a single pooled student-level ML model.
outcome_summary: This integrative data analysis synthesizes individual participant data from ICILS 2013 and ICILS 2018 for grade-8 students across 32 country samples (total N = 105,981). title: What key contextual factors contribute to students’ reading literacy among top-performing countries and economies? Statistical and machine learning analyses
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for reading literacy and constructs an analytic sample consisting of students from B-S-J-Z (China), Singapore, and Macau, plus a comparison analysis using all 79 participating countries/economies. The authors report using PV1READ (first plausible value for reading) as the outcome and exclude students with reading scores below 262. For missing values, they impute missing factor values using the median of each factor. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights; given the use of ML (GBDT) and PV-based outcomes, the analysis appears to be conducted without explicit complex-survey weighting, which may affect population-representativeness and uncertainty estimates.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 reading literacy using PV1READ as the dependent variable, focusing first on students from the top three high-performing economies (B-S-J-Z/CHN, Singapore/SGP, Macau/MAC) and then comparing results with the full PISA 2018 dataset across all 79 countries/economies. For contextual-factor decomposition, it applies Shapley value decomposition and reports that metacognitive strategies account for the largest relative contribution (53.83%), with assessing credibility and summarizing information among the most influential factors. For prediction, it trains a gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT) using a random 80/20 train-test split and 10-fold cross-validation for tuning; the combined top-performing subset achieves R² = 0.499 (RMSE = 68.34), while all 79 countries achieve R² = 0.48 (RMSE = 73.26). Missing factor values are imputed via median imputation, and students with reading scores below 262 are excluded. The paper does not report using PISA sampling/replicate weights, and the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation of the ML-derived importance patterns.
sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic samples were drawn from PISA 2018: (1) a combined subset of students from the top three high-performing countries/economies—B-S-J-Z (China), Singapore, and Macau—for the main joint analysis; (2) separate analyses for each of the three economies; and (3) an additional analysis using the full PISA 2018 dataset across all 79 participating countries/economies. The outcome was PV1READ (first plausible value for reading). Students with reading scores below 262 were excluded. Missing values in contextual factors were imputed using the median of each factor.

title: Being female and being well-situated implies higher performance on creative thinking tests: Evidence across 62 countries from PISA 2022
authors: B. Goecke; M. Benedek; J.G. Diedrich; B. Forthmann; S. Patzl; S. Weiss
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses secondary microdata from PISA 2022 and restricts it to the 62 country/economy samples that include the innovative domain (creative thinking), excluding Cyprus (no creative thinking data) and excluding Costa Rica (missing SES variables). Analyses are conducted with design-based weighted regression to respect PISA’s complex sampling design, explicitly accounting for the nested structure of students within schools. The authors apply student-level sampling weights and replicate weights and estimate robust standard errors using Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR) with Fay’s adjustment. Effect estimates are then pooled across multiple imputations using Rubin’s rules, and the subsequent cross-country synthesis is performed via a two-stage individual-participant meta-analytic approach with cluster-robust random-effects models.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 microdata for 62 countries/economies that administered the innovative domain creative thinking, alongside mathematics and reading. It uses a two-stage individual-participant meta-analytic approach: within each country, weighted regressions predict z-standardized plausible values (PVs) for creative thinking, mathematics, and reading from Gender, ESCS (and Gender×SES), with science competence used as an auxiliary variable in nested Bayesian multiple imputation for ESCS missingness. Effects are synthesized across countries using cluster-robust random-effects meta-analysis and pooled across imputations using Rubin’s rules. Key results show female students outperform male students in creative thinking and reading (gender main effects), while SES is a strong positive predictor in all three domains (≈0.33–0.36 SD per 1 SD ESCS). The paper also finds creative-thinking gender/SES disparities are comparatively stable across macro moderators (OECD membership, HDI, GGGI, power distance), whereas mathematics and reading show more context sensitivity. Limitations include reliance on observational cross-sectional associations and the fact that the analysis is not a machine-learning predictive pipeline (no ML model metrics such as accuracy/AUC are reported).
null_fields_interpretation: This is an observational, design-based comparative analysis using weighted regressions and two-stage meta-analytic synthesis across countries, not a machine-learning predictive modeling study. sample_filtering_criteria: Used a subset of PISA 2022 microdata for the innovative domain creative thinking plus the core domains mathematics and reading. title: Predicting Key Factors Influencing Students’ Creative Thinking: A Machine Learning Analysis Based on PISA 2022 Data from East Asia

outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 creative thinking for five East Asian economies (Singapore, South Korea, Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Macao; N=29,208) using a two-stage ML pipeline: LASSO for variable selection followed by Random Forest regression for variable importance (%IncMSE) and predictive performance. title: Understanding students’ mathematical achievement through feature selection and machine learning: Evidence from PISA 2018
authors: U.H. Yildirim; Y. Kayhan Atilgan; D. Turfan
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Turkish subset of PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) and extracts a student-level analytic dataset of 6,863 students from 186 schools. Although PISA is collected using a complex survey design with stratification, clustering, and unequal selection probabilities, the authors explicitly do not incorporate PISA sampling and replicate weights into the ML classification models because the aim is an exploratory, sample-oriented predictive approach rather than population-level estimation. Plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) are used to address uncertainty in mathematics achievement, and all feature selection and model training/evaluation are conducted separately for each plausible value. The manuscript therefore treats the ML results as patterns in the extracted sample; it does not apply complex-survey variance estimation via weights/replicates, which may affect generalizability and uncertainty quantification.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes the Turkish subset of PISA 2018 (n=6,863 students from 186 schools) and converts ten mathematics plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) into a binary outcome using the PISA Level 2 threshold (below 420.07 = low-performing; ≥420.07 = high-performing). After imputing missing predictor values with MissForest (excluding the dependent variables to avoid target leakage), the authors apply three feature-selection methods (Boruta, Mutual Information, ReliefF) and train five supervised classifiers (DT, Bagging, Random Forest, AdaBoost, SVM) using repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation (5 folds, 5 repetitions) separately for each PV. Across all 62 predictors, AdaBoost attains the highest mean F1-score (0.7509 ± 0.0046), while Random Forest is close (0.7437 ± 0.0048) and shows stable performance. In feature-selection experiments, RF combined with MI-selected top-20 variables reaches substantially higher F1-score (0.8352 ± 0.0038) and AUC (0.8370 ± 0.0037). The study uses conditional SHAP and related plots for interpretability, but the authors explicitly do not incorporate PISA sampling/replicate weights, so findings reflect sample-based patterns rather than population-level estimates, and SHAP-based importance is not causal evidence.
ml_all_techniques: Decision Tree, Bagging, Random Forest, AdaBoost, SVM
sample_filtering_criteria: Used publicly available PISA 2018 data and extracted the Turkish sample only (6,890 students from 186 schools). Excluded 27 students (0.39%) with no valid responses to any student-level variables, yielding a final analytic sample of 6,863 students. Mathematics achievement was operationalized using the ten PISA mathematics plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH), and analyses were run separately for each PV; PVs were not missing. For predictors, missing values in the 62 retained independent variables were imputed using MissForest, with the dependent variables explicitly excluded from the imputation process to avoid target leakage.

title: The essence of creative thinking in PISA 2022: An item-level machine learning approach to construct validity at the facet level
authors: Elisabeth Barbara Kraus; Benjamin Goecke; Ann-Kathrin Jaggy
weight_fields_interpretation: The study reanalyzed PISA 2022 microdata and restricted the analytic sample to students who completed the creative thinking assessment. The authors describe PISA’s two-stage stratified sampling (schools sampled with probability proportional to size, then students randomly selected within schools), but in the methods they do not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the random-forest modeling. Because the predictive models are implemented as random forests in R (ranger via tidymodels) and the paper does not mention weight-aware estimation, the analysis appears to proceed without complex-survey weighting. They also preprocess by merging PISA files, excluding character variables with long text and excluding sampling weights, removing creative-thinking plausible values in favor of raw item scores, and restructuring data into a long item–person format.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper uses plausible values for mathematics, reading, and science competences but explicitly selects one randomly chosen PV per competence domain for modeling (single_pv). However, it does not describe how missing data in predictors or outcomes were handled (e.g., whether cases with missing questionnaire/process variables were excluded or imputed), which is a reporting gap given the large number of predictors and the long-format restructuring. This omission prevents assessing potential bias from missingness mechanisms and the robustness of the predictive relationships.
outcome_summary: The study reanalyzed PISA 2022 creative thinking microdata, restricting to 142,564 students who completed the creative thinking assessment and modeling raw item scores (not the official composite PV-based creative thinking score). Using a multi-level predictive modeling strategy implemented as random forests on long-format item–person data, the authors trained separate models for each facet (GDI, GCI, EII) and predicted three ordered score categories (no/partial/full credit). Predictive performance was moderate (accuracy 67.5% for GDI, 64.5% for GCI, 65.8% for EII), with permutation variable importance and ALE-based XAI used to interpret effects. Across facets, the strongest predictors were item characteristics, behavioral engagement indicators (e.g., time on task, number of actions, latency), general academic competence (reading/mathematics/science PVs), and socioeconomic background (e.g., HOMEPOS, ISCEDP), while creativity self-report measures were not among the top predictors. The paper also reports small, threshold-like interactions between item domain and academic competences. Limitations include the apparent omission of complex-survey weights in the ML models and the use of single randomly selected PVs for competences, plus the fact that XAI feature importance supports prediction-oriented validity evidence rather than causal claims.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 reanalysis restricted to students who completed the creative thinking assessment. The final analytic sample contains 142,564 students from 63 countries/economies. Preprocessing excluded character variables with lengthy text entries (e.g., open-ended parental occupation fields) and excluded sampling weights; creative-thinking plausible values were removed and replaced by raw item scores plus process indicators. Data were restructured into long format (one row per item–person combination) and then split into three facet-specific datasets (GDI, GCI, EII) with facet-specific student-level mean predictors for the other facets.

title: Interpretable machine learning reveals key determinants of creative thinking among East Asian students: Evidence from PISA 2022
authors: Hui Chen; Hongji Deng; Hao Yu; Yan Dong; Huazhen Wang
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 creative thinking scores constructed from 10 plausible values (PVs) under PISA’s IRT scaling procedure, and it pools PVs using Rubin’s rules to obtain a single composite creative thinking score per student. The authors also state that the PV pooling approach is designed to maintain measurement properties under PISA’s complex survey design, but they do not report applying explicit student sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight variance estimation. Because the paper’s ML models (Elastic Net, Random Forest, SVR, XGBoost, LightGBM) are trained on preprocessed features and evaluated via resampling, the manuscript does not document whether survey weights were incorporated into model fitting or only reflected through the PV construction. Preprocessing included label encoding for gender and Z-score standardization for continuous variables, plus KNN-based missing value imputation performed within each training fold to reduce data leakage.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 creative thinking for five East Asian economies (HKG, MAC, TWN, KOR, SGP; N=29,208), predicting a student-level creative thinking composite derived from 10 plausible values pooled with Rubin’s rules. A robustness check using Leave-One-Group-Out CV showed reduced generalization (LightGBM R²=0.3898), suggesting economy-specific patterns. Because the analysis is correlational and SHAP explains predictive contributions rather than causality, policy translation should be treated as hypothesis generation rather than causal proof.
ml_all_techniques: Elastic Net, Random Forest, SVM, XGBoost, LightGBM
sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses PISA 2022 data for five East Asian economies: Hong Kong (China), Macau (China), Chinese Taipei, South Korea, and Singapore. Japan was excluded because it did not participate in the creative thinking assessment module. The dependent variable is the PISA 2022 creative thinking composite score derived from 10 PVs; predictor variables were restricted by excluding variables with missing-data rates exceeding 10%. primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 creative thinking data for East Asian students, the study leveraged reading performance, science performance, ESCS, math performance, and gender to predict creative thinking, finding that reading performance was the most influential global predictor and that overall predictive fit was moderate (LightGBM R²≈0.63 in random splits). title: Educational Data Mining: Identification of Factors Associated With School Effectiveness in PISA Assessment
authors: F. Martínez-Abad; A. Gamazo; M.-J. Rodríguez-Conde
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 panel data for Spain and restricts the analytic sample to 15-year-old students within 896 schools (after excluding schools with fewer than 20 participants). In the first phase (multilevel models in HLM 7), the authors state that they used student and school sampling weights to ensure correct representation of the PISA-eligible population, but they could not use replicate weights; instead they applied robust (Huber-White) estimators to compensate for related bias. In the second phase (decision trees in Weka/J48), the authors aggregate student-level variables to the school level and apply data weighting based on available school sample weights because the school is the unit of analysis. Missingness is handled within HLM7 via regression imputation at the school level (with none of the final-model variables having missing values) and within J48 via a weighting approach that distributes instances with missing predictor values across branches proportionally to training counts.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 Spain (15-year-olds) using a two-phase approach aligned with the CIPO school-effectiveness model. First, three input-only multilevel models (mathematics, reading, science) are estimated in HLM 7 using the 10 plausible values for each domain and sampling weights; schools are then labeled high- or low-effectiveness based on whether their residuals fall in the first vs last quartile across all three domains. Second, the authors train a decision tree (J48/C4.5) in Weka to classify schools as high vs low effectiveness using 59 PISA process/context variables, ultimately selecting 11 variables in a tree with 25 branches and 13 leaves. In 10-fold stratified cross-validation, the global model reached COR=0.916, Kappa=0.747, and ROC AUC≈0.916, with training COR=0.947 and Kappa=0.849. Limitations include the cross-sectional nature (no causal inference) and the use of aggregated student-level variables at the school level, which may mask within-school variability.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2015 Spain sample of 15-year-old students. The initial PISA Spain sample contained 32,330 students and 976 schools; the analytic sample was reduced to 31,236 students and 896 schools by excluding all schools with fewer than 20 participants. After the first-phase multilevel modeling (input-only models for mathematics, reading, and science), schools were classified as high- or low-effectiveness based on whether their school-level residuals fell in the first quartile (high) or last quartile (low) across all three domain models. The second-phase decision-tree analysis then used a subsample of 8,347 students from 239 schools (109 high-effectiveness, 130 low-effectiveness).
effect_size: Decision tree (J48/C4.5). Training set: High-effectiveness TP=0.906, Precision=0.929, COR=0.947; Low-effectiveness TP=0.941, Precision=0.922, COR=0.947; Global Kappa=0.849, RRSE=0.515. primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 Spain the study leveraged additional lessons, cooperation-related student perceptions, ICT use/autonomy, and reading time to predict whether a school was high- vs low-effectiveness (based on residuals from input-only multilevel models). This indicates that school effectiveness in PISA can be meaningfully profiled from process- and context-related questionnaire indicators, suggesting that education authorities could target ICT use patterns, reading-time alignment, and the structure of extracurricular academic support when designing school improvement strategies, while noting that the design is cross-sectional and predictive (not causal).

title: Predictive insights into U.S. students’ mathematics performance on PISA 2022 using ensemble tree-based machine learning models
authors: Li Zhu; Hyesun You; Minju Hong; Zhenhan Fang
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 U.S. student microdata and merges student and school files using the school identifier (CNTSCHID), assigning school-level predictors to students within the same school. The analytic sample comprises 4,552 students in 154 schools, with grade information reported (primarily 10th grade). The authors explicitly state they did not include sampling weights in the ML analyses, arguing that weighting may be less critical for ML model configuration than for traditional regression and citing prior work; thus complex multistage/cluster design weights were omitted. For data preparation, they removed predictors with >50% missingness, removed identical and redundant variables (including excluding components used to compute ESCS), then imputed remaining missing predictor values using missForest (RF-based imputation) before training/testing split and 5-fold cross-validation.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 mathematics performance for U.S. 15-year-olds (N=4,552 students in 154 schools) and predicts mathematics achievement using 10 plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) as separate outcomes, then averages estimates across PVs. After cleaning predictors (dropping variables with >50% missingness, removing identical/redundant variables) the authors impute remaining missing predictor values using missForest (RF-based imputation), split data into training (80%) and test (20%), and train three ensemble tree models: Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. Using reduced predictor sets selected via an ARE criterion, XGBoost performed best on both accuracy and efficiency, with reduced-model rMSE=66.39 and training time=4.14s (vs. RF rMSE=69.82, 129.27s; LightGBM rMSE=66.36, 22.93s). The most consistent top predictors across models include mathematics self-efficacy and ESCS, plus familiarity with math concepts and family support. A key limitation is that sampling weights were not incorporated, so results may not fully reflect the complex survey design; additionally, interpretability via ALE supports predictive understanding rather than causal claims.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 data for the United States (15-year-old students). Merged student and school questionnaires using CNTSCHID so that school-level predictors were attached to students in the same school. For predictors, removed variables with >50% missing values; removed identical variables (same values for all students); removed redundant variables to avoid collinearity (e.g., retained ESCS and excluded the three component DVs used to compute it). After cleaning, imputed missing values for remaining predictors using missForest, then split the overall dataset into training (80%, N=3644) and test (20%, N=908).
effect_size: Model comparison using reduced predictor sets: RF (5 predictors) rMSE=69.82, XGBoost (10 predictors) rMSE=66.39, LightGBM (10 predictors) rMSE=66.36; efficiency (training time): RF=129.27s, XGBoost=4.14s, LightGBM=22.93s. Best model by accuracy+efficiency: XGBoost.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data for U.S. students, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy, ESCS, familiarity with math concepts, expected occupation status, and family support for self-directed learning to predict mathematics achievement (averaged across PV1MATH–PV10MATH), finding that XGBoost achieved lower prediction error than Random Forest and LightGBM when using ML-selected predictors. This indicates that data-driven predictor selection can identify actionable student- and home-related levers for improving U.S. mathematics performance, though the results are predictive associations rather than causal effects and the analysis omits sampling weights.

title: Using machine learning approaches to predict Taiwanese eighth graders’ computational thinking performance in ICILS 2023 study
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICILS 2023 microdata for Taiwanese eighth graders (ICILS 2023 CT test and student questionnaire) with a two-stage sampling design (stratified random sampling of junior high schools, then cluster sampling at the class level). The manuscript describes that the IEA cleaned and pre-processed the final dataset and that CT scores were standardized using Rasch IRT scaling (international mean 483, SD 112). However, the authors do not report applying ICILS sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures in their ML training/evaluation pipeline, and they do not name any weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or BRR/jackknife method. Given the use of scikit-learn and tree/boosting classifiers, the analysis appears to be conducted without explicit complex-survey weighting; therefore, results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than fully population-representative estimates.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a binary classification derived from students’ standardized CT scores using a threshold based on the mean of the first plausible value (PV1) from the ICILS 2023 international database. While the paper specifies this PV-based thresholding approach, it does not describe how missing questionnaire/test data were handled during feature filtering (e.g., whether cases with missing predictors were removed or imputed). This is a reporting gap because ICILS datasets typically contain missingness in questionnaire variables, and the ML results can be sensitive to the missing-data strategy.
outcome_summary: The study uses ICILS 2023 microdata from 5211 Taiwanese eighth graders, combining the ICILS CT performance test (two randomly assigned CT modules per student) with an ICILS student questionnaire and a 15-item CT disposition scale (CTDS). Students’ CT performance was dichotomized into below- vs above-average using a PV1-based threshold (541), and 18 predictors spanning socio-demographic, student-related, and school-related categories were selected after derived-index aggregation, missingness-based variable removal, and VIF multicollinearity screening. In model comparison with a 10-fold cross-validation on an 80/20 train-test split, Logistic Regression yielded AUC=0.76 and accuracy=0.69, while XGBoost, LightGBM, and Stacking achieved the highest AUC=0.79 and accuracy=0.72. XGBoost performed best overall (AUC=0.79; F1≈0.72 for below-average), and SHAP-based feature importance highlighted CTDS and ICT self-efficacy as top predictors. Limitations include the binary PV1-threshold outcome, no reported missing-data strategy, and no explicit complex-survey weighting, so results should be treated as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
ml_all_techniques: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, LightGBM, XGBoost, Stacking
sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample consists of the 5211 Taiwanese students who participated in ICILS 2023. The authors report a multi-stage feature filtering process: (1) aggregating overlapping/highly correlated items into derived indices following IEA guidelines (e.g., CTDS, S_HOMLIT), (2) removing variables with excessive missingness and variables with little theoretical connection to CT performance (e.g., country identifiers not relevant to Taiwan), (3) screening retained predictors for multicollinearity using VIF (retaining variables with VIF below 5), and (4) selecting 18 final features across socio-demographic, student-related, and school-related categories. For the outcome, students were dichotomized into below-average vs above-average CT based on a threshold of 541 (around 52.8% below, 47.2% above), where the threshold was decided using the mean of PV1 from the ICILS 2023 international database.

primary_finding: Using ICILS 2023 Grade 8 (Taiwan) computational thinking the study leveraged CT disposition (CTDS), ICT self-efficacy (general and specialist), specialist classroom application learning, and academic media multitasking to predict CT performance (below vs above average using a PV1-based threshold), finding that XGBoost achieved the highest overall AUC (0.79) and accuracy (0.72) and that CTDS was the most influential predictor across models. This indicates that strengthening students’ computational thinking dispositions and digital self-efficacy—alongside curriculum emphasis on specialist classroom applications—may be more actionable than relying on basic socio-demographic factors for improving CT outcomes, though the binary PV1-thresholding and lack of documented missing-data/weight handling limit causal interpretation.

title: The Effect of the Weight Variable on Predicting Reading Comprehension Achievement in PISA 2018: A Data Mining Approach
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 Turkey microdata and constructs models to predict reading comprehension achievement using 34 student-questionnaire variables plus (in one condition) the student-level sampling weight W_FSTUWT (Final Trimmed Nonresponse Adjusted Student). The analytic sample consists of 6,890 students from 186 schools across 12 regions of Turkey, selected via PISA’s multi-stage stratified sampling (schools selected first, then students/classes within schools). The authors explicitly compare weighted vs unweighted analyses by running CART and Random Forest twice: once including W_FSTUWT and once excluding it. Missing data were handled via a multiple assignment method in SPSS, and outliers were checked with no outliers detected; however, the paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty estimation is not described in replicate-weight terms.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 Turkey microdata (6,890 students from 186 schools) to predict reading comprehension achievement using PV1 from the reading test, recoded into a binary 'successful' vs 'unsuccessful' outcome. Using 34 student-questionnaire variables, the authors train CART and Random Forest models in two conditions: with the student-level sampling weight W_FSTUWT and without it. For CART, overall classification/prediction performance remains high and changes only slightly when weights are included (e.g., PCC ~85.8 vs ~85.9 on all data; Kappa decreases from 0.346 to 0.314). For Random Forest, performance is extremely high on all data (PCC and Kappa reported as 100 and 1), while validation/test Kappa is lower and shows differences by weighting (test Kappa 0.220 weighted vs 0.164 unweighted). The paper reports missing-data handling via SPSS multiple assignment and does not describe replicate-weight uncertainty estimation; additionally, the study focuses on predictive performance and variable importance rather than causal effects.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2018 Turkey dataset and restricted the analytic sample to 15-year-old students represented by the official Turkey PISA sample: 6,890 students attending 186 schools across 12 regions. The dependent variable was PV1 from the PISA 2018 reading comprehension test, which was then categorized into 'successful' vs 'unsuccessful' using the PISA reading proficiency level table (0–552.999 vs 553–1000). The models used 34 independent variables derived from the PISA 2018 student questionnaire. Outliers were checked and none were detected; missing data were eliminated using SPSS multiple assignment.

primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 Turkey reading comprehension data (PV1 categorized as successful vs unsuccessful), the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS), perceived test difficulty, parental occupational status, home possessions, and reading enjoyment to predict achievement category using CART and Random Forest, finding that including the student weight variable W_FSTUWT slightly decreased prediction performance but did not significantly reduce overall accuracy. title: Which Teachers Adopt AI in Teaching? An Interpretable Machine Learning Analysis of East Asian Data from TALIS 2024
authors: Jiheng Wu; Baiwei Liu; Qian Zhao
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2024 teacher questionnaire data from four East Asian economies (Singapore, Shanghai (China), Korea, Japan) and defines the dependent variable from the teacher item on AI use in the last 12 months. The analytic sample is restricted to teachers with no missing values on the dependent variable (TT4G36), and predictors are imputed after examining missingness patterns. For the main analyses, the authors apply the final teacher weight (TCHWGT) to account for TALIS’s two-stage stratified probability sampling (schools then teachers) and non-response within each economy. For robustness, they also construct and test an economy-balanced rescaled weight (W_BAL_ECON) and compare with unweighted results; they further use Fay-BRR replicate weights (TRWGT1–TRWGT100) within the initial survey-weighted logit step to estimate uncertainty under the complex design.

Therefore, plausible values handling is not applicable. Missingness is addressed for predictors using missForest, which is a random-forest-based imputation procedure; the paper does not describe multiple imputation draws and pooling rules, so the exact MI framework is not fully specified, but the imputation is clearly model-based rather than listwise deletion.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2024 teacher data from four East Asian economies (Singapore, Shanghai (China), Korea, Japan) to predict whether teachers used AI in teaching during the last 12 months (TT4G36; binary). After filtering to teachers with no missing dependent-variable values, predictors with missingness were imputed using missForest, and the main models used the TALIS final teacher weight (TCHWGT) with Fay-BRR replicate weights in the initial survey-weighted logit step. For machine learning, the authors sequentially apply LASSO for parsimonious feature selection and then AutoML (H2O) to compare GBM, DRF, and XRT, selecting GBM as the leader model based on cross-validated AUC; interpretability relies on SHAP and partial dependence plots. Exact AUC/accuracy/F1 values are not present in the provided text, but the SHAP rankings consistently highlight teaching self-efficacy and collaboration as key drivers across samples. The paper is cross-sectional and emphasizes associations rather than causal effects; SHAP-based importance is predictive, not causal, and the study’s reliance on a single binary AI-use item limits conclusions about frequency or depth of AI integration.

title: Do Key Predictors of Academic Resilience Differ Across Cultures? Evidence From Korea and the US
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students in South Korea and the United States, then restricts the analytic sample to students in the bottom 25% of ESCS within each country. The dependent variable is a binary indicator of reading resilience (at or above Level 3 in reading literacy, coded 1, among students in the bottom ESCS quartile, coded 0 otherwise). The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the random forest estimation; instead it describes model fitting in R using the randomForest package and performance evaluation (sensitivity, specificity, accuracy) across 10 plausible-value-based models. Missing values are imputed using na.roughfix (mode for categorical, median for continuous), but the paper does not specify any complex-survey-weight adjustments for the ML models.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 reading literacy to model academic resilience as a binary outcome: students in the bottom 25% of ESCS who achieve at or above Level 3 in reading. Random forest models were fit separately for South Korea and the US on the restricted samples (KOR n=1,654; USA n=1,175), using 10 plausible values for reading and averaging variable-importance rankings across plausible-value-based models. Model performance was moderate: in Korea, sensitivity ranged 0.68–0.78, specificity 0.72–0.78, and accuracy 0.71–0.76; in the US, sensitivity ranged 0.83–0.92, specificity 0.50–0.65, and accuracy 0.73–0.79. The most influential predictors were largely individual factors (especially meta-cognition and joy of reading), while some predictors differed by country (e.g., self-efficacy and educational expectations in Korea; fixed mindset and meaning in life in the US). The paper is cross-sectional and uses ML feature importance (permutation %IncMSE), so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects, and the manuscript does not report complex-survey weight application for the ML models.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 student data for reading literacy. Restricted to students in the bottom 25% of ESCS within each country (South Korea and the US). Defined academic resilience as achieving at or above Level 3 in reading literacy while belonging to the bottom 25% of ESCS; created a binary DV (resilient=1, non-resilient=0).
effect_size: Random Forest (R randomForest, 5,000 trees). title: Tools as well-being? AI teaching applications and teacher work stress: Evidence from TALIS 2024

title: Comparison of Statistical and Machine Learning Approaches for Predicting Mathematical Literacy: Evidence from PISA 2022 Türkiye
journal: Journal of Measurement and Evaluation in Education and Psychology
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 Türkiye international student microdata (15-year-olds in formal secondary education) and constructs a student-level dependent variable (PVORT) from the ten mathematics plausible values. The authors report that PISA provides student sampling weights, but they explicitly state that design-based weights could not be fully integrated into the predictive models due to PISA’s complex sampling design and the modeling approach. Therefore, the ML and regression models are trained on the filtered analytic sample without fully weight-integrated estimation. Preprocessing includes removing cases with >30% missingness, imputing remaining missing values under MAR using missForest, trimming 5% of outliers, and re-standardizing all predictors and PVORT as z-scores within the Türkiye subsample before fitting models in the same 10-fold cross-validation partitions.
outcome_summary: The study predicts PISA 2022 mathematics mathematical literacy for Turkish 15-year-olds using 13 standardized predictors spanning cognitive, affective, and contextual dimensions, with the dependent variable PVORT created by averaging the ten mathematics plausible values. Using 10-fold cross-validation in R, stacking (GLMNET meta-learner) achieved the best out-of-fold performance (R²=0.319, RMSE=0.777, MAE=0.633), followed by XGBoost (R²=0.313, RMSE=0.781) and random forests (R²=0.304, RMSE=0.786). Linear models were weaker (MLR R²≈0.270; LASSO R²≈0.273) and showed more variable error across folds. Variable-importance rankings were consistent across methods, with ESCS as the strongest predictor, then mathematics self-efficacy and disciplinary climate. Limitations include cross-sectional design (predictive, not causal), simplified PV handling via averaging (not Rubin’s rules), and incomplete integration of PISA sampling weights into predictive models.
ml_all_techniques: Stacking, XGBoost, Random Forest, Neural Network, LASSO, Linear Regression
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 Türkiye student microdata and restricted to student questionnaire variables only (omitting school and parent questionnaires). title: Education Data Mining on PISA 2015 Best Ranked Countries: What Makes the Students go Well
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 student questionnaire and achievement information for a restricted set of “best-ranked” countries by discipline. The analytic sample is created by extracting country-level subsets (top 5 countries per domain) and then preprocessing each knowledge field separately, including computing grade averages from PV items and discretizing into quartiles. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure; instead, it applies WEKA’s J48 decision trees with ten-fold cross-validation. For each domain, the authors compute an average achievement score from the ten plausible-value items (PV1–PV10), exclude the PV attributes afterward, discretize the averaged scores into quartiles (Q1–Q4), and exclude attributes with missing values. The decision trees are trained using ten-fold cross-validation, and the paper reports domain-specific quartile success rates by country (e.g., Mathematics quartile success rates up to ~56% in the top quartile for Chinese Taipei; Sciences up to ~60.9% for Singapore), but it does not provide standard predictive metrics such as accuracy, AUC, or RMSE. Key predictors repeatedly include educational aspiration, socioeconomic resources (ESCS/HOMEPOS/books), motivation/anxiety, ICT use patterns, and domain-specific epistemic/science knowledge. Because the analysis is unweighted and uses discretized PV averages, the results should be interpreted as correlational patterns rather than causal policy effects.

title: Young people’s civic engagement in Italy: evidence on grade 8 students from the international civic and citizenship education study (ICCS) 2016
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICCS 2016 microdata for Italy (grade 8) and applies student/sampling weights in all analyses, as stated in the Data analysis section. The authors normalize the total student weight so that the sum of weights equals the student sample size, and then run descriptive/correlational analyses in IDB Analyzer 5.0. For the latent profile analysis (LPA) and the subsequent logistic regressions, the manuscript indicates the analyses were conducted using the student weights, but it does not report replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife). The analytic sample is restricted to students with complete data on explanatory variables (missing values excluded), with an overall exclusion rate of 3%, and all participating schools in Italy are included.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes ICCS 2016 Italy grade 8 data to identify distinct civic engagement profiles and test how school-context and student-attitude/behavior factors relate to profile membership. Using latent profile analysis, the authors select a three-profile solution (disengaged 7%, moderately engaged 61%, engaged 32%) with entropy reported as 0.79 and fit indices (AIC/BIC/ABIC) supporting the three-class interpretability. In follow-up logistic regressions comparing disengaged and engaged groups to the moderately engaged reference, citizenship self-efficacy emerges as the most relevant differentiator (Group 3 vs Group 2 OR=1.5), while trust in civic institutions, social media engagement, open classroom discussion, and civic learning at school also show positive associations with the engaged profile. Civic knowledge is modeled as the dependent outcome using all five plausible values, but no statistically significant differences are found across profiles. The analysis excludes students with missing explanatory variables (3% overall exclusion) and is cross-sectional, so results describe associations rather than causal effects.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used ICCS 2016 Italy grade 8 student data. All participating schools in Italy were included (170 schools). Students with missing values for one or more explanatory variables were excluded from the analysis (overall exclusion rate 3%). The final analytic sample consists of 3329 eighth-grade students aged 12.3–17.1 years.
effect_size: Latent profile analysis fit: 3-profile solution (AIC/BIC/ABIC decreased; entropy 0.79). Logistic regression: odds ratios (OR) reported; effect sizes mostly weak; no overall classification accuracy reported. Additional analysis (Civic knowledge differences across engagement profiles (PVs)): Logistic regression results for civic knowledge: OR=1.00 (SE=0.01) for Group 1 vs Group 2 and OR=1.00 (SE=0.01) for Group 3 vs Group 2; no statistically significant associations reported.
primary_finding: Using ICCS 2016 Grade 8 (Italy) the study leveraged citizenship self-efficacy, trust in civic institutions, engagement with social media, open classroom discussion, and civic learning at school to model civic engagement profile membership, finding that students in the engaged profile were characterized by higher citizenship self-efficacy (Group 3 vs Group 2 OR=1.5) and generally higher levels of the other school-context and attitude/behavior variables, while civic knowledge showed no statistically significant association. This indicates that strengthening students’ perceived capability to act civically—supported by open classroom discussion and school learning opportunities—may be more actionable for improving civic engagement than focusing primarily on civic knowledge alone, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.
confounders: Citizenship self-efficacy; Engagement with social media; Trust in civic institutions; Civic learning at school; Open classroom discussion; Civic knowledge

title: How Learning Time Allocation Make Sense on Secondary School Students' Academic Performance: A Chinese Evidence Based on PISA 2018
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students from mainland China, with a two-stage sampling design (schools then students) and sampling weights assigned to both schools and students. The authors state that, after excluding missing or invalid cases, they used a final analytic sample of 9343 students and that student weights and school weights were incorporated in their OLS models. The manuscript does not report the exact weight variable names, but it explicitly indicates that PISA sampling weights were applied to account for sampling and measurement error. No replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is described, and the analysis is conducted in STATA 16 using OLS/threshold/quantile/2-stage regressions rather than ML algorithms that would require special weighting support.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 microdata for mainland China (four participating provinces/cities: Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) and models subject achievement in mathematics, science, and reading for 15-year-olds. The authors incorporate PISA’s IRT-based achievement information by generating 10 plausible values per student and using student and school sampling weights in STATA 16. They estimate (i) OLS models with linear and quadratic learning-time terms, (ii) threshold regression to identify optimal subject-specific learning-time ranges, (iii) quantile regression to assess heterogeneity across achievement levels, and (iv) a two-stage OLS mediation model via attitude toward school and subjective well-being. Results show inverted U-shaped effects with optimal ranges of about 200–240 minutes/week for math, 440–520 for science, and ~200 for reading, plus diminishing marginal benefits for top performers. Limitations include potential endogeneity (non-tracking design) and self-report bias in learning-time measures, so the findings support guidance on time allocation rather than causal claims.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 data for mainland China, focusing on four participating cities/provinces (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang). The authors report excluding missing or invalid samples from the PISA database and then selecting an analytic sample of 9343 students.
effect_size: OLS: R2=0.195 (Model 1) and R2=0.202 (Model 2); threshold regression: optimal math learning time 200–240 min/week (single threshold 200 min/week; double threshold 200–240 min/week).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 China the study leveraged learning time (math minutes/week) together with gender, urban/rural location, school type, and ESCS to model mathematics achievement, finding that learning time shows an inverted U-shaped relationship with significant positive effects up to an optimal range and negative/ineffective effects beyond it. This indicates that policies under the “double reduction” framework should target an evidence-based upper bound for subject-specific study time (about 200–240 minutes/week for math) rather than assuming that more time always improves achievement.

title: Capturing the spark: PISA, twenty-first century skills and the reconstruction of creativity
weight_fields_interpretation: This article does not conduct a student-level empirical analysis of PISA microdata; instead, it performs a thematic analysis of OECD materials and media coverage related to the development of the PISA 2022 creativity domain. Because no estimation model is fit to a sampled student dataset, there is no sampling-weight application (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and no replicate-weight procedure (e.g., BRR/jackknife) to describe. The paper also does not report plausible-value (PV) scaling or scoring model estimation steps that would normally require PV-combining rules. Consequently, there is no analytic subsample defined for statistical inference beyond the qualitative corpus of documents and media sources.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the study does not analyze PISA achievement outcomes at the student level; it is a qualitative thematic analysis of OECD documentation and media discourse about the introduction of creativity into PISA 2022. As a result, there is no PV-based dependent variable and no PV-combining procedure to report. Missing-data handling is also not reported because no quantitative model is estimated on an ILSA micro-dataset.
outcome_summary: This paper is not an empirical ML study of PISA student performance; it is a critical thematic analysis of how the OECD has responded to the challenge of measuring creativity within PISA and how creativity is framed in policy and media discourse. It draws on OECD documents (from early formalisation through pilot materials and the 2019 draft framework) and on media sources (OECD webcasts/YouTube and media coverage) using Multimodal Discourse Analysis to interpret linguistic and semiotic messaging. The article argues that the forthcoming PISA 2022 creativity metric is likely to operationalize creativity as a narrow, convergent, easily measured cognitive competence linked to human capital and economic productivity, rather than capturing broader, more polysemic conceptualizations. It also discusses how PISA’s existing high-performer stereotypes in media (e.g., East Asian 'lack of creativity') motivated the move toward a direct creativity domain. Limitations include the absence of student-level scoring, PV scaling, or performance metrics, so no quantitative benchmark or causal impact on achievement can be estimated.
null_fields_interpretation: The extraction yields no student-level sample, PV handling, missing-data strategy, or ML model outputs because the manuscript is a qualitative critical analysis rather than an empirical predictive/causal study using PISA microdata. The paper does not report any algorithmic training, validation metrics, or statistical estimation results; instead, it analyzes the development and communication of the creativity assessment concept and its implications for PISA’s role as a global benchmark.
sample_filtering_criteria: No student sample is analyzed. The study’s 'data' consist of (1) OECD materials documenting the development of the creativity measure (reports, pilot materials, and draft framework) and (2) media materials (OECD YouTube/webcasts and media coverage of PISA results).

title: A new perspective on memorization practices among East Asian students based on PISA 2012
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 microdata for seven East Asian educational systems and relies on PISA’s two-stage complex survey design (schools sampled with probabilities proportional to size, then students sampled within schools). The manuscript describes the complex design and the questionnaire rotation/booklet design, but it does not report applying any explicit student/sampling weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight variance estimation. Instead, it uses full information maximum likelihood (FIML) to address questionnaire missingness induced by the rotation design and uses all five plausible values for mathematics achievement in the regression analyses. Because no survey-weight variable is named, the weighting approach for population-representative estimation is not transparent in the text.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2012 mathematics learning strategies among 15-year-olds in seven East Asian educational systems using the PISA Student Questionnaire and mathematics achievement scores. Learning strategies (memorization, elaboration, metacognition) were measured with a forced-choice format and modeled with latent class analysis, yielding four strategy profiles: memorization+metacognitive (17.49%), metacognitive+memorization (50.70%), elaboration only (10.33%), and metacognitive+elaboration (16.47%). Mathematics achievement was modeled via regression using all five plausible values (scaled to mean 500, SD 100) and covariates ESCS and gender; the Macau regression did not converge, so coefficients were not reported there. The results show that Class 2 is positively associated with mathematics performance in all systems, and Class 4 is positively associated in all systems except Singapore. A key limitation is that learning strategies are self-reported and the study is correlational (no causal identification), so the findings should not be interpreted as proving that metacognitive instruction causes higher achievement.
null_fields_interpretation: The paper does not train predictive machine-learning models; instead, it uses latent class analysis to identify strategy profiles and then runs regressions to compare mathematics achievement across profiles. Therefore, ml_techniques are intentionally left empty and the research design is classified as exploratory rather than predictive.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2012 Student Questionnaire and mathematics achievement for 15-year-old students in seven East Asian educational systems (Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea, Macau, Shanghai of China, Singapore, Taiwan). The study addresses questionnaire missingness due to the PISA rotation design for learning-strategy items (each student answered only a subset), using full information maximum likelihood (FIML). For the regression stage, it reports no missing data on class membership, gender, ESCS, and mathematics scores; the Macau regression did not converge, so Macau coefficients were not reported.
effect_size: Not reported (LCA model selection via BIC/a_BIC/LMR; class proportions: 17.49%, 50.70%, 10.33%, 16.47%).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged Economic, social, cultural status and Gender to contextualize learning-strategy class membership derived via latent class analysis, finding four distinct learning-strategy classes with the largest class being metacognitive strategies with memorization (50.70%). title: On the Choice of the Item Response Model for Scaling PISA Data: Model Selection Based on Information Criteria and Quantifying Model Uncertainty
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2009 microdata and performs country-level scaling analyses for three cognitive domains (mathematics, reading, science). For all country-level analyses, student weights are taken into account; within each country, weights are normalized to contribute equally across countries (normalized to a sum of 5000). For uncertainty quantification of the plausible-value-based country estimates, the paper draws plausible values for each country using sampling weights and then computes standard errors using balanced half sampling (instead of balanced repeated replication). The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that student weights are used in both the country scaling step and the plausible-value drawing step.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe a missing-data strategy for student covariates or item responses (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation, or explicit handling of missing item responses). This is likely because the analysis is based on PISA 2009 scaling and plausible-value drawing procedures, where missingness is handled implicitly by the IRT estimation/scaling workflow rather than by a separately documented imputation rule in the manuscript. However, the absence of an explicit missing-data handling description is a reporting gap for reproducibility.
outcome_summary: This paper empirically evaluates how the choice of unidimensional IRT scaling model affects PISA 2009 country-level distribution parameters. Using PISA 2009 mathematics, reading, and science, the author compares 11 functional forms (1PL through 4PL variants, including 3PLQ and 3PLRH) with information criteria (AIC, BIC, and ∆GHP) and then quantifies model uncertainty via model error (ME), bias-corrected model error (MEbc), and error ratios ER=MEbc/SE, plus total error TE. For reading, model error is small for country means (ER≈0.24) but substantial for standard deviations (ER≈0.60, max 2.05) and for percentiles (ER≈0.60 for Q10 and 0.84 for Q90). The study uses student weights and plausible-value drawing with Rubin rules, but it does not provide an explicit missing-data handling strategy, and the results are descriptive about scaling-model sensitivity rather than causal effects of model choice.
sample_filtering_criteria: The empirical calibration and scaling procedure uses PISA 2009 data for 26 countries and three cognitive domains (mathematics, reading, science). For model fitting and information-criterion comparisons, the authors draw an international calibration sample by randomly sampling 500 students from each of the 26 countries for each domain, yielding 13,000 students per domain for the model-comparison step. All polytomous items are dichotomously recoded (only the highest category treated as correct). In the subsequent country-specific scaling step, item parameters are fixed from the international calibration sample and country-specific plausible values for the latent ability distribution are drawn; the paper states that no student covariates are included when drawing plausible values.
effect_size: Model comparisons via AIC, BIC, and ∆GHP across 11 IRT models (1PL, 1PCL, 1PLL, 1PGL, 2PL, 3PL, 3PLQ, 3PLRH, 4PGL, 4PL, 4PLQ). Model uncertainty quantified using model error (ME), bias-corrected model error (MEbc), error ratio (ER=MEbc/SE), and total error (TE=√(SE^2+MEbc^2)). For mathematics, the error ratio for country means was on average 0.24 (max 0.66) and for country standard deviations on average 0.77 (max 1.58).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2009 mathematics the study compared 11 unidimensional IRT scaling models to obtain country means and standard deviations, finding that model choice had limited impact on country means on average (error ratio ER≈0.24) but substantial impact on country standard deviations (ER≈0.77, with some countries showing model error exceeding sampling error). This indicates that reporting uncertainty for dispersion parameters should incorporate model-uncertainty measures rather than relying on sampling standard errors alone.

title: Evaluating the Results of PISA Assessment: Are There Gaps Between the Teaching of Mathematical Literacy at Schools and in PISA Assessment?
weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a purposive sample of 100 ninth-grade students from two junior high schools in Semarang City, Indonesia, and administered a 24-item mathematical literacy test constructed from PISA 2012, 2015, and 2018 items. The manuscript states that sampling followed PISA technical standards, but it does not report any use of PISA student/sampling weights or replicate weights, nor any specific weight variable names. Because the analysis is based on a small, locally selected sample rather than an international PISA microdata extract, complex survey weighting is not documented and should not be assumed. The reported scoring relies on Rasch fixed item parameters and WLE reliability, so the key preparation step is test scoring and categorization (mathematical competence, precision, and self-perception), not survey-weighted estimation.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are derived from a locally administered 24-item mathematical literacy test and from questionnaire/interview measures (self-perception and precision coding), rather than from PISA-provided plausible values (PVs). The paper does not describe any missing-data rule for questionnaire items, test responses, or interview coding (e.g., complete-case selection or imputation), which is a reporting gap given that missingness can occur in Likert responses and test items. Therefore, missing-data handling cannot be reconstructed from the text.
outcome_summary: This study used a locally administered 24-item mathematical literacy test based on PISA 2012, 2015, and 2018 items, together with a 20-item Likert self-perception questionnaire and precision coding from students’ answer sheets, in a purposive sample of 100 grade 9 students (age 15) from two schools in Semarang City, Indonesia. Students’ overall mathematical literacy mean was 55.4 (SD=8.62), with Group A (state) higher than Group B (private): 58.1 vs 52.7. The paper reports strong Pearson correlations among mathematical competence, precision, self-perception, and mathematical literacy (e.g., Math Competency–Math Literacy r=0.904; Precision–Math Literacy r=0.874; Self-Perception–Math Literacy r=0.793). It also documents that most students performed at low proficiency levels (levels 1–2 dominate) and that teachers’ instruction emphasized formulas and procedural practice rather than PISA-style reasoning. Limitations include the small, single-city sample, the absence of documented missing-data handling, and the correlational nature of the relationships (no causal identification).
sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample comprised 100 ninth-grade students aged 15 years from two junior high schools in Semarang City, Indonesia (50 from state schools and 50 from private schools). Inclusion criteria required students to be male or female, 15 years old, and ninth-grade junior high school students; sampling was purposive. The mathematical literacy test contained 24 PISA-based items (drawn from PISA 2012, 2015, and 2018) and students’ responses were scored using PISA international coding rules and Rasch fixed item parameters; precision was coded from students’ answer sheets and self-perception from a 20-item Likert questionnaire.

title: Exploring school leadership profiles across the world: a cluster analysis approach to TALIS 2018
journal: International Journal of Leadership in Education
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 school- and teacher-level data collected via a two-stage sampling design (random sample of schools within each country, then random sample of teachers within schools). Prior to clustering, the authors standardized the 12 leadership-for-learning scales using “senate weights” so that all countries contribute equally to the scale metric. Factor scores for the TALIS scales were calculated using Mplus with TYPE = COMPLEX and school weights to account for non-independence and unequal probability of selection. For the clustering stage, the paper does not report additional explicit application of student/school sampling weights beyond the earlier standardization and the use of senate weights for equal country contribution.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variables are leadership-for-learning scale factor scores (and one derived factor score) used for descriptive clustering, not cognitive achievement outcomes with PVs. The paper also does not report any PV-based achievement modeling; instead, it uses standardized scale scores and then applies k-means clustering to form school leadership profiles.
outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 (lower secondary; teachers and principals) to construct leadership-for-learning profiles across schools and to examine whether country-level groupings emerge. After standardizing scales using senate weights, they aggregated teacher variables to the school level and applied k-means clustering, selecting k=5 via elbow and silhouette methods. Variance decomposition showed that most variability lay between schools rather than between countries, leading to a school-level clustering solution. The five-cluster solution accounted for 25.9% of variability in school profiles; 790 schools (15%) had negative silhouette coefficients, and the authors excluded these for cluster purification. The study reports that country-level cluster membership does not align with geographic/linguistic/political proximity, while leadership profiles are present in most countries and show teacher–principal perception gaps in distributed leadership.

title: Factors Predicting Collaborative Problem Solving: Based on the Data From PISA 2015
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for CPS from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Guangdong, with a probability proportionate to size (PPS) school sampling design. It states that a student-level sampling weight (W_FSTUWT) and a school-level sampling weight (W_FSCHWT, computed as the sum of student weights within each school) were employed to reduce unequal selection probabilities and non-response bias. The CPS outcome is based on 10 plausible values, and the authors follow OECD guidance by estimating models separately for each plausible value and then averaging the resulting statistics. For the hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) approach, the manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so replicate-weight handling is not documented.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 Collaborative Problem Solving (CPS) for 15-year-olds in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Guangdong, using hierarchical linear models to account for students nested within schools. CPS is measured via a computer-based CPS test and summarized using 10 plausible values; the authors estimate models for each plausible value and average the resulting statistics. Missing data reduced the sample from 9841 students (268 schools) to 9328 students (259 schools). At the student level, gender, grade, ESCS, enjoyment of cooperation, teacher unfair treatment, and ICT resources significantly predicted CPS, with grade and ESCS showing positive associations and teacher unfairness showing a negative association; sports time was not significant. At the school level, school location, school ESCS, and the proportion of fully certified teachers were significant predictors, with the largest incremental variance explained at the school level coming from teacher certification. The paper does not report any machine-learning algorithms; therefore, results should be interpreted as correlational model-based associations rather than ML predictive performance.
null_fields_interpretation: This paper uses hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) with plausible values and does not train or evaluate any machine-learning predictive algorithms (no RF/XGBoost/SVM/NN, etc.). Consequently, the ML technique fields are intentionally empty, and main_findings summarize the statistical associations rather than ML model performance.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 CPS assessment data for 15-year-olds from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Guangdong. The initial sample comprised 9841 students from 268 schools, but cases with missing data were deleted automatically by HLM, leaving 9328 students from 259 schools for analysis.
effect_size: Hierarchical linear models (HLM); variance explained at student level: 5.98% (Model 2 with gender/grade/ESCS), 2.21% (Model 3 with cooperation attitudes), 1.74% (Model 4 with teacher unfairness), 1.18% (Model 5 with ICT resources), 0.51% (Model 6 with sports time). Coefficients (selected): gender β=-20.32 (p<0.001), grade β=28.64 (p<0.001), ESCS β=9.21 (p<0.001), enjoyment of cooperation β=11.44 (p<0.001), value of cooperation β=-4.16 (p<0.05), teacher unfairness β=-1.34 (p<0.01), ICT resources β=8.65 (p<0.001), sports time β=1.74 (ns).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 CPS data for 15-year-olds in Beijing/Shanghai/Jiangsu/Guangdong, the study leveraged gender, grade level, ESCS, cooperation attitudes, teacher unfair treatment, and ICT resources to predict CPS achievement (averaging across 10 plausible values). It found that higher grade and higher ESCS were associated with higher CPS scores, ICT resources and enjoyment of cooperation were positive predictors, while teacher unfair treatment and the “value of cooperation” scale were negative (and sports time was not significant). This indicates that improving learning conditions—especially ICT access and fair teacher-student relationships—alongside grade-appropriate CPS instruction may strengthen collaborative problem-solving performance, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.
