title: Explaining gender differences in mathematics achievement: Cross-country evidence from PISA
weight_variable_name: senate weights (rescaled PISA student sampling weights)
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for mathematics and applies senate weights throughout both the ML (CatBoost) and regression stages. Senate weights are described as rescaled student sampling weights that are normalized so each participating country contributes equally to the pooled analysis, rather than proportionally to its student population size. The ML stage retains students with incomplete covariate information (CatBoost can handle missing values), while the regression stage uses a restricted complete-case subsample of 43 countries and 173,059 students. Country fixed effects are included in regression specifications, and the authors interpret results as pooled internal validation within the observed multinational sample under the senate-weighted framework.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper explicitly states that CatBoost can handle missing data without requiring imputation, but it does not provide a formal missing-data handling label for the overall analytic pipeline (e.g., whether any additional missingness filtering or complete-case restrictions were applied beyond the regression stage). For the regression stage, the authors do report a complete-case subsample, but the manuscript does not clearly specify the missing-data handling strategy for the full ML stage in a way that maps to the schema’s missing-data categories. This is a reporting gap because the PV pooling is described (OECD/Rubin), yet the missing-data treatment is only partially operationalized across stages.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 mathematics microdata for 15-year-olds pooled across 77 countries/economies (597,345 students) and models two outcomes: continuous mathematics achievement using PV1MATH–PV10MATH and a binary indicator of high performance at Levels 5–6 (>=607 points). The main ML approach is CatBoost with gender-specific cross-features (covariate × girl/boy indicators), estimated separately for each plausible value and then averaged; senate weights are applied so each country contributes equally to pooled estimates. Predictive performance is reasonably strong for the continuous outcome (R²=0.62; RMSE=65.07; MAE=51.52) and strong for ranking the binary outcome (ROC AUC=0.899; Accuracy=0.924) but more modest for identifying the high-performing class at a threshold (F1=0.356; balanced accuracy=0.618). The most salient gender-differentiated correlates include expected occupational status (EOS), perceived test difficulty, and several learning-environment/ICT and home-experience variables. The authors emphasize that results are descriptive/predictive rather than causal, and regression follow-ups use a complete-case subsample (173,059 students across 43 countries), so differences across stages may reflect both functional-form restrictions and sample composition.
sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA 2018 mathematics microdata pooled across 77 countries/economies (597,345 students). For the ML stage, the full 77-country pooled sample is used and missing covariates are retained because CatBoost can handle missing values without imputation. For the regression stage, analyses are restricted to a complete-case subsample with available observations for at least 43 countries and 173,059 students (complete-case restriction is explicitly stated). High-performance is defined as mathematics proficiency Level 5 or 6 (>=607 points), and the ML models are estimated separately for PV1MATH–PV10MATH and then averaged.
effect_size: CatBoost (PV-specific models averaged): RMSE=65.07, MAE=51.52, R-squared=0.62
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics data (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) pooled across 77 countries/economies, the study leveraged gender-specific interaction components of Expected occupational status (EOS), Perceived test difficulty, Cultural possessions at home, Eudaemonia, and Reading self-concept (competence) to predict continuous mathematics achievement, finding that EOS is the most salient gender-differentiated correlate and that perceived test difficulty and ICT-related perceptions also show systematic gender-specific association patterns. This indicates that strengthening girls’ STEM-related career expectations and addressing perceived test difficulty/anxiety in learning environments may be key levers for reducing gender disparities in high-stakes mathematics performance, though the study remains descriptive and does not establish causal effects.
confounders: Expected occupational status (EOS); Perceived test difficulty; Cultural possessions at home; Eudaemonia; Reading self-concept (competence); Perceived autonomy in ICT use; Experience of being bullied; Perceived ICT competence; Reading self-concept (difficulty); Sense of belonging to school; ICT use outside of school; Interest in ICT; Parental ESCS; Parents' emotional support; ICT available at home; Family wealth; Mathematics learning time; Gender indicator (girl/boy)

title: The impact of gender differences in teachers’ teaching practices and attitudes on students’ math and science achievement in Saudi Arabia: Evidence from TIMSS 2019 data
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 international database data for Saudi Arabia, focusing on fourth-grade mathematics and science achievement and linking them to teacher-reported attitudes and teaching style plus student-reported teaching practices. The manuscript reports sample composition (students and teachers) and administration dates, but it does not describe the application of TIMSS complex survey weights or any replicate-weight procedure. Because the analysis is presented as multiple regression with reported F-tests and R², the paper does not provide the weight variable name(s) (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate design details needed to reproduce population-representative estimates. Analysts using TIMSS microdata should apply TIMSS sampling weights and replicate weights when estimating standard errors and model fit; however, this paper’s weighting strategy is not documented, so it is unclear whether weighted estimation was performed.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are students’ TIMSS mathematics and science achievement scores, but the manuscript does not state whether these were analyzed using TIMSS plausible values (PV) with Rubin’s combining rules, averaged PVs, or an alternative scaling approach. Similarly, the paper does not report any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., complete-case exclusion, imputation, or PV-specific missingness rules). Given that TIMSS datasets typically include missing questionnaire responses and PV-based achievement scoring, the absence of explicit PV and missing-data documentation is a reporting gap that limits transparency and reproducibility.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 data from Saudi Arabia, focusing on fourth-grade mathematics and science achievement and examining whether teacher-related factors explain gender differences in student performance. Across both domains, multiple regression models were statistically significant (Math: F5, 8313 = 99.764, R² = 0.057; Science: F5, 8062 = 146.804, R² = 0.083), with teaching practices (student-reported) emerging as the strongest predictor (partial R = 0.180 for math; partial R = 0.206 for science). Teaching style and teaching attitudes were also among the top predictors and were positively associated with achievement, while years of experience was not significant for science. The paper further reports that female teachers scored higher on these teacher variables, which the authors interpret as a partial reflection of the girls’ higher achievement. However, the manuscript does not report how TIMSS plausible values were handled or how missing data were treated, and it uses correlational/regression evidence rather than causal identification.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 data from Saudi Arabia, restricted to fourth-grade students and their associated teachers in the TIMSS 2019 administration (9–10 April 2019). The analytic focus is on five teacher-related predictors: teaching practices (measured via student questionnaire items), teaching style (teacher questionnaire), teaching attitudes (teacher questionnaire), years of teaching experience, and teacher major/specialization (math vs science). The manuscript reports that the sample is nearly split by student gender and that teacher gender counts are available, but it does not specify additional exclusions (e.g., missing questionnaire items, school/teacher eligibility rules, or PV availability filters).
effect_size: Multiple regression: model significant (F5, 8313 = 99.764, p < 0.001), R² = 0.057. Best predictor: teaching practices (partial R = 0.180), implying ~3.2% of unique variation explained. Coefficients: teaching practices (B = -30.810, Beta = -0.179, p < 0.001), teaching style (B = -20.801, Beta = -0.096, p < 0.001), teaching attitudes (B = -21.762, Beta = -0.078, p < 0.001).
primary_finding: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics data from Saudi Arabia, the study leveraged teaching practices (student view), teaching style (teacher view), teaching attitudes, years of teaching experience, and teacher major to predict students’ math achievement, finding that teaching practices, teaching style, and teaching attitudes were the three highest predictors and were positively associated with achievement. This indicates that strengthening high-quality instructional practices and supportive teacher dispositions may help reduce the gender achievement gap, though the study’s regression design and undocumented PV/weighting strategy limit causal interpretation.
confounders: Teaching practices (student view); Teaching style (teacher view); Teaching attitudes; Years of teaching experience; Teacher major (math specialization); Teacher major (science specialization); gender; Teacher gender

title: Using Machine Learning Approaches to Explore Non-Cognitive Variables Influencing Reading Proficiency in English among Filipino Learners
authors: A.B.I.B.; M.O.C.II; R.I.G.L.; J.M.M.T.; S.A.Y.; U.C.C.
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Philippines national sample from PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) downloaded as a public-use file from OECD. The original PISA design is described as a two-stage stratified random selection of schools (187 schools across 17 regions) followed by random sampling of students within schools, but the manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML training/testing pipeline. For modeling, the authors rescaled variables to 0–1, imputed missing values using k-nearest neighbors (k=7), and then trained multiple classifiers on an 80/20 random split with five-fold cross-validation for training performance. Because the paper does not state weight usage, the safest interpretation is that complex survey weighting was not incorporated into the ML estimation, which may limit population-representativeness and under/over-estimate uncertainty under the nested school design.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 Philippines data (7233 students) and predicts a binary reading proficiency label derived from PV1READ: low proficiency corresponds to Levels 1b and below, while high corresponds to Levels 1a and above. After converting PISA missing tags to nulls, the authors dropped variables with 100% missingness and imputed remaining missing values using k-nearest neighbors (k=7), then rescaled variables to 0–1. Multiple classifiers were trained and tuned via grid search, with five-fold cross-validation for training performance and an 80/20 random split for testing. The SVM with an RBF kernel performed best, reaching 81.20% test accuracy and AUC-ROC of 0.89, outperforming other models including logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting, AdaBoost, and kNN. Interpretation relies on SHAP for feature importance, but the paper’s predictive focus and the lack of explicit reporting on survey-weight use mean results should be treated as correlational and potentially limited in generalizability under the nested PISA design.
ml_all_techniques: SVM, Logistic Regression, Neural Network, Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, AdaBoost, k-NN
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the complete nationally representative PISA 2018 Philippines student sample (7233 15-year-olds) selected via two-stage stratified sampling (187 schools across 17 regions). For ML, students were labeled into low vs high reading proficiency groups using PV1 for reading (low = Levels 1b and below; high = Levels 1a and above). From the 122 candidate variables, variables with 100% missingness were dropped; remaining variables with missing values were imputed using k-nearest neighbors with k=7 after converting PISA missing tags ("M"/"N") to nulls. Variables were rescaled to 0–1 prior to model training.
effect_size: SVM (RBF kernel) — best average test accuracy: 81.20%; AUC-ROC: 0.89. Worst AUC-ROC reported: 0.5; best AUC-ROC reported: 1.0. Five-fold cross-validation used for training performance; hyperparameters selected via grid search.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 Philippines reading the study leveraged SCREADDIFF, BEINGBULLIED, WORKMAST, ICTRES, and JOYREAD to classify students into low vs high reading proficiency groups, finding that the SVM achieved the best test performance (accuracy 81.20%, AUC-ROC 0.89) and that higher perceived reading difficulty and bullying exposure were associated with low proficiency while mastery motivation was associated with higher proficiency. This indicates that interventions targeting reading self-beliefs (reducing perceived difficulty), school social climate (bullying reduction and belonging/cooperation), and mastery-oriented motivation may be high-leverage for improving English reading outcomes among Filipino students, though the results are predictive and not causal and may be sensitive to the unreported use of PISA sampling weights.

title: Prediction of the Factors Affecting PISA Mathematics Literacy of Students from Different Countries by Using Data Mining Methods
authors: Nurşah Aksu; Gökhan Aksu; Seda Saracaloğlu
journal: International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for mathematics literacy and constructs an analytic sample restricted to six countries (Singapore, Japan, Norway, the USA, Turkey, and the Dominican Republic). The dependent variable is PV2MATH (a PISA mathematics plausible value) and the authors report using WEKA (M5P decision-tree regression) and MATLAB (feed-forward artificial neural network) with a hold-out validation scheme (70% train, 15% test, 15% validation) within each country. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) and does not name any weight variables, so weighting strategy is unclear. Because the models are implemented in WEKA/MATLAB and the paper does not discuss complex survey design adjustments, the analysis should be treated as potentially unweighted and may not fully account for PISA’s clustered sampling design.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper specifies that the dependent variable is PV2MATH, but it does not describe how missing questionnaire or predictor values were handled (e.g., imputation vs. complete-case filtering) in the WEKA/MATLAB pipeline. Although the authors mention that M5P can deal with missing data, they do not report the exact missing-data rule used (and whether it was applied consistently across countries and train/test splits), which is a reporting gap for reproducibility.
outcome_summary: The study predicts PISA 2015 mathematics literacy using a single plausible value (PV2MATH) as a continuous target and 15 student questionnaire variables, estimating models separately for six countries (Singapore, Japan, Norway, the USA, Turkey, and the Dominican Republic). In the first stage, it trains a regression-based decision tree (M5P in WEKA) and reports country-specific decision-tree rules and fit (e.g., Matthews correlation coefficients). In the second stage, it uses a feed-forward artificial neural network in MATLAB (TRAINLM and LEARNGDM) and evaluates external validity via a hold-out split (70% training, 15% test, 15% validation). Predictive performance varies substantially by country: ANN overall R2 ranges from 0.861 (Singapore) to 0.264 (Turkey), with RMSE values from 17.57 to 43.20. The paper does not report survey-weight usage or a detailed missing-data procedure, so results may be sensitive to unweighted estimation and undocumented preprocessing choices; moreover, the findings are predictive associations rather than causal effects.
sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is restricted to students from six countries that the authors selected based on different proficiency levels in PISA 2015: Singapore (Level 4), Japan (Level 3), Norway (Level 3), the USA (Level 2), Turkey (Level 1), and the Dominican Republic (below Level 1). The dependent variable is PISA mathematics literacy taken as a continuous outcome using PV2MATH. The study then runs separate country-specific models and evaluates external validity using a hold-out split within each country (70% training, 15% test, 15% validation).
effect_size: M5P (WEKA): Matthews correlation coefficient = 0.464; average absolute error = 64.58; RMSE (reported as square root of average errors) = 87.72. ANN (MATLAB): Training R2 = 0.927, Test R2 = 0.861, Validation R2 = 0.861; Overall R2 = 0.861; regression equation y=0.86x+78; RMSE = 17.57; correct prediction ≈ 92.8% (93.18% train, 91.96% test, 91.86% validation).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 Mathematics literacy (PV2MATH) data for Singapore, the study leveraged Socio-economic status (ESCS), Teacher fairness, Mathematics learning time, and Total learning time to predict mathematics literacy, finding that socio-economic status was the root driver and that the ANN achieved high overall fit (Overall R2 = 0.861) with low prediction error (RMSE = 17.57). This indicates that strengthening equity-oriented supports (reducing socioeconomic disadvantages) alongside improving perceived teacher fairness and sustaining mathematics learning time may be especially important for high-proficiency contexts, though causality cannot be inferred from predictive modeling.

title: How are maths-anxious students identified and what are the key predictors of maths anxiety? Insights gained from PISA results for Korean adolescents
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 student questionnaire data for South Korea and constructs an analytic dataset of 3,355 students from 156 schools, then further splits it into 70% training (2,351) and 30% test (1,004). The paper does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML training/evaluation; therefore, the analysis appears to rely on unweighted model fitting and standard train/test partitioning. Because the dependent variable is a binary classification of “maths-anxious” status derived from a maths anxiety score, the authors’ main data preparation steps are (i) selecting 194 questionnaire variables as predictors, (ii) defining the anxiety group using a one-standard-deviation-below-mean threshold, and (iii) performing multiple imputation for missing predictor values. The hierarchical nature of students nested in schools is addressed via a hierarchical generalized linear model (HGLM) baseline, but the manuscript does not specify survey-weight adjustments for the random forest or logistic regression.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is students’ maths anxiety classification (a questionnaire-based affective construct), not a cognitive achievement score for which PISA provides plausible values. Missing data handling is reported as multiple imputation with 10 replications using the R “mice” package, so the main transparency issue is not PVs but whether imputation was performed within the training folds versus on the full dataset (the paper does not explicitly state this). This omission matters because imputation performed before splitting can introduce leakage into the test set.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2012 South Korea student questionnaire data (3,355 students from 156 schools) and defines a binary outcome for “potential maths anxiety” using a threshold of one standard deviation below the mean on a maths anxiety score (634 students; 18.9%). It trains and compares three supervised prediction models—random forest, logistic regression, and a two-level hierarchical generalized linear model (HGLM)—using 194 questionnaire predictors, with a 70/30 train/test split (2,351/1,004). Model discrimination is high across approaches: AUC is 0.854 for HGLM and logistic regression and 0.851 for random forest; overall accuracy is 0.839 (HGLM), 0.836 (logistic), and 0.823 (random forest). The random forest shows the highest sensitivity (0.681), while sensitivity for HGLM/logistic is 0.628, indicating better identification of at-risk students at the cost of lower specificity. Missing predictor data are handled via multiple imputation (10 replications, mice), but the paper does not clarify whether imputation was nested within training folds, which could affect generalization estimates.
ml_all_techniques: Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Hierarchical General Linear Model
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2012 South Korea student questionnaire dataset. The analytic sample includes 3,355 students from 156 schools. Maths-anxious students were operationally defined by categorizing students whose maths anxiety score was one standard deviation below the mean; this yields 634 (18.9%) students classified as “potential maths anxiety” and 2,721 as “without maths anxiety.” Predictors were restricted to 194 selected questionnaire variables spanning learning experiences/strategies, attitudes, perceived teacher and school/classroom climate, ICT use, and student background/demographics; item-level responses were used as predictors.
effect_size: HGLM: Proportion accurate=0.839, Sensitivity=0.628, Specificity=0.888, AUC=0.854. Logistic regression: Proportion accurate=0.836, Sensitivity=0.628, Specificity=0.884, AUC=0.854. Random forest: Proportion accurate=0.823, Sensitivity=0.681, Specificity=0.856, AUC=0.851.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2012 South Korea student questionnaire the study leveraged negative maths self-concept, attributions to failure (lack of ability/task difficulty/bad luck), and enjoying maths to predict whether students were classified as potential maths-anxious. It found that self-concept and attributions to failure were the most influential predictors across models, with the random forest achieving the highest sensitivity (0.681) while HGLM/logistic regression had slightly higher overall accuracy and AUC (~0.854). This indicates that interventions targeting maladaptive self-beliefs and failure attributions may be more effective for identifying and supporting maths-anxious students than relying on performance-only or single-factor screening, though the study’s binary thresholding and potential imputation/splitting leakage limit causal interpretation.

title: Identifying patterns of students' performance on simulated inquiry tasks using PISA 2015 log-file data

title: Are schools becoming more unequal? Insights from exploratory data mining of international large-scale assessment, TIMSS 2003-2019
authors: Farhan Ali; Yook Kit Ow-Yeong; Jacqueline L. Tilley
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS science scale scores for Grade 4 and Grade 8 across five cycles (2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019) and computes school-level statistics from student-level plausible values. For representativeness, the authors explicitly state that they used total student weight when computing average scale scores for each school (via intsvy.mean.pv), and they filtered out schools with fewer than 10 tested students. The paper does not report replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty estimation at the replicate level is not documented here. Because the analysis is exploratory and focuses on variance decomposition and distributional modeling at the school level, the key weighting step is the use of total student weights to form weighted means/variances rather than a separate replicate-weight variance estimation procedure.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper describes how TIMSS plausible values (five PVs) were computed per student and then averaged to obtain the final relevant statistic at the school level, but it does not explicitly document how missing questionnaire/background variables or missing PVs were handled. This is a reporting gap because missingness handling can affect variance and distributional measures, especially when aggregating to schools across multiple cycles. The authors also do not state whether they used complete-case filtering beyond the school-level exclusion criterion (schools with fewer than 10 tested students).
outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS general science achievement data for Grade 4 and Grade 8 across five cycles (2003–2019) in 10 countries with complete data across cycles and grades. It computes school-level achievement inequality by decomposing total variance into between-school and within-school components using weighted plausible-value-based scale scores, excluding schools with fewer than 10 tested students. Across both grades, the dominant pattern is that within-school inequality is much larger than between-school inequality, and between-school inequality does not show consistent worsening over nearly two decades. The study also finds a stable, moderate-to-large negative relationship between within-school average achievement and within-school inequality, and distributional modeling suggests that lower-achieving schools often contain multiple subpopulations (bimodality), with a clearer rise in such subpopulations for Grade 4 by 2019. Limitations include limited class sampling per school (hindering finer within-school decomposition) and lack of explicit documentation of missing-data handling beyond the school exclusion rule.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS general science achievement data for Grade 4 and Grade 8 across five cycles (2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019). Restricted to 10 countries that had complete data for all five cycles at both grade levels. Focused on general science (not specific science subjects) to ensure comparability across systems. Excluded schools with fewer than 10 students tested, yielding 7474 schools (Grade 4) and 7567 schools (Grade 8) with adequate sample sizes across cycles. For within-school distribution modeling, the analysis was conducted at the school level (with supplementary checks using classes due to limited class sampling per school).

title: Equity lost: Sweden and Finland in the struggle for PISA scores
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA microdata for science achievement for Sweden and Finland in 2000, 2009, and 2015, estimating separate cross-sectional multilevel linear regression models for each year. The authors explicitly state that they calculate and apply student weights provided by the OECD to compensate for missing observations at the student level, indicating complex survey considerations in the estimation. No replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported in the provided text, so replicate-weight usage cannot be confirmed. The analytic sample is further restricted by the modeling strategy (student-level and school-level predictors, plus governance indices and interaction terms), and the authors report robustness checks and diagnostics (z-standardization, normality checks, and VIF for heteroscedasticity), with some effects described as influenced by outliers.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports the use of OECD-provided student weights to compensate for missing observations, but it does not specify the exact missing-data mechanism or the concrete missing-data handling rule (e.g., listwise/pairwise deletion or an imputation strategy) for the regression variables. Because the dependent variable is PISA science achievement (which is typically based on plausible values), the manuscript does not document the PV-combining procedure used in the multilevel regressions, representing a transparency gap for reproducibility.
outcome_summary: The article tests two hypotheses derived from the global educational reform movement (GERM) by analyzing OECD PISA science achievement for Sweden and Finland in 2000, 2009, and 2015. The authors estimate separate cross-sectional multilevel linear regression models with student-level and school-level predictors, using OECD student weights to address missing observations and applying z-standardization for comparability. Across years, the strongest and most robust associations with science achievement come from socioeconomic status (student ESCS and school mean ESCS), with explained variance and ICC indicating increasing stratification in Sweden earlier than in Finland. Governance-tool indices (school autonomy, educational leadership, accountability) do not show a systematic positive effect on performance or on reducing the ESCS gradient; instead, Hypothesis H2 is confirmed in both countries, implying that advantaged students are better positioned to benefit from these reforms. Limitations include incomplete reporting of plausible-value handling and missing-data rules for reproducibility, and the study’s observational design prevents causal claims about governance tools.
sample_filtering_criteria: The authors conduct separate cross-sectional multilevel linear regression analyses for Sweden and Finland using PISA science scores for the years 2000, 2009, and 2015. The dependent variable is PISA science achievement, and the models include student-level and school-level predictors (ESCS, migration background indicators, disciplinary climate, and governance-tool indices), plus interaction terms for socioeconomic status and disciplinary climate. Beyond this modeling structure, the provided text does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., grade restrictions, school-type restrictions, or explicit complete-case criteria), so the analytic sample is best described as the available PISA student and school data for the specified countries and years with OECD student weights applied.

This indicates that, in these Nordic contexts, marketization/accountability-style governance tools did not measurably improve science performance or reduce socioeconomic achievement gaps, and equity gains were not supported by the governance mechanisms proposed in the global reform agenda.

title: The influence of SES, migration background, and non‑cognitive abilities on PISA reading and mathematics achievement: evidence from Sweden
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Sweden and applies a two-level multilevel modeling approach to account for the nested sampling of students within schools. The authors state that level-1 models (student background factors) were weighted with student weights and that level-2 models (school-level aggregated factors) were weighted with school weights, but they do not report the exact weight variable names in the provided text. Plausible values are handled by using all ten plausible values for reading (PVREAD) and mathematics (PVMATH) and combining estimates across plausible values using Rubin’s (1987) method implemented in Mplus. Missing data are handled in Mplus using Maximum Likelihood Robust (MLR) estimation, which is consistent with model-based handling rather than listwise deletion for the multilevel analyses.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes Sweden’s PISA 2018 microdata to explain within-school and between-school differences in reading and mathematics achievement using multilevel models with all ten plausible values (PVREAD and PVMATH) combined via Rubin’s method in Mplus. For reading, the intraclass correlation is 0.075 and the multilevel model yields within-school R2 = 0.263 and between-school R2 = 0.575, with reading self-concept, SES (books at home and mother’s education), migration background, gender, and growth mindset emerging as significant predictors. For mathematics, the intraclass correlation is 0.105 and the model yields within-school R2 = 0.214 and between-school R2 = 0.483, with SES and migration background showing large effects and non-cognitive factors (notably growth mindset and reading self-concept) also significant. The authors report no meaningful interaction effects for SES×migration background or SES×growth mindset, and they emphasize that cross-sectional PISA data cannot establish causality. Missing data are handled using MLR estimation in Mplus, and the study does not present any machine-learning predictive modeling or accuracy-type metrics.
null_fields_interpretation: This is an empirical multilevel regression study using PISA plausible values and Rubin’s combining rules, not a machine-learning predictive modeling paper. Consequently, no ML algorithms are trained or evaluated, so ml_techniques.primary is intentionally null and all_techniques is empty. The extraction still reports substantive multilevel regression findings for reading and mathematics achievement.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used Sweden’s PISA 2018 student sample (students aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) from the OECD PISA microdata. title: Exploring the effect of digitization on education: An empirical analysis based on PISA 2022
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata (student questionnaire and ICT-related items) and constructs latent/scale variables from questionnaire items (e.g., IC172, ST326, ST273, ST283, ST272). The manuscript reports selecting 53,908 valid cases after deleting questionnaires with missing/invalid/inapplicable responses, but it does not describe the use of PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure. Because the analysis is conducted with SmartPLS (bootstrap-based path significance testing) rather than an explicit survey-weighted estimation workflow, the paper does not document whether complex survey design weights were applied; therefore, weighting cannot be verified from the provided text. Analysts using the PISA database should apply the official PISA student/sampling weights (and replicate weights if required by the software/workflow) when estimating population-representative effects, especially given the multistage school-based sampling design.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables in this study are questionnaire-based constructs (digitization level, teaching behavior, learning level, and perceived quality of math instruction), not PISA cognitive achievement scores reported via PVs. The paper does not provide a detailed missingness mechanism or item-level missingness rates, so the impact of listwise deletion on bias and representativeness cannot be assessed from the excerpt.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2022 questionnaire data to model how education digitization relates to educational effectiveness, using digitization construction (IC172) and digitization application (ST326) as predictors, teaching behavior (ST283) and learning level (ST273) as mediators, and perceived math instruction quality (ST272) as the effectiveness outcome. title: Discrimination of the Contextual Features of Top Performers in Scientific Literacy Using a Machine Learning Approach

The analytic sample is further restricted to students with available student and principal questionnaire responses, and the authors report cleaning to remove a large proportion of missing values. For the binary target (top performers vs non-top performers), the authors explicitly state that PISA student sampling weights were fully considered to obtain unbiased population estimates. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the ML pipeline (SVM with SVM-RFE and 10-fold cross-validation) is implemented in Python/scikit-learn; thus, the paper’s handling of complex-survey variance estimation for ML metrics is not fully specified beyond the use of PISA weights.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 science literacy for 380,771 secondary students from 58 countries/economies, restricting to those using the computer-based science assessment components and using only student and principal questionnaires. The authors apply SVM with SVM-RFE to rank 141 contextual variables and select an optimal top-20 feature set, then evaluate classification via 10-fold cross-validation. The top-20 set achieves about 69.52% accuracy in the initial selection stage and 77.50% (recall 78.48%) and 75.80% (recall 76.39%) in two follow-up 10-fold CV rounds. title: A scoping review of the relationship between students’ ICT and performance in mathematics and science in the PISA data
authors: Maria Cutumisu; Bryce Odell; Mark Gierl
weight_fields_interpretation: This article is a scoping literature review that synthesizes secondary quantitative studies using PISA data (2000–2015) rather than re-analyzing a student-level dataset. Because no original PISA microdata are analyzed in this review, there is no reported application of PISA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) within the review’s own analyses. The included studies vary in their analytic approaches (e.g., HLM, MLR, SEM, propensity score matching), and the review does not standardize or re-compute weighted estimates across studies. For interpreting the synthesized findings, readers should consult each primary study’s documentation for how PISA’s complex survey design and plausible-value scaling were handled.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because this work is a scoping review that does not conduct an original empirical analysis of PISA achievement scores. Instead, it summarizes results reported in 25 secondary publications that used PISA ICT Familiarity Questionnaire variables as predictors and mathematics/science outcomes as reported by those studies. Missing-data handling is not reported at the review level because the review does not fit models to a pooled dataset; it only aggregates conclusions from prior papers.
outcome_summary: This scoping review synthesizes 25 secondary quantitative studies that used PISA data (2000–2015) and the PISA ICT Familiarity Questionnaire to examine how students’ ICT interactions relate to mathematics and science performance for 15-year-olds. title: Factors affecting teacher job satisfaction: a causal inference machine learning approach using data from TALIS 2018
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the English subset of TALIS 2018, restricting the full international teacher/principal dataset to England and to primary and lower-secondary teachers (total n=4385). To obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors, the authors applied TALIS sampling weights and used the Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR) procedure described in the TALIS technical report. This indicates complex survey design handling rather than a simple unweighted analysis. Missingness in questionnaire variables was addressed via missRanger imputation before fitting the causal BART models, but the authors note that imputation uncertainty is not fully propagated into the main analysis, implying slightly optimistic confidence intervals.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is a continuous teacher job satisfaction scale constructed from eight Likert items using confirmatory factor analysis by TALIS organisers, rather than a PV-based cognitive achievement score. Missing data handling is reported: the authors imputed missing responses using missRanger (a single imputation approach) to retain cases, but they explicitly state that uncertainty from imputation is not captured in the main analysis, which may widen true intervals.
outcome_summary: The study applies causal inference machine learning using the bartCause package with Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) to estimate average treatment effects on a continuous teacher job satisfaction scale in the English subset of TALIS 2018 (n=4385 teachers; 2009 primary, 2376 lower-secondary). The authors define multiple binary “treatments” (e.g., CPD participation in the past year, induction at a new school, observing other teachers, team teaching, mentoring, public school, class size threshold, out-of-field teaching, and part-time contracts) and estimate each treatment’s ATE independently while controlling for a common covariate set and including a propensity score estimated via BART. sample_filtering_criteria: Used the TALIS 2018 dataset restricted to England only, including primary and lower-secondary teachers (2009 primary teachers and 2376 lower-secondary teachers). The outcome is teacher job satisfaction measured from eight Likert items combined into a continuous scale by TALIS organisers. title: A decade of PISA: student perceived instructional quality and mathematics achievement across European countries
authors: Xin Liu; Kajsa Yang Hansen; Martin Valcke; Jan De Neve

Mathematics achievement is handled via PISA plausible values (five PVs in 2012; ten PVs in 2022) estimated in Mplus using TYPE=IMPUTATION and then averaged across PV datasets, which is the standard approach for PV-based achievement modeling. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the structural models; instead, it focuses on measurement invariance and uses Mplus TYPE=COMPLEX to adjust standard errors and chi-square statistics for clustering. Because survey-weight variables are not explicitly named or used, readers should treat the results as model-based associations rather than fully design-weighted population estimates unless weights are confirmed in the full methods section.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2012 and PISA 2022 mathematics data for 15-year-olds in ten European education systems (Belgium-Flanders, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden). Mathematics achievement is modeled using PISA plausible values (five PVs in 2012; ten PVs in 2022) with Mplus TYPE=IMPUTATION and averaged estimates, and the structural models are estimated with Mplus TYPE=COMPLEX to adjust standard errors for clustering. Across both cycles, teacher support and disciplinary climate show positive associations with mathematics achievement, and cognitive activation is beneficial overall, but its sub-dimensions in 2022 diverge: encouraging mathematical thinking is often negative while fostering reasoning is positive. SES has significant direct effects and also indirect effects through instructional quality dimensions, with patterns that consistently benefit low-SES students for teacher support, disciplinary climate, and reasoning-based cognitive activation. Limitations include the absence of explicit reporting on survey-weight application and the correlational nature of SEM paths (no causal identification).
null_fields_interpretation: The manuscript reports structural equation modeling (CFA/SEM) and trend analyses rather than training/evaluating machine learning predictive models; therefore, no ML algorithms are extracted (ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty and primary is null). title: Cross-Cultural Comparisons of the Factors Influencing the High Reading Achievement in Turkey and China: Evidence from PISA 2018

The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML steps (Random Forest feature selection and ARF subgroup identification), so it is unclear whether complex survey design was accounted for in estimation. title: Sampling weights in multilevel modelling: an investigation using PISA sampling structures
weight_fields_interpretation: The study is based on PISA’s two-stage stratified cluster sampling (schools sampled first via PPS with stratification, then students sampled within schools). It discusses and operationalizes PISA sampling weights at both levels: final student weights (combining school and student selection probabilities with non-response adjustments) and final school weights (level-two weights reflecting school selection probabilities adjusted for school non-response). In the simulation and application, the authors compare multiple ways of incorporating these weights into two-level multilevel models, including scenarios with no weights, unscaled weights, and several scaling rules for level-one (student) weights, while keeping level-two (school) weights as the key component. The recommended approach is to use only the final school weights at level two (i.e., no student-level weights at level one), because this best recovers population parameters under the simulated PISA sampling structure; the paper does not report replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) as part of the estimation.
handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not perform missing-data imputation for student-level outcomes; instead, it focuses on how sampling weights are incorporated into two-level multilevel models under simulated PISA sampling and non-response mechanisms. Missingness is handled through simulated non-response adjustments (e.g., student participation probabilities by grade and gender) rather than through an explicit missing-data imputation strategy for analysis variables. Therefore, a standard missing-data handling label (e.g., listwise deletion or multiple imputation) is not applicable as a documented procedure for the analysis dataset.
outcome_summary: This methodology paper investigates how to incorporate PISA sampling weights into two-level multilevel (hierarchical) models, using both simulation and an application to PISA 2015 data for Germany. The authors simulate a German PISA-like population with two-stage stratified cluster sampling (schools sampled via PPS with stratification; students sampled within schools) and generate student achievement (PISA competence in science) and socioeconomic background (ESCS) under three scenarios differing in between-school variance (ICC 0.05, 0.52, 0.79). They compare nine weighting scenarios (e.g., no weights, unscaled weights, only student weights, only school weights, and several scaling rules for student weights) across three two-level model specifications, estimating parameters and their uncertainty using pseudo maximum likelihood with sandwich-type variance estimation in two software packages (Mplus and SAS PROC GLIMMIX). Across scenarios, the recommended approach is to use only final school weights at level two; scaling of student weights yields nearly identical results when school weights are used, and software differences are small under the recommended weighting scheme. The study is not a predictive ML analysis; its key contribution is methodological guidance for valid multilevel inference under complex LSA sampling designs.
null_fields_interpretation: This is a simulation/methodology investigation of weighting and estimation procedures for multilevel models rather than a machine-learning predictive study. As a result, there is no ML target variable with predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) and no ML algorithm training/evaluation pipeline to extract; consequently, ml_techniques is empty and main_findings is left as an empty array per the schema rules for non-ML methodological papers. title: The influence of ICT use and related attitudes on students’ math and science performance: multilevel analyses of the last decade’s PISA surveys
authors: Matthew Courtney; Mehmet Karakus; Ersozlu; Nurumov
weight_fields_interpretation: The study merges student and school data from PISA 2009, 2012, 2015, and 2018 for countries that administered the ICT questionnaire modules. Analytic samples exclude schools with fewer than ten students and account for missing ICT-related data, yielding cycle-specific totals of students and schools. To make countries contribute equally, the authors use “senate weights” and then rescale them within each country so the sum of student senate weights equals 5000 per country (constant computed using the number of students in the final analyses after missing-data accounting). The manuscript reports using normalized weights in all multilevel models; replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is not described, and the analysis is implemented in R using lme4 maximum-likelihood estimation.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes four PISA cycles (2009, 2012, 2015, 2018) using merged student and school data to examine how ICT availability, ICT use (inside and outside school), and ICT-related attitudes relate to mathematics and science achievement. Achievement is modeled using PISA plausible values, and the authors fit three-level linear mixed-effects models with students nested in schools and schools nested in countries, using maximum likelihood estimation. They report that ICT availability and ICT use are generally neutral or negatively associated with math and science performance, while ICT attitudes and beliefs—particularly perceived autonomy related to ICT use—show the strongest positive associations (e.g., autonomy coefficients around b≈8.93–9.43 for math and b≈10.20–11.90 for science in 2015/2018). The models explain up to about 9.5% of student-level residual variance, and country-level GDP per capita shows inconsistent associations (significant mainly in 2012). Because PISA is cross-sectional and ICT questionnaire items vary across cycles, the results support associations rather than causal claims.
null_fields_interpretation: The paper does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models; it uses three-level linear mixed-effects modeling with plausible values. Therefore, ML technique fields are intentionally empty (no ML algorithms to extract), while the study still provides substantive multilevel association results across PISA cycles.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used merged PISA 2009, 2012, 2015, and 2018 student and school datasets for countries that opted into the ICT survey modules. For each cycle, schools with fewer than ten students were removed. The authors also account for missing ICT-related data (and other variables used in the models), and the senate weights are rescaled using the number of students included in the final analyses after accounting for missing data. Analyses are run separately by year and subject (math/science) using all available plausible values for that cycle.

title: Factors predicting mathematics achievement in PISA: a systematic review
authors: Sarah Wang; L. P.; A. M.; T. I.
weight_fields_interpretation: This study is a systematic literature review of peer-reviewed articles analyzing PISA mathematics achievement; it does not conduct a new student-level analysis of PISA microdata. Therefore, there is no application of PISA sampling weights (e.g., student weights) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) within this review. Instead, the review synthesizes reported associations across primary studies that used different analytical approaches and (in some cases) different missing-data and significance-threshold decisions. For interpreting the synthesized findings, readers should note that differences in how primary studies handled complex survey design and plausible values can contribute to mixed results across factors.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because this paper does not estimate PISA mathematics achievement from student-level plausible values; it synthesizes results from 156 previously published studies. Missing-data handling is not reported at the review level because the authors do not re-analyze microdata and instead summarize associations reported in the included primary studies, each of which may have used different missing-data strategies.
outcome_summary: This paper is a PRISMA-guided systematic review synthesizing 156 peer-reviewed studies that investigated predictors of PISA mathematics achievement. The included primary studies analyzed PISA mathematics scores from multiple PISA cycles (2000, 2003, 2006, 2009, 2012, 2015, 2018), with most studies using PISA 2012 and fewer examining multiple cycles. Across the synthesized evidence, the authors identify 135 factors grouped into five ecological levels and report seven factors that are consistently associated with math achievement: student grade level and overall family SES (positive), and absenteeism/lack of punctuality, grade repetition and dropout rate, school misbehavior prevalence, shortages of teachers/general staff, and student-centered instruction (negative). The review also reports 14 factors with predominantly positive or negative associations, while many others show mixed findings due to methodological differences across studies (e.g., measures, analytical methods, missing-data handling, and significance thresholds). Because this is a review rather than a re-analysis, no single predictive model, accuracy metric, or causal identification strategy is estimated here; the findings should be interpreted as patterns of association across heterogeneous studies rather than as causal effects.
null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to student-level ML and sampling because the article is a systematic review rather than an empirical analysis of PISA microdata. As a result, there is no analytic sample of students, no country-level per-cell Ns, no plausible-values estimation procedure, and no ML model training/evaluation reported by the authors themselves. The review synthesizes reported associations from included studies, so fields tied to predictive modeling performance and survey-weighted estimation are not applicable at the review level.
sample_filtering_criteria: No student-level PISA sample is analyzed by the authors. The review includes peer-reviewed English-language journal articles published between 1 September 2011 and 30 September 2021 (with a second screening window 31 August 2021 to 1 July 2022) that examined factors predicting PISA mathematics performance using any main PISA cycle (2000, 2003, 2006, 2009, 2012, 2015, 2018). title: Mediating effects of motivation and socioeconomic status on reading achievement: a secondary analysis of PISA 2018
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 reading literacy scores for 15-year-olds from 38 European countries (n=237,366) and runs uni-level SEM models separately within each country using EQS 6.4. For the reading achievement outcome, the authors report that they considered only the student weights in the analysis to account for different sampling probabilities, while conducting uni-level SEM (students nested within schools acknowledged but not modeled with multilevel SEM). The paper does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that student weights were used. No replicate-weight procedure (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is mentioned, and the analysis is not framed as a machine-learning pipeline that would require weight-aware resampling.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper describes plausible value handling for PISA reading (ten plausible values, run 10 times, then averaged with attention to measurement error), but it does not report any explicit strategy for missing data (e.g., listwise/pairwise deletion or imputation). Because the analysis relies on SEM/CFA with multiple questionnaire indicators and a reading PV outcome, missingness could occur at both the item/scale level and the PV level; the absence of a documented missing-data rule is a reporting gap that limits reproducibility.
outcome_summary: This secondary analysis uses PISA 2018 reading literacy for 15-year-olds from 38 European countries (n=237,366) to test a theory-driven mediation model linking ESCS to reading achievement through three motivation elements. Reading achievement is based on ten PISA plausible values; the authors run the analysis across plausible values and average results while accounting for measurement error, and they use student weights to address sampling probabilities. Within each country, CFA and multigroup CFA are used to validate the measurement structure, but metric invariance is not supported, so mediation is estimated separately by country using uni-level SEM in EQS 6.4. The mediation results show that expected occupational status mediates the SES–reading relationship in all countries, enjoyment of reading in 37/38, and mastery-approach orientation in 11/38, with the direct SES effect reduced in all models. Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causal inference) and a missing-data strategy that is not reported.
sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample includes 15-year-old students who participated in PISA 2018 reading. The authors restrict the analysis to European countries: from 41 PISA 2018 participating countries, 38 provided sufficient data for the study, yielding 237,366 students. The paper does not specify additional exclusions beyond the requirement of sufficient data for the mediation model; it also acknowledges that CFA/SEM were conducted within each country and that mediators were excluded when they were not statistically significant in the mediation paths.

title: Does teachers’ motivation have an impact on students’ scientific literacy and motivation? An empirical study in Colombia with data from PISA 2015
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for Colombia, with students nested within schools, and applies a multilevel modeling framework. For the hierarchical models, the authors report that only the final school weights (W_SCHGRNRABWT) were applied at level two, following recommendations for two-level modeling with PISA. The manuscript does not clearly state whether student-level sampling weights were also applied; therefore, student-weight usage is not explicitly documented. Plausible values for science were handled by running analyses across the ten PVs and aggregating results, which is consistent with PISA scaling practice; no additional preprocessing exclusions beyond the multilevel/PV workflow are described.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper describes how plausible values (ten PVs for science) were analyzed and aggregated, but it does not report a specific missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise/pairwise deletion or imputation) for questionnaire or PV-related variables. Given PISA’s complex survey design and typical item nonresponse, this omission is a reporting gap that prevents assessing potential bias from missingness patterns.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 microdata for Colombia (8095 students, 313 schools, 1314 science teachers) to examine whether teachers’ motivation affects students’ scientific literacy and intrinsic motivation, framed by Self-Determination Theory. Using two-level hierarchical linear modeling, the authors regressed students’ science plausible-value achievement (ten PVs aggregated across PVs) and an intrinsic motivation index on student, teacher, and school variables, with teacher variables aggregated to the school level. For scientific literacy, teacher motivation showed no significant association (β = -4.37, p = 0.372), while directed science instruction (β = 56.35, p < 0.001) and school ESCS (β = 21.18, p < 0.001) were significant predictors. For intrinsic motivation, teacher motivation was again non-significant (β = -0.102, p = 0.462), but inquiry-based teaching was positively associated (β = 0.631, p = 0.020). Limitations include cross-sectional inference (no causal identification) and the use of job satisfaction as a proxy for teacher intrinsic motivation, plus missing-data handling not being reported.
null_fields_interpretation: The paper uses multilevel hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) rather than machine-learning predictive algorithms; therefore, the ML technique fields are intentionally empty. Because the extraction is not an ML-prediction study, plausible values are handled for the achievement outcome, but no ML model selection/accuracy metrics apply.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 Colombia student, teacher, and school responses (8095 students; 1314 science teachers; 313 schools). Teacher-level variables were aggregated to the school level and merged into the student file; scientific literacy was analyzed using the ten science plausible values for each student. No additional analytic exclusions (e.g., missing-variable rules) are explicitly described in the provided text.
effect_size: Two-level hierarchical linear model (HLM). Teacher motivation effect: β = -4.37, p = 0.372. Directed instruction effect: β = 56.35, p < 0.001. Inquiry-based teaching effect: β = -16.67, p = 0.092. School ESCS effect: β = 21.18, p < 0.001. Teacher support effect: β = -23.66, p = 0.036. Model variance decomposition (unconditional): 28.1% between schools, 71.9% within schools.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 Colombia Grade 15 Science the study leveraged directed science instruction (TDTEACH), school ESCS (ESCSSCHO), inquiry-based teaching (IBTEACH), science self-efficacy (SCIEEFF), and teacher motivation (TEACHMOT) to model students’ scientific literacy (PVSCIE), finding no significant relationship between teacher motivation and scientific literacy (β = -4.37, p = 0.372). This indicates that, at least with the job-satisfaction proxy available in PISA 2015, policy efforts solely targeting teacher motivation may not translate into higher science achievement, while instructional practice and school socioeconomic context show stronger associations.

title: Metacognitive reading strategies and its relationship with Filipino high school students’ reading proficiency: insights from the PISA 2018 data
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Philippines national sample from PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) and reports descriptive statistics “using sampling weights,” indicating complex survey weighting was applied in at least some analyses. The analytic sample is restricted to students with complete data on the main variables (metacognitive strategy usefulness items) and the control variables (sex, ESCS, number of books at home), yielding 6591 students out of the full 7233. For reading outcomes, the authors use PISA plausible values (PV1) for overall reading proficiency and for three cognitive process subscales, treating these as the dependent variables in hierarchical regression models. The manuscript does not report the specific weight variable name or replicate-weight method, so replicate-weight-based inference cannot be confirmed from the provided text.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes the Philippines’ PISA 2018 reading data for 15-year-olds (analytic sample N=6591) to examine how perceived usefulness of 11 metacognitive reading strategies relates to reading proficiency in English as a second language. Reading proficiency is operationalized using PISA plausible values, specifically PV1 for overall reading and for three cognitive process subscales (locate information, understand, and evaluate/reflect). Using hierarchical regression with controls for gender, ESCS, and number of books at home, the authors report that adding the 11 strategy usefulness items explains an additional 18% of variance in overall reading proficiency (final R2=0.40; ΔR2=0.18). For subscales, the incremental variance is ΔR2=0.16 (locate information), ΔR2=0.18 (understand), and ΔR2=0.14 (evaluate/reflect), all with p<0.001. Limitations include reliance on perceived usefulness (which may reflect teacher/classmate messaging rather than actual strategy use) and the use of single PVs, so results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Philippines PISA 2018 nationally representative sample of 15-year-olds (complete nationally representative sample: 7233). The analysis was restricted to participants with complete data on all main variables (11 metacognitive reading strategy usefulness items) and control variables (sex, ESCS, number of books at home), resulting in a final analytic sample of 6591 students.
effect_size: Hierarchical regression: Model R2 = 0.40 (final); baseline R2 = 0.22; additional explained variance by adding 11 strategies: ΔR2 = 0.18, ΔF = 181.28***. Strategy-level standardized coefficients (β) reported for each of the 11 items; overall model F(14, 6576) = 292.50*** (from reported hierarchical regression summary).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for Filipino 15-year-olds (PV1 for overall reading proficiency), the study leveraged Gender, ESCS, number of books at home, and perceived usefulness of 11 metacognitive reading strategies to predict overall reading proficiency, finding that adding the 11 strategies explained an additional 18% of the variance (ΔR2 = 0.18) beyond the controls. This indicates that metacognitive strategy awareness is meaningfully associated with reading achievement in English as a second language, suggesting that reading instruction and assessment alignment should explicitly teach and model effective strategies while also addressing students’ miscalibrated perceptions of strategy usefulness (e.g., some low-level or ineffective strategies were rated as useful yet were negatively associated with proficiency).
confounders: Gender; Socioeconomic status (ESCS); Number of books at home

title: Similarities and differences in social and emotional profiles among students in Canada, USA, China, and Singapore
authors: Virginia M. C. Tze; Johnson C.-H. Li; Lia M. Daniels
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata from four countries (Canada, United States, China, Singapore) and focuses on students in the computer-based assessment mode who completed the Collaborative Problem-Solving (CPS) assessment. For achievement outcomes (reading, mathematics, CPS), the authors use OECD-provided plausible values and explicitly compute composite scores as the mean of the 10 plausible values per domain. The paper does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the latent profile estimation or BCH comparisons; therefore, the weighting strategy for population-representativeness is not documented. Analysts using the same PISA extracts should apply PISA complex survey weights when estimating country-level means or uncertainty, but this manuscript’s latent-profile/BCH workflow is primarily described in terms of PV averaging and Mplus estimation rather than explicit weight variables.
outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2015 microdata from four countries (Canada, United States, China, Singapore) restricted to students in the computer-based assessment mode who completed the Collaborative Problem-Solving (CPS) assessment. The authors operationalize four CASEL social-emotional competencies using selected PISA Likert items (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills), test a four-factor measurement model with multigroup CFA, and then estimate latent social-emotional profiles using latent profile analysis (LPA). For achievement outcomes (reading, mathematics, CPS), they use OECD-provided plausible values (10 per domain) and compute student-level composite scores as the mean of the plausible values; profile differences are evaluated using the BCH approach with Wald tests. Across Canada/US/Singapore, the Sociable profile generally shows the highest reading and maths scores and higher CPS than Reserved and Withdrawn, while China shows a different pattern where Solitary and Team-oriented profiles can outperform Reserved depending on the domain. Limitations include reliance on PISA proxies for social-emotional skills (few items per factor) and the absence of explicit reporting of PISA sampling-weight usage in the latent-profile/BCH estimation.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 data restricted to two OECD countries (Canada, United States) and two partner countries (China, Singapore) and further restricted to students participating in the computer-based assessment mode (CBA) who completed the Collaborative Problem-Solving (CPS) assessment. The analytic sample comprises 15-year-old students (born 1999–2000) from these four countries; all selected students completed the student background questionnaire. For achievement outcomes, the authors used OECD-provided plausible values for reading, mathematics, and CPS and then derived student-level composite scores by averaging the 10 plausible values per domain. Missing data in the latent-variable estimation was handled using Mplus default estimation with Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML).
effect_size: BCH/Wald tests of mean differences among latent profiles (p-values reported). Canada/USA/Singapore: Sociable > Reserved and Sociable > Withdrawn (ps < .01); Reserved > Withdrawn on reading and maths in Western countries. Singapore: no significant Sociable vs Reserved difference on CPS (not reading); reading differences follow the Western pattern. China: Solitary > Team-oriented and Solitary > Reserved on reading (Wald X2 (1) = 15.398, p < .0001; Reserved vs Solitary: Wald X2 (1) = 59.485, p < .0001).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 (CBA) the study leveraged latent social-emotional profiles derived from self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and relationship skills to compare reading achievement across profiles via the BCH approach. It found that in Canada, the United States, and Singapore the Sociable profile consistently obtained higher reading scores than the Reserved and Withdrawn profiles, with Reserved also outperforming Withdrawn on reading. This indicates that aligning social-emotional learning messages with culturally appropriate expectations may support reading achievement, though the direction of profile–achievement associations differs in China (Solitary outperforms Team-oriented and Reserved), limiting simple “more is better” policy generalizations.
confounders: Self-awareness (PISA proxies); Self-management (PISA proxies); Social awareness (PISA proxies); Relationship skills (PISA proxies)

title: From Meals to Marks: Modeling the Impact of Family Involvement on Reading Performance with Counterfactual Explainable AI
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for the United Arab Emirates (UAE), drawing on both reading achievement and student background questionnaire items. The analytic sample is described as 24,600 students in the UAE, and the dependent variable is the PISA reading plausible value (READING). The methodology reports handling missing data via listwise deletion and does not mention applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the ML training, SHAP computation, or counterfactual simulations. Because the paper applies standard ML regressors (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and MLP) using scikit-learn and does not discuss complex survey design adjustments, the analysis is treated as unweighted; this is a limitation given PISA’s clustered sampling design.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 UAE data (n=24,600) to predict reading achievement (READING plausible value) from ten family-engagement questionnaire variables. Three ML regressors were trained (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and an MLP neural network) using an 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation on the training set and hyperparameter tuning via GridSearchCV. Gradient Boosting performed best, with test R² ≈ 0.1879 (MAE=90.29; RMSE=111.61) and CV R² (mean) ≈ 0.1882, while Random Forest showed lower test R² (0.1342). SHAP interpretation of the Gradient Boosting model indicated that EATMEAL, SPENDTALK, and DISSWELL were the strongest predictors. Counterfactual simulations (holding other variables at medians) suggested that increasing SPENDTALK from 1 to 5 could raise predicted reading scores by about 89.75 points (95% CI [85.2, 94.3]) and increasing EATMEAL by about 84.61 points (95% CI [80.1, 89.1]); the authors caution that these are quasi-causal simulations rather than causal identification.
ml_all_techniques: Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Neural Network
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 UAE student microdata (15-year-olds) and modeled reading achievement using the PISA reading plausible value (READING). Missing data were handled using listwise deletion prior to exploratory analysis and model training, ensuring consistency across model training, SHAP analysis, and counterfactual simulations. No additional grade/school-type restrictions are reported beyond the PISA 2022 15-year-old sample and the inclusion of the ten family-engagement predictors.
effect_size: Gradient Boosting (GBR) — Test R²: 0.1879, Test MAE: 90.29, Test RMSE: 111.61; CV R² (mean): 0.1882. Random Forest — Test R²: 0.1342, Test MAE: 92.42, Test RMSE: 115.24. Neural Network — Test R²: 0.1876, Test MAE: 89.96, Test RMSE: 111.63.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 (UAE) reading plausible value the study leveraged family meal frequency, time talking with parents, and discussions about how school is going (plus other family-engagement items) to predict reading achievement, finding that Gradient Boosting achieved the best generalization (R² ≈ 0.188) and that counterfactual increases in SPENDTALK and EATMEAL could raise predicted reading scores by roughly 90 and 85 points respectively; however, the counterfactuals are univariate ceteris paribus simulations and SHAP-based importance is not causal evidence. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

title: Student and school-level factors to predict science literacy for two top-performing countries in PISA 2015 Finland and Singapore
authors: Ulas Ustun; Mustafa Cansiz; Ertugrul Ozdemir; Nurcan Cansiz
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for Finland and Singapore, with students nested within schools, and applies a multilevel modeling strategy (HLM) to account for hierarchical clustering. The manuscript describes PISA’s two-stage stratified random sampling at the country level (schools then students), but it does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme. Because the analysis is model-based (HLM) rather than PV-based ML, the paper does not specify a weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) for complex-survey variance estimation. Analysts using the PISA international database should apply the provided student sampling weights and replicate weights when estimating standard errors and variance components, especially given the school-level nesting and cross-country comparisons.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable (science literacy) is estimated using 10 plausible values in PISA 2015, but the manuscript does not describe the exact combining procedure across plausible values (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or any explicit missing-data strategy for questionnaire/index variables. This is a reporting gap because PISA typically involves nontrivial item nonresponse and missingness in background indices, which can affect multilevel estimates if not handled consistently. The paper therefore provides insufficient transparency to verify how missingness and PV combining were implemented in the final HLM models.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 science literacy for two top-performing countries—Finland and Singapore—using a multilevel (HLM) framework to model students nested within schools. Science literacy is estimated using 10 plausible values, and the models explain about 43% (Finland) and 40% (Singapore) of within-school variance, while between-school variance is substantial in Singapore (ICC = 0.38) compared with Finland (ICC = 0.13). At the student level, affective variables are most influential: interest in broad science topics for Finland and enjoyment of science for Singapore, alongside epistemological beliefs and ESCS. At the school level, the average school ESCS is the strongest predictor in both countries, explaining 61.5% (Finland) and 63.7% (Singapore) of between-school variance. Limitations include the cross-sectional nature of PISA (no causal claims) and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling and the exact plausible-value combining procedure.
null_fields_interpretation: This paper uses hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) rather than machine-learning algorithms from the schema’s ML list, so ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty and primary is left null. The extraction therefore focuses on multilevel predictive modeling results (variance explained and significant predictors) without treating HLM as an ML technique under the provided constraints.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 student sample for the two specified countries (Finland and Singapore). The analytic sample consists of 15-year-old students participating in the science major domain assessment, with students clustered within schools. The paper does not report additional task/module restrictions beyond the PISA 2015 science literacy outcome and the inclusion of the listed student- and school-level indices; it also describes trimming outliers based on standardized residuals (>3) and Mahalanobis distance after fitting HLM.
effect_size: HLM variance explained: 43% of within-school variance; between-school variance explained reported via ICC and variance components (between-school variance proportion ICC = 0.13).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 science literacy data for Finland, the study leveraged interest in broad science topics, epistemological beliefs, science learning time, expected occupational status, and ESCS to predict students’ science literacy (10 plausible values), finding that affective engagement and epistemic beliefs were among the strongest student-level predictors while school ESCS dominated school-level differences. This indicates that policies aiming to strengthen students’ science interest/enjoyment and epistemological understanding—alongside reducing socioeconomic stratification across schools—may support both achievement and equity in high-performing systems, though causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional PISA data.
