title: Educational Data Mining: Identi cation of factors associated with school e ectiveness in PISA assessment
authors: F. Martínez-Abad; Adriana Gamazo; M.-J. Rodríguez-Conde
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for Spain and restricts the analytic sample to students aged 15 within 896 schools (after excluding schools with fewer than 20 participants). For the multilevel phase, the authors state that HLM 7 enabled the use of student and school sample weights to ensure correct representation of the PISA-eligible population, and they apply robust Huber-White adjustments because student replicate weights could not be used. For the decision-tree phase, the unit of analysis is the school, so student-level predictors are aggregated to school means; the authors then weight the decision-tree learning based on the available school sample weights. Missingness is handled within HLM7 at student level (low missing percentages) and via regression imputation at school level (with no missing values in final multilevel models), while the decision-tree algorithm (J48/C4.5 in Weka) uses a weighting approach to route instances with missing predictor values across branches.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 Spain data for 15-year-old students and uses a two-phase school-effectiveness approach. First, multilevel models (HLM 7) estimate expected performance from input variables and compute school residuals to select high- and low-effectiveness schools; the authors report ICCs above 10% for science, mathematics, and reading. Second, the authors train a decision tree (J48/C4.5 in Weka) using school effectiveness (high vs low) as a dichotomous target and process/context variables from PISA 2015 questionnaires as predictors, aggregating student-level variables to the school level. The resulting tree (25 branches, 13 leaves) shows strong performance: global cross-validation COR=0.916, Kappa=0.747, RRSE=0.647, and ROC AUC=0.916, with correct predictions around 87.5%. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and reliance on aggregated predictors, which may mask within-school variability.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2015 Spain sample of 15-year-old students. Excluded all schools with fewer than 20 assessment participants, reducing the sample from 32,330 students and 976 schools to 31,236 students and 896 schools. In phase 2 (decision trees), further restricted to the selected high- and low-efficacy schools, yielding 8,347 students across 239 schools (3,801 in high-efficacy schools; 4,546 in low-efficacy schools).
effect_size: Decision tree (J48/C4.5, Weka): Training set — High: TP=0.906, Precision=0.929, COR=0.947; Low: TP=0.941, Precision=0.922, COR=0.947; Global: Kappa=0.849, RRSE=0.515. Cross-validation (10-fold stratified): Global — COR=0.916, Kappa=0.747, RRSE=0.647; Correct predictions=0.875, ROC AUC=0.916 (high/low maintained at high levels). primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 (Spain) the study leveraged additional lessons (curricular), cooperative learning value, ICT use outside school, reading lesson minutes, and ICT autonomy to classify schools as high- vs low-effectiveness, finding that the decision tree achieved high classification fit (global cross-validation COR=0.916; Kappa=0.747; ROC AUC=0.916). This indicates that school effectiveness in secondary education is strongly associated with a small set of process- and context-related factors (extracurricular academic time, ICT use patterns, and reading time-on-task), suggesting that education authorities can prioritize targeted guidance on instructional time and ICT practices rather than relying only on socioeconomic inputs, while noting the study is cross-sectional and uses aggregated school-level predictors.

title: The mediating–moderating model of inquiry-based learning and science self-efficacy: evidence from PISA 2015
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 student questionnaire constructs that were scaled with Item Response Theory (IRT) and reported as weighted likelihood estimates (WLE) transformed to a mean of 0 and SD of 1 across OECD countries. The sampling design is described as a two-stage stratified design with schools selected using systematic PPS sampling and students selected with equal probability within schools, implying a complex survey structure. However, the manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights (e.g., student design weights) or replicate-weight procedures for variance estimation; instead, it focuses on PROCESS macro mediation/moderation with standardized WLE scores. For replication, analysts should use the official PISA sampling weights and appropriate variance estimation when estimating uncertainty, while treating WLE as the IRT-based scaling of questionnaire constructs rather than a substitute for survey-weighted estimation.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are WLE-based IRT scores from PISA student questionnaires (science self-efficacy, inquiry-based science teaching/learning practices, science interest, teacher support), not achievement plausible values. The paper does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., listwise/pairwise deletion or imputation), so the approach to missing questionnaire responses is not transparent. This is a reporting gap because missingness can affect mediation/moderation estimates in large-scale survey data.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 student questionnaire data from 57 participating countries and economies (N=346,109) to test a mediating–moderating model linking inquiry-based learning to science self-efficacy. The constructs (inquiry-based learning, science interest, science self-efficacy, teacher support) are scaled using IRT and expressed as weighted likelihood estimates (WLE), standardized across OECD countries. Using PROCESS macro mediation (Model 4) and moderated mediation (Model 59) with 5,000 bootstrap samples, the authors report a significant positive total effect of inquiry-based learning on science self-efficacy (B=0.194, p<.001), with partial mediation via science interest (indirect effect B=0.039; 20.1% of total). Teacher support moderates the direct effect positively (B=0.049) but moderates the indirect effect negatively (B=-0.015), yielding R2=0.111 for the self-efficacy outcome model. Limitations include lack of reported missing-data handling and no explicit discussion of applying PISA sampling weights/replicate variance estimation; results are correlations due to cross-sectional data.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 student data from 57 participating countries and economies. The analytic sample includes 346,109 students who had administered questions measuring all variables of interest in the PISA 2015 context questionnaires (inquiry-based learning, science interest, science self-efficacy, teacher support) plus the control variable (disciplinary climate) and demographic gender. The paper does not report additional grade/school-type restrictions beyond the PISA target population of 15-year-old students, nor does it specify an explicit missing-data rule beyond stating that the included sample had measures for all variables of interest.
effect_size: Mediation (PROCESS Model 4, 5,000 bootstraps): total effect B=0.194 (p<.001), direct effect B=0.155 (p<.001), indirect effect B=0.039 (20.1% of total; 95% CI above 0). Moderated mediation (PROCESS Model 59, 5,000 bootstraps): interaction IBTEACH×TEACHSUP predicting science self-efficacy B=0.049 (p<.001); interaction INTBRSCI×TEACHSUP predicting science self-efficacy B=-0.015 (p<.001). Model fit: R2=0.111 for the science self-efficacy outcome model (standardized). Effect size: Cohen’s f2 for final model = 0.125 (small).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) science context questionnaire the study leveraged inquiry-based learning (IBTEACH), science interest (INTBRSCI), and teacher support (TEACHSUP), controlling for disciplinary climate and gender, to model science self-efficacy (SCIEEFF; WLE). It found that inquiry-based learning had a significant positive direct association with science self-efficacy (B=0.155), and that science interest partially mediated this relationship with an indirect effect accounting for 20.1% of the total effect (indirect B=0.039). Teacher support strengthened the direct effect of inquiry-based learning on science self-efficacy (interaction B=0.049) while weakening the indirect pathway through science interest (interaction B=-0.015), indicating a mediating–moderating pattern. This indicates that improving inquiry-based science instruction should be paired with strategies that sustain students’ science interest while leveraging teacher support to maximize self-efficacy gains, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
confounders: Gender; Disciplinary climate (science)

title: Influential factors on mathematical literacy of Turkish students: An educational data mining study using PISA 2015 data.
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata restricted to Turkey’s participating students and then applies a supervised classification pipeline with 10-fold cross-validation. The manuscript does not report whether complex survey sampling weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate weights were applied, nor does it name any weight variables. Because the analysis is based on standard ML classifiers (SVM, Multi-Layer Perceptron, J48, Naïve Bayes), the paper may have proceeded without weight-aware estimation; however, this is not explicitly documented. For replication, analysts should use the official PISA student sampling weights and replicate-weight procedures when estimating performance and uncertainty, and should ensure that any preprocessing (e.g., feature selection/variable filtering) is performed within each cross-validation fold to avoid leakage.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a binary classification of students as successful vs unsuccessful in mathematical literacy, rather than a PV-based achievement score. The paper does not describe any missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically contain missingness in background and questionnaire variables. Without documentation, it is unclear whether missing values were excluded, imputed, or handled via model-specific mechanisms.
outcome_summary: The study classifies Turkish students’ mathematical literacy into successful vs unsuccessful categories using PISA 2015 data and educational data mining classifiers. It evaluates multiple algorithms—Support Vector Machine, Multi-Layer Perceptron, J48 (decision tree), and Naïve Bayes—under 10-fold cross-validation, reporting Precision, Recall, F-measure, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), and ROC. Across methods, the highest ROC value reported is 0.720 (Naïve Bayes), while the lowest precision value reported is 0.645 for the Multi-Layer Perceptron. The most important predictors for classification are learning time per week in total and father’s education level, with additional influential variables drawn from questionnaire scales (e.g., test anxiety, motivation, belonging). The paper does not report a missing-data strategy or whether PISA sampling/replicate weights were used, limiting the interpretability of performance estimates and any policy inference.
ml_all_techniques: Support Vector Machine, Neural Network, Decision Tree, Naive Bayes
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the full available PISA 2015 student sample for Turkey ("all Turkish students who participated in PISA 2015"). The paper reports classification into successful vs unsuccessful mathematical literacy groups and includes grade and questionnaire-derived variables (e.g., learning time, motivation/affect scales), but it does not specify additional task/module restrictions or explicit missing-data exclusions.
effect_size: 10-fold cross-validation. Naïve Bayes — ROC: 0.720 (highest reported ROC); Precision (successful): 0.771; Precision (unsuccessful): 0.543; MCC: 0.318 (successful/unsuccessful). Multi-Layer Perceptron — lowest precision reported: 0.645 (overall table).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 (Turkey) the study leveraged learning time per week (total) and father education level (plus affect/motivation variables such as test anxiety and achievement motivation) to classify students as successful vs unsuccessful in mathematical literacy, finding that learning time per week and father education level were the most important variables and that the highest ROC value reached 0.720. This indicates that strengthening students’ sustained learning time and addressing socioeconomic barriers linked to parental education may improve the likelihood of mathematical literacy success, though the study’s binary classification and limited reporting of weighting/missing-data handling constrain causal interpretation.

title: A Machine Learning Approach to Assess Differential Item Functioning of PISA 2018 ICT Engagement Questionnaire
journal: International Journal of Curriculum and Instruction (IJCI)
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 ICT engagement questionnaire items administered to 15-year-old students in EECA countries (Bulgaria, Georgia, Croatia, Kazakhstan, Turkey). The analytic approach is DIF detection using the GPCMlasso regularization method for generalized partial credit models, which estimates item-level DIF parameters conditional on grouping variables (country, gender, ESCS). The manuscript does not report whether PISA sampling/student weights or replicate weights were applied, nor does it name any weight variables; therefore, weighting cannot be confirmed from the provided text. Analysts using PISA microdata should apply the official PISA student/sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) when estimating DIF parameters to account for the complex survey design; however, this paper’s weighting strategy is not documented.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are DIF indicators/parameters for polytomous ICT engagement questionnaire items (modeled via a generalized partial credit model with lasso regularization), not PV-based cognitive achievement scores. As a result, plausible values are not part of the DIF estimation target in this study. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure for questionnaire responses (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap because DIF estimation can be sensitive to missing item responses.
outcome_summary: This study examines differential item functioning (DIF) for the PISA 2018 ICT engagement questionnaire using a generalized partial credit model with lasso regularization (GPCMlasso). The analytic sample includes 29,277 fifteen-year-old students from EECA countries, focusing on the five ICT-participating countries (Bulgaria, Georgia, Croatia, Kazakhstan, Turkey). DIF was assessed at the item level across four ICT engagement subscales (interest in ICT, perceived ICT competence, perceived ICT autonomy, and social media use) using BIC-selected tuning for the lasso penalty; items were flagged as DIF when grouping-variable coefficients were non-zero and/or coefficient paths crossed the optimal λ line. Results indicate that only items 10 and 11 are completely DIF-free, while DIF is pervasive by country, present for gender with both male- and female-favoring items, and comparatively rare for ESCS (about 3/21 items). The paper does not report missing-data handling or whether PISA sampling/replicate weights were applied, limiting the precision and generalizability of DIF prevalence estimates.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 ICT engagement questionnaire responses from EECA countries, focusing on the five countries that participated in the ICT questionnaire (Bulgaria, Georgia, Croatia, Kazakhstan, Turkey). The sample comprises 15-year-old students (total N=29,277) and includes gender and ESCS as covariates for DIF detection. The paper reports gender-specific frequencies and ESCS means/SDs in Table 1 for the five ICT-participating countries; it does not specify additional exclusions beyond the ICT-questionnaire participation restriction.
countries_formatted: AZE; BLR; BGR (2574); HRV (4835); GEO (2613); KAZ (13775); MDA; ROU; TUR (5480); UKR
effect_size: GPCMlasso coefficients with BIC-selected tuning parameter λ; DIF diagnosed when lasso coefficients for grouping variables are non-zero and/or coefficient paths cross the optimal λ line. Reported counts: 2/21 items show DIF overall by country+gender+ESCS; by country all items except items 10 and 11 are DIF-flagged (only items 10,11 completely DIF-free). Additional analysis (Country-pair DIF burden relative to Bulgaria (reference group)): Reported DIF proportions based on GPCMlasso coefficients (Bulgaria reference): Georgia 28%, Croatia 71%, Kazakhstan 33%, Turkey 33% of all items hold DIF. Pairwise comparison narrative: most DIF-prone items between Bulgaria and Croatia; fewest between Bulgaria and Georgia.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 ICT engagement questionnaire data from EECA countries, the study leveraged Country (dummy-coded with Bulgaria as reference), Gender (male vs female), and ESCS to assess uniform DIF across 21 polytomous ICT items via GPCMlasso, finding that nearly all items exhibit DIF by country while only a small subset shows DIF by ESCS and a larger subset shows DIF by gender. This indicates that cross-country comparisons of ICT engagement using these items may be biased unless country-specific measurement non-equivalence is addressed (e.g., through DIF-aware scoring or revised item sets), though the study is descriptive and does not establish causal effects.
confounders: Country (EECA); dummy-coded; Gender (male vs female); Economic; social; cultural status (ESCS)

title: School effectiveness and high reading achievement of Spanish students in PISA 2018: a machine learning approach
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Spain and defines the analytic sample as Spanish students aged 15–16, with a further restriction for the multilevel logistic regression stage (schools with more than 20 students). The authors report imputing missing values via multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) and then standardising continuous predictors before fitting models. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the ML stage (Random Forest in H2O) is described without any weight-aware estimation. Therefore, readers should treat the results as conditional on the modelling choices and preprocessing described, rather than as fully population-representative estimates unless weights are applied in the underlying PISA dataset extraction pipeline.
outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of PISA 2018 reading for Spain, defining “high performance” as reaching reading levels 5–6 and modelling it as a dichotomous outcome. For variable selection and ranking, it trains a Random Forest classifier in H2O using 10-fold cross-validation and evaluates performance across plausible values, selecting PV9 as the most accurate (AUC = 0.827). It then estimates multilevel binary logistic regression models (student level 1; school level 2) after excluding schools with 20 or fewer students, using robust standard errors and reporting odds ratios and explained variance (PEV). Context-only predictors explained about 41% of variance, process-only predictors about 38–41%, and the combined model about 54.676% (PEV ≈ 54.356%). The authors emphasize that metacognition: credibility assessment is the strongest predictor (OR ≈ 1.989), but they also note that results cannot be interpreted causally and that questionnaire-based constructs may have validity limitations.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 database and restricted to Spanish students (initially 35,943). For the Random Forest stage, the entire dataset was utilised after preprocessing; for the multilevel binary logistic regression stage, schools with 20 or fewer students were omitted, yielding a refined sample of 34,411 students across 976 schools. The outcome was dichotomised as high reading performance (PISA reading level 5–6) vs average/low (levels below 5), with 1,797 high-performing students and 34,146 low/average in the Spanish sample. Predictors were reduced from 159 to 137 by removing variables with over 20% missingness, except learning-time variables (LMMINS, MMINS, SMINS) which were retained despite ~24–25% missingness; missing values were then imputed using MICE.
effect_size: Random Forest (H2O) — best PV selected as PV9 with AUC = 0.827; contextual-only set (15 variables) AUC = 0.839 (Accuracy = 0.952); multilevel logistic regression explained variance: context-only PEV = 38.258% and process-only PEV = 40.909% (zero-inflated baseline PEV = 40.909); full model PEV ≈ 54.356% with odds ratio for METASPAM ≈ 1.989 (model 3).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for Spanish students, the study leveraged enjoyment of reading (JOYREAD) and metacognition (especially credibility assessment, METASPAM), along with reading self-concept and learning time, to predict high reading performance (Level 5–6). It found that process variables dominated relative importance and that the full context+process model explained about 54% of reading success, with METASPAM showing the largest effect (roughly twice the effect of key context/input indices). This indicates that strengthening reading enjoyment and metacognitive instruction (e.g., teaching students to evaluate text credibility) may increase the proportion of high-performing readers in Spain, though the study is correlational and cannot establish causality.

title: Identifying Key Predictors of Resilience in Mathematics Engagement: Global Evidence From PISA 2022 Using Machine Learning
authors: Xu Wei; Yuxin Liu; Kan Guo
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata and restricts the analytic sample to students whose ESCS is in the bottom quartile within each of 80 economies, yielding 153,412 students. The dependent variable is a binary resilience indicator based on ESCS quartile membership and top-quartile mathematics engagement (MATHPERS) within each economy. For model training and evaluation, the authors report applying final student weights (W_FSTUWT) to account for PISA’s complex sampling design, and they stratify the sample by the dependent-variable category before splitting into training and test sets. In addition, missing values were imputed prior to modeling using iterative imputation by chained equations; the paper also notes that Table 1 means/SDs were calculated without applying weights, but the predictive modeling used weights.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 mathematics engagement resilience among socioeconomically disadvantaged students (ESCS bottom quartile within each economy), defining resilience as those whose mathematics engagement (MATHPERS) is in the top quartile within the same economy. Using 153,412 students from 80 economies, the authors trained three tree-based ensemble classifiers—Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM—on 115 predictors (including PV1MATH as a candidate feature) with 5-fold cross-validation and a 7:3 train/test split. Model discrimination was assessed primarily with AUC due to class imbalance (~1:3.69): Random Forest achieved the highest AUC (0.7616), outperforming XGBoost (0.7396) and LightGBM (0.7480), and exceeding a logistic regression baseline (AUC 0.7384). Accumulated local effects (ALE) plots from Random Forest revealed non-linear/threshold patterns, including diminishing returns for key predictors and a non-linear school-size effect. The paper is explicitly predictive rather than causal, and it uses imputation for missing values and applies PISA sampling weights (W_FSTUWT) for the modeling stage.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 student and school questionnaire data and restricted to students whose ESCS falls in the bottom quartile within each economy (socioeconomically disadvantaged). Engagement resilience was then defined within each economy as ESCS bottom-quartile students whose mathematics engagement (MATHPERS) ranks in the top 25% among all students in that economy; these were coded as resilient (1). The remaining students from the bottom ESCS quartile were coded as non-resilient (0). Missing values were imputed via iterative chained equations before training/testing; the paper does not report additional grade/school-type restrictions beyond the PISA 15-year-old target population.
effect_size: Random Forest (best): AUC = 0.7616; XGBoost: AUC = 0.7396; LightGBM: AUC = 0.7480. Logistic regression baseline (12 predictors): AUC = 0.7384. Cross-validation: 5-fold; train/test split: 7:3; class imbalance ratio ~1:3.69; performance primarily evaluated via AUC.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 the study leveraged perseverance, curiosity, mathematics self-efficacy, mathematics anxiety, and familiarity with mathematical concepts (among other multi-level predictors) to predict mathematics engagement resilience, finding that higher perseverance/curiosity/self-efficacy/familiarity and lower mathematics anxiety were associated with a higher probability of being classified as engagement-resilient. This indicates that equity-oriented interventions for disadvantaged students should prioritize socioemotional supports and math-related beliefs (e.g., anxiety reduction and self-efficacy building), while recognizing the analysis is predictive (not causal) and relies on cross-sectional PISA data.

title: Cognitive and non-cognitive efficiency gaps between private and public schools and their determinant
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 school-level efficiency analysis for nine Latin American countries, constructing school averages from student and school questionnaires and then estimating DEA efficiency scores separately for private and public schools. The analytic sample is restricted to schools with complete inputs/outputs for the DEA formulations (including non-cognitive soft-skills outcomes), resulting in 2,034 schools (1,548 public; 486 private). The manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures in the DEA or the second-stage ML; therefore, weighting strategy is not documented. In the second stage, the authors train binary classifiers (logit, neural networks, gradient boosted trees) with stratified 5-fold cross-validation and select models using AUROC and AUPRC; these ML methods are typically run without native survey-weight incorporation, and the paper does not specify any weight-aware training or post-stratification corrections.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in the second stage are binary indicators derived from DEA technical efficiency scores (above vs. below the regional mean), not directly from PV-based achievement scores. While PISA achievement inputs are used to construct school-average cognitive outputs, the paper does not document how missing item responses or any PV-related missingness were handled when building those school-level outputs, which is a reporting gap for transparency. Because the analysis relies on aggregated school measures and DEA/ML rather than explicitly reported PV estimation procedures, the missing-data strategy is not clearly traceable from the text provided.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2022 school-level data from nine Latin American countries (2,034 schools) to estimate DEA technical efficiency separately for private and public schools, using two output sets: cognitive outputs (school-average math/reading/science) and non-cognitive outputs (a soft-skills well-being index). It finds a sizable cognitive efficiency gap favoring private schools (mean TEBC 0.865 vs 0.768; gap ≈ 0.10) and a smaller non-cognitive gap (0.685 vs 0.640; gap ≈ 0.045). To explain determinants, the author converts DEA efficiency into a binary outcome (top half vs bottom half) and trains interpretable ML classifiers (logit, neural networks, and gradient boosted trees/XGBoost), selecting the best model by AUROC and AUPRC with stratified 5-fold cross-validation. SHAP is used for global and local interpretability, highlighting home learning resources, school autonomy, climate, repetition, truancy, and COVID-related remote-learning barriers as key correlates. Limitations include lack of documented survey-weight use and missing-data/PV handling transparency, and SHAP-based explanations are predictive rather than causal.
sample_filtering_criteria: The working sample includes nine Latin American countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Panama, Peru, Uruguay) from PISA 2022. The analysis is conducted at school level: the author constructs averages of key student and school variables and merges them into a school-level dataset for DEA. The resulting school sample contains 2,034 schools total (1,548 public; 486 private). Two additional LAC countries are excluded: Costa Rica (missing the household SES covariate used as an input for the DEA formulation) and Paraguay (missing non-cognitive outputs). The DEA is estimated separately for private and public schools and for two output sets (cognitive: school-average math/reading/science scores; non-cognitive: a soft-skills well-being index), implying that schools must have the required output/input information for each DEA model.

effect_size: Gradient boosted trees (GBT/XGBoost) — AUROC and AUPRC reported in Appendix A; example for private cognitive model: AUROC=0.769, AUPRC=0.855 (logit AUROC/AUPRC ranges 0.727–0.792; NN AUROC/AUPRC 0.678/0.721).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 school-level the study leveraged Books at home, ICT home resources, School autonomy, Bad school climate, and Paid work intensity to predict whether a school is in the top half of cognitive efficiency, finding that private schools have higher cognitive technical efficiency (0.865 vs 0.768; gap ≈ 0.10) and that resource-rich and autonomy-supportive contexts (e.g., books/ICT at home, higher autonomy, lower engagement in paid work) are key drivers of high efficiency. This indicates that strengthening home learning resources and school autonomy—alongside reducing barriers to engagement during and after disruptions—may narrow private-public efficiency gaps, though the SHAP-based interpretation is predictive rather than causal.

title: Effects of the “highly adaptive testing design for PISA” on plausible value-based population estimates
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 public-use cognitive achievement and background data to simulate two alternative Reading test designs (PISA 2018 MST vs PISA HAT) across 18 OECD countries. For the PV-based population statistics (country means, standard deviations, and proficiency-level proportions), the authors apply the operational PISA scaling settings and use the final student and replicate weights included in the PISA 2018 public use files. They implement balanced repeated replication (BRR) with a Fay factor of 0.5 to estimate sampling variances and associated error-variance components. Because the analysis is simulation-based but explicitly follows PISA’s operational PV-generation and variance estimation procedures, weights are treated as essential for the sampling-variance component; the paper does not indicate any omission of weights.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are central to the study: the authors draw 10 PVs per domain and repeat PV drawing 200 times, then average PV-based estimates across draws, consistent with Rubin-style combining. However, the paper does not explicitly state a missing-data strategy for the PV-generation/variance estimation stage (e.g., whether any cases are listwise deleted or whether missingness is handled via the PV model). This is a reporting gap because PV-based procedures typically require clear documentation of how omitted responses (e.g., not-reached items) are treated in the estimation pipeline.
outcome_summary: The paper evaluates whether the highly adaptive testing (HAT) design for PISA 2018 Reading improves the precision of plausible value (PV)-based population statistics used for reporting. Using simulated administrations based on PISA 2018 public-use item pools and background/cognitive data, the authors compare the operational multistage testing (MST) design against HAT across 18 OECD countries (N=110,958 students; 5,723,330 after weighting). They follow PISA’s PV-generation and variance decomposition procedures, including BRR with Fay’s factor 0.5 for sampling variance and PV draws for imputation variance. Results show HAT reduces imputation variance for country means by ~19% and for country standard deviations by ~16%, with smaller but significant reductions in total error variance. For proficiency-level proportions, HAT reduces imputation variance by ~8–13% and total error variance by up to ~9%, and it shifts top-level (V/VI) proportions downward, suggesting MST overestimation of very high performers. Limitations include reliance on simulation and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling specifics in the PV pipeline.
sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses the PISA 2018 main survey public-use files and selects a subset of 18 OECD countries (plus specific language groups within countries where applicable) that implemented PISA as a computer-based assessment without financial literacy and global competence. The analytic sample is generated from the PISA 2018 public-use cognitive achievement and background data for Reading as the major domain, then simulated under two Reading test designs (MST and HAT). For each country and student, the authors simulate item administration and recode responses coded as not-reached as missing in the simulated response vectors; these omitted responses are implicitly accounted for in the generation of the students’ true ability vectors. The paper does not report additional exclusions beyond the country/language subset and the simulated not-reached-to-missing recoding.
effect_size: HAT vs MST: mean imputation variance decreased by 19% on average (range: 16% to 23%); total error variance of country means was ~2% smaller on average; sampling variances showed no significant differences across designs.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 Reading the study compared PV-based country-specific means under the MST and HAT test designs, finding that HAT significantly reduced the imputation variance of country mean Reading proficiency by about 19% (with total error variance ~2% lower). This indicates that adopting more adaptive operational test designs can improve the precision of reported cross-country benchmarking statistics, even when sampling variance remains largely unchanged.

title: Predictors of Cognitive Skills Underlying Global Competences of Filipino Students in PISA 2018: A Machine-Learning Approach
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Philippine sample from PISA 2018, which is based on a two-stage stratified random sampling design (schools selected first, then students within schools). Although PISA provides sampling and replicate weights, the authors explicitly did not use student weights or replicate weights in the machine-learning analysis because the models were trained for prediction and feature-importance interpretation rather than population-parameter estimation. Consequently, all observations were treated with equal weight during training, cross-validation, hold-out testing, and SHAP-based ranking. For preprocessing, the authors standardized predictors and applied k-nearest neighbors (k=5) imputation within each cross-validation fold to avoid using validation/test information during preprocessing.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are three Warm likelihood estimate (WLE) indices derived from self-report questionnaire items (perspective taking, cognitive flexibility/adaptability, and intercultural communication ability), rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores produced by PISA. Missing data handling is reported: outcome values were not imputed and cases with missing target index values were excluded, while missing predictor values were imputed using k-nearest neighbors (k=5) within the cross-validation pipeline.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes the Philippine PISA 2018 dataset (15-year-olds; N=7233) to predict three self-report cognitive skill indices underlying global competence: perspective taking (PERSPECT), cognitive flexibility/adaptability (COGFLEX), and intercultural communication ability (AWACOM). For each target, the authors used an outcome-specific modeling approach with kNN imputation for missing predictors (k=5) inside a cross-validation pipeline and excluded predictors that overlapped with the target index construction. Among three candidate regression algorithms (support vector regression, XGBoost, and multilayer perceptron), XGBoost consistently outperformed the others, with training R2 between 0.4953 and 0.5394 and test R2 between 0.3896 and 0.4469. SHAP was used to rank influential predictors, showing strong overlap between perspective taking and cognitive flexibility, while intercultural communication relied more on immigrant attitudes, global values, and global-issue knowledge. Limitations include the absence of survey-weighted inference and the fact that SHAP explains predictive contribution rather than causal impact.
sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic data come from the Philippine PISA 2018 sample (15-year-old students). For each outcome-specific model, the authors excluded predictors that were used to construct the target index and also excluded the other global competence indexes to avoid mechanical prediction. Observations with missing values in the target outcome index were excluded (no outcome imputation). Missing predictor values were imputed within the machine-learning pipeline using k-nearest neighbors (k=5), with preprocessing (standardization and imputation) fitted only on the training portion of each cross-validation fold.

title: AI-related measures and self-reported lesson-aim attainment: an explainable machine-learning analysis of TALIS 2024
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the TALIS 2024 teacher public-use file and constructs an analytic sample of teachers with valid AI-module routing responses and valid outcome/grouping fields (country/economy, ISCED stratum, and school identifier). For the primary conditional prediction models, the authors fit LightGBM models without final teacher weights, explicitly stating that the models are not design-based population estimates. As a sensitivity analysis, they recalculated evaluation metrics using the final teacher weights at test/evaluation time while leaving model fitting unchanged, showing that weighted AUROC/AUPRC increments differ from unweighted results. Because the primary models are tree-based ML methods (LightGBM) and the manuscript does not report a weight variable used during training, the main findings should be interpreted as conditional prediction for the analytic sample rather than fully design-based inference for TALIS populations.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable (SLAA) is constructed from TALIS self-report items and then dichotomized/treated as a continuous mean, rather than using PV-based cognitive achievement scales. Missing data handling is implemented via train-only median imputation for numerical predictors and mode imputation (plus one-hot encoding) for categorical predictors, while outcomes are never imputed; the paper also uses missingness/routing indicators for AI task breadth. The manuscript reports the extent of missingness by construct and explains that multiple imputation was not used because most task-breadth missingness follows questionnaire routing rather than ordinary item nonresponse.
outcome_summary: This secondary cross-sectional study uses TALIS 2024 teacher public-use data (ISCED 1–3) and constructs SLAA from seven self-report lesson-aim items (item 58), aggregating to a continuous mean and then defining a binary “relatively high” outcome as teachers at or above the 75th percentile within each country/economy × ISCED stratum. The primary model is a matched nested LightGBM contrast: Model 1 predicts SLAA from teacher background, country/economy, and a broad work-related stress index, while Model 2 adds AI-related predictors (perceived AI benefits/risks, breadth of AI task use, and AI-use barriers). On the independent test set, AI-added information improved AUROC from 0.6021 to 0.6299 (+0.0277) and AUPRC from 0.4138 to 0.4476 (+0.0338), with Brier score and log loss also improving. Calibration curves were close to the diagonal, supporting descriptive group-level probability assessment. The authors report that weighted evaluation changes the magnitude of increments and that SHAP provides fitted-model attribution rather than causal or actionable effects; additionally, task-breadth missingness is largely routing-related, which can confound attribution.
ml_all_techniques: LightGBM, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, Extra Trees, Logistic Regression
sample_filtering_criteria: Secondary cross-sectional analysis of TALIS 2024 teacher public-use data. title: Can Teacher AI Literacy Reach Those Who Need It Most? Professional Learning, Realised Access, and Cumulative Advantage in TALIS 2024
authors: F. Javier Murillo; Angel C. Herrero
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2024 lower-secondary teacher data (teachers nested within schools, schools nested within 55 education systems) and incorporates teacher sampling weights in all multilevel models. The analytic sample is constructed by sequentially restricting the initial teacher working file to those in questionnaire forms containing the AI-related professional learning participation item (TT4G21G) and the declared need item (TT4G24G), and then excluding cases with missing/non-applicable values for the outcome, key predictors, weights, or clustering identifiers. Because the outcome is binary and models are linear probability multilevel specifications (with logistic robustness checks), the weighting is used for prevalence estimation and regression estimation rather than for any PV-combining procedure.

outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2024 lower-secondary teacher and principal questionnaires across 55 education systems, analyzing a binary outcome: whether teachers reported participating in professional learning on “Using artificial intelligence for teaching and learning” during the previous 12 months (TT4G21G). Associations are also patterned by teacher digital self-efficacy and structured collaboration, and by school digital leadership and digital resource shortages; the paper uses linear probability multilevel models with logistic robustness checks. Limitations include cross-sectional, self-reported measures and no direct measurement of objective AI literacy or the quality/content of professional learning, so causality cannot be inferred.
sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses use TALIS 2024 lower-secondary teacher questionnaire data. The initial working file contains 129,617 teacher records across 55 education systems. The analytic sample is restricted to teachers in questionnaire forms that include both the AI-related professional learning participation item (TT4G21G) and the declared need item (TT4G24G), then further restricted to teachers with valid information on reported participation, valid information on declared need, valid teacher-level predictors including teaching experience, and successful linkage to school-level predictors from the principal questionnaire. Final restrictions exclude cases with missing/non-applicable values in the outcome, declared need, teacher- or school-level predictors, missing school-level information from the principal questionnaire, invalid sampling weights, or missing clustering identifiers. The authors describe PISA’s two-stage sampling (schools then students) but do not report applying any PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML training/evaluation. Because the models are standard scikit-learn classifiers (LR, RF, SVM) and the manuscript does not mention weight-aware estimation, the analysis appears to be unweighted. Preprocessing includes dropping students with missing feature values (~3% removed), imputing specific questionnaire response categories with the mode, one-hot encoding categorical variables, and min-max scaling numerical features to [0,1].

It constructs a student-level binary target by converting mathematics PVs into “success” when the PV is at or above the OECD math average (489), using 5 PVs sampled from the 10 available and repeating model training/evaluation across PV draws. Three classifiers—logistic regression, random forest, and SVM—are tuned via grid search with 5-fold cross-validation on a 90/10 train/test split per country, and evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1; SVM is reported as the best-performing algorithm with about 73% accuracy, while mean accuracies across countries are very similar across models. title: Optimizing automated scoring in ILSAs with prompt compression
authors: J.Y. Jung; Ummugul Bezirhan; Matthias von Davier
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses digital PIRLS 2021 constructed-response (CR) item responses from 27 countries and 29 languages, but it does not report applying PIRLS sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation in the automated scoring evaluation. Instead, the authors draw a randomly selected 20% subset of the full dataset for each country to conduct exploratory analyses, and then run GPT-4o-based automated scoring with prompt compression variants. Because the evaluation is based on agreement between automated scores and human scores (accuracy, Cohen’s kappa, hallucination rate) rather than estimating population parameters, the manuscript provides no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and no discussion of complex survey design adjustments. As a result, the reported performance should be interpreted as model-scoring agreement on the sampled responses, not as a nationally representative estimate of PIRLS reading literacy distributions.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are binary 1-point constructed-response scores (human scoring vs automated scoring) for PIRLS CR items, not PV-based cognitive achievement scales. The paper also does not describe any missing-data handling strategy (e.g., how incomplete responses, translation failures, or absent fields were treated), which is a reporting gap given that multilingual responses and API-based translation/summarization can produce missing or unusable outputs. The evaluation therefore focuses on scoring agreement metrics computed on the available item responses after the authors’ subset selection, without documenting a formal missing-data protocol.
outcome_summary: This study evaluates automated scoring (AS) for PIRLS 2021 digital Grade 4 reading constructed-response items using GPT-4o with prompt compression and optimization. The authors score five 1-point CR items across 27 countries/29 languages, using a randomly selected 20% subset per country for exploratory analysis. They compare a baseline prompt (original passages and original scoring guides) against three variants that refine scoring guides (extractive vs abstractive) and compress reading passages via question-based summarization, all using Zero-Shot-CoT with an internal validation step and JSON output constraints. Across items, Model 3 achieves the highest average accuracy (92.87%) and low hallucination rate (0.12%), closely approximating baseline accuracy (92.62%) while reducing prompt token lengths to ~18% (passages) and ~15% (scoring guides). Limitations include the absence of documented missing-data handling and survey-weighted representativeness, and the fact that kappa can be suppressed by skewed item difficulty distributions.
sample_filtering_criteria: The dataset consists of multilingual responses from all participating countries in digital PIRLS 2021, but the analytic dataset is restricted to five 1-point CR items (trend items) used for PIRLS 2026 preparation. The authors further select a randomly chosen 20% subset of the full dataset for each country to conduct exploratory analyses while maintaining representation across countries and languages. The evaluation is then performed on these item responses across the specified countries/languages, with additional post-processing to fix misformatted JSON outputs and to detect/flag hallucinated translations based on response-length ratios (Latin-alphabet vs non-Latin thresholds), reassigning flagged cases to score 0.
effect_size: Model 3 (RefinedSG_AT + question-specific passage summaries): average accuracy 92.87%; baseline average accuracy 92.62%; Model 1 average accuracy 92.19%. Item-level accuracy (baseline vs Model 3): Item 1 90.83% vs 91.13%, Item 2 91.11% vs 90.26%, Item 3 95.05% vs 94.36%, Item 4 92.18% vs 94.85%, Item 5 93.95% vs 93.77%.
primary_finding: Using PIRLS 2021 digital Grade 4 reading data for five multilingual 1-point constructed-response items, the study leveraged prompt compression (question-based passage summaries) and refined scoring guides (RefinedSG_AT) together with Zero-Shot-CoT prompting and hallucination post-processing to predict binary automated scores aligned to human scoring, finding that Model 3 achieved the highest average accuracy (92.87%) and closely approximated the baseline despite substantial compression. This indicates that compressing long PIRLS prompts can preserve scoring agreement while improving operational efficiency, supporting scalable automated scoring workflows for multilingual reading assessments.

title: Comparative analysis of global education performances based on PISA 2022 results: an assessment with statistical and machine learning methods
authors: Emel Şaşmaz; Sadullah Çelik; Bilge Doğanlı
weight_fields_interpretation: The study does not use PISA student microdata; instead it uses OECD-published country-level aggregated average scores for Mathematics, Reading, Science, and overall PISA achievement. Because the unit of analysis is the country (one observation per country), there is no student-level sampling frame and no complex survey design to weight at the analysis stage. The paper reports preprocessing steps such as standardizing score variables and treating missing values during preprocessing, but it does not report any application of PISA sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures. Consequently, weighting is not applicable to the analytic dataset as constructed from published aggregates.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The analysis is performed on country-level aggregated mean scores published by OECD, not on student-level PISA plausible values (PVs). As a result, PV handling is not applicable because the dependent variables are already aggregated achievement summaries rather than PV-based student achievement estimates. The paper states that missing values were treated in preprocessing, but it does not specify whether missingness was handled via deletion, imputation, or another rule, which is a reporting gap for reproducibility.
outcome_summary: The study uses OECD-published PISA 2022 country-level average scores in Mathematics, Reading, Science, and overall PISA achievement (one observation per country/economy; 81 participants). It first applies Pearson correlations and PCA to summarize the strong co-movement among the three domain scores (e.g., very high correlations with the overall score). In regression, three linear variants (Linear, Ridge, Huber) all achieve R²=1.0, with the smallest errors for Classical Linear Regression (RMSE=0.309, MAE=0.283); permutation importance indicates Mathematics is the most decisive sub-score (significance 0.268 vs 0.226 and 0.216). For clustering, K-Means yields four clusters (k=4), and supervised validation via stratified 5-fold cross-validation shows extremely high separability, with Extra Trees reaching mean accuracy=1.000 and macro F1=1.000. Limitations include reliance on aggregated data (no student PVs), unspecified missing-value treatment, and the fact that cluster labels are data-derived rather than externally validated, so results support typology stability rather than causal policy effects.
ml_all_techniques: Random Forest, Extra Trees, SVM, Neural Network
sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic dataset is constructed from OECD-published PISA 2022 country-level aggregated average scores (Mathematics, Reading, Science, and overall PISA score). Each observation corresponds to a single country/economy that participated in PISA 2022 and submitted the necessary data to OECD; the paper states that 81 countries/economies participated in PISA 2022. title: Machine learning evidence from PISA 2018 data to integrate global competence intervention in UAE K–12 public schools
authors: Xin Miao; Ali Nadaf; Zhuotong Zhou
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses publicly available PISA 2018 microdata for UAE students (public and private schools) and models a per-student academic performance output derived from PISA cognitive-test plausible values (PVs). The authors explicitly describe PV aggregation as a weighted average for each PV within subpopulations, then averaging across PVs, which is consistent with PISA’s recommended approach for unbiased statistics. However, the manuscript does not report whether complex survey sampling weights (e.g., student/school weights) or replicate weights were applied in the CatBoost training and SHAP computation. The analysis also excludes questionnaire features with more than 50% missingness, indicating a preprocessing step that changes the effective feature set used for prediction.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper explains how academic performance is constructed from PISA plausible values by taking a weighted average across PVs, but it does not report a specific missing-data strategy for the remaining questionnaire variables beyond excluding features with >50% missingness. This creates a reporting gap: it is unclear whether remaining missing values were imputed, set to defaults, or handled via CatBoost’s internal missing-value handling. Given that PISA questionnaire items typically have non-trivial item nonresponse, the absence of a documented missing-data method limits reproducibility and may affect SHAP-based feature contribution estimates.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata and trains a CatBoost boosted-regression-tree model on 80 PISA questionnaire features (excluding any feature with >50% missingness), using a per-student academic performance output constructed as the mean of plausible values (PV-weighted within each PV) across reading, mathematics, and science. The model is validated on a 70/30 split and achieves RMSE 47.74, MAE 37.2, and R² 0.75, which the authors interpret as substantial predictive accuracy. SHAP (TreeExplainer) is then used to quantify feature contributions, showing that three global competence indicators—awareness of global issues (GCAWARE), self-efficacy on global issues (GCSELFEFF), and awareness of intercultural communication (AWACOM)—are the main contributors, while perspective-taking, flexibility, and respect contribute less. Subgroup SHAP patterns suggest different intervention priorities by gender and school type in the UAE. Limitations include the absence of a documented missing-data handling method beyond feature exclusion, and the fact that SHAP explains predictive contribution rather than causal effects.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 student questionnaire data (80 survey features) for UAE K–12 students (public and private schools) and excluded global competence cognitive-test data because the UAE did not participate in the cognitive test. Excluded any survey features with more than 50% missing data across the whole dataset. Defined the analytic output as a per-student academic performance score computed as the mean of all PVs for reading, mathematics, and science, using a weighted average within each PV before averaging across PVs. Trained a CatBoost boosted-regression-tree model on the resulting dataset of 600,821 student rows.
effect_size: CatBoost validation: RMSE 47.74, MAE 37.2, R² 0.75 (70/30 train/validation split; 2,000 estimators; depth 10; learning rate 0.05). SHAP used for feature contribution; no additional predictive metrics reported for SHAP-based subgroup comparisons.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 UAE student questionnaire the study leveraged awareness of global issues, self-efficacy on global issues, and awareness of intercultural communication (among other global competence indicators) to predict an academic performance score derived from reading, mathematics, and science plausible values, finding that these three indicators contributed positively to academic performance in both the UAE and other OECD-participating countries. This indicates that global-competence-focused interventions targeting these specific skills may support academic achievement and help inform UAE K–12 public-school reform priorities, though the SHAP-based evidence is predictive rather than causal.

weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses country-average PISA performance profiles (low–medium–high classes) and country-year economic freedom indicators, so it does not analyze student-level microdata from PISA. For model training and evaluation, the authors apply final student weights (W_FSTUWT) to correct for non-response bias and sampling error arising from the two-stage stratified sampling design. primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 data for 15-year-olds, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy, stress resistance, self-directed learning problems, and mathematics achievement (PV1MATH) to predict mathematics anxiety, finding that self-efficacy and stress regulation variables were the strongest predictors while mathematics achievement had relatively weak predictive power. title: Artificial Intelligence in Educational Data Mining and Human-in-the-Loop Machine Learning and Machine Teaching: Analysis of Scientific Knowledge
weight_fields_interpretation: This article is a bibliometric analysis and qualitative systematic review of publications indexed in Scopus (2006–2024), not an analysis of student microdata from an ILSA such as PISA/TIMSS. title: Predictive insights into U.S. students’ mathematics performance on PISA 2022 using ensemble tree-based machine learning models
authors: Li Zhu; Hyesun You; Minju Hong; Zhenhan Fang
weight_fields_interpretation: The study analyzed PISA 2022 mathematics performance for the United States, merging student and school files using the school ID (CNTSCHID) so that school-level predictors were assigned to students within the same school. The analytic sample comprised 4,552 students in 154 schools, with grade information reported (primarily 10th grade). Although the authors followed PISA user guidance for computing estimates for each plausible value, they explicitly did not include sampling weights in the ML analyses, arguing that weighting might be less critical for ML model configuration and citing evidence that ML can still produce reliable results under complex multistage clustered designs. The paper therefore treats the ML training/testing as effectively unweighted with respect to PISA sampling weights, while still using the official PV framework for the outcome.
outcome_summary: The study used PISA 2022 mathematics plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) for U.S. 15-year-olds (N=4,552 in 154 schools) and trained three ensemble tree-based ML models—Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM—to predict mathematics achievement. After cleaning predictors (dropping >50% missing predictors, removing identical/redundant variables) and imputing remaining missing values with missForest, the authors split data into training (80%) and test (20%) and performed five-fold cross-validation within training. For each PV, they fitted each model with all predictors, then used forward selection with an absolute relative error (ARE) criterion of 0.1 to obtain reduced predictor sets; results were averaged across the 10 PVs. Reduced-model performance showed high accuracy for all models, with XGBoost identified as best by both accuracy and efficiency (reduced-model rMSE=66.39; training time=4.14s), slightly outperforming LightGBM (rMSE=66.36; 22.93s) and RF (rMSE=69.82; 129.27s). The study uses ALE plots for interpretation and does not apply sampling weights in ML, so findings should be treated as associations rather than causal effects.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 microdata for 15-year-old students in the United States. Merged student and school questionnaires using CNTSCHID so that school-level predictors were attached to students in the same school. The analytic dataset was then reduced via preprocessing: removed predictors with >50% missing values; removed identical predictors (same values for all students); removed redundant predictors (e.g., retained ESCS and excluded the component DVs used to compute it); and imputed remaining missing predictor values using missForest (RF-based imputation). The final modeling dataset was split into training (80%, N=3644) and test (20%, N=908), and models were trained separately for each of the 10 PVs (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) with results averaged.

LightGBM (selected 10 predictors) rMSE full=60.43 vs reduced=66.36; training time full=44.28 vs reduced=22.93. Best model by accuracy+efficiency: XGBoost with reduced-model rMSE=66.39 and ARE≈9.79%.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data for U.S. students, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy, ESCS, familiarity with math concepts, expected occupation status, and family support for self-learning to predict mathematics achievement (across PV1MATH–PV10MATH), finding that all three ensemble tree models achieved high accuracy with substantially reduced predictor sets and that XGBoost performed best (lowest reduced-model rMSE among the compared models and fastest training time). This indicates that focusing instructional and support efforts on a small set of high-yield factors—especially self-efficacy and foundational math familiarity—may be a more efficient strategy for improving math outcomes, though the study is predictive (not causal) and does not incorporate PISA sampling weights in the ML training.

title: Using machine learning approaches to predict Taiwanese eighth graders’ computational thinking performance in ICILS 2023 study
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICILS 2023 microdata for Taiwanese eighth graders (ICILS 2023 CT test and student questionnaire) and applies a two-stage sampling design at the school and class levels (stratified random sampling of schools, then cluster sampling of classes). The analytic dataset is further restricted to 8th graders in Taiwan and to 18 derived questionnaire/scale predictors after aggregating correlated items, removing variables with excessive missingness, and screening multicollinearity using VIF. The manuscript does not report applying ICILS sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML training/evaluation pipeline, and it does not name any weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT). Because the models are standard supervised ML classifiers (tree-based ensembles and stacking) trained in scikit-learn, the analysis likely proceeds without complex-survey weighting; therefore, results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than fully design-weighted population estimates.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that variables with excessive missingness were removed during feature selection, but it does not specify the missing-data rule used for the remaining predictors (e.g., listwise deletion vs. imputation) or the proportion of cases excluded. Because the dependent variable is a binary classification derived from CT scores using the first plausible value threshold, missingness handling can affect both the class balance and the learned decision boundaries. This omission is a reporting gap that limits reproducibility and may bias predictive performance if missingness is not handled consistently across features.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes ICILS 2023 Grade 8 computational thinking (CT) for Taiwan (N=5211) and converts CT performance into a binary outcome (below vs above average) using a threshold based on the mean of the first plausible value (PV1) from the international database. Using supervised ML with an 80/20 train-test split and 10-fold cross-validation on the training set, the authors compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, LightGBM, XGBoost, and a Stacking Ensemble. XGBoost and the Stacking Ensemble reach the top AUC (0.79) and accuracy (0.72), with XGBoost showing the strongest precision/recall/F1 overall. Limitations include binary simplification of CT, reliance on PV1 for the threshold, and missing-data handling not being fully specified, so results should be treated as predictive associations rather than evidence of causal effects.

title: Predicting Teachers’ AI Usage in Education Based on Machine Learning: Evidence from TALIS 2024
