The manuscript does not report any use of TALIS sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures, nor does it name any weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or describe complex survey design handling. Because the models are tree-based ensembles (Random Forest, XGBoost) and SHAP is applied for interpretation, the paper does not provide evidence that survey weights were incorporated into estimation. Analysts should therefore treat the reported predictive performance as potentially unweighted and interpret generalizability cautiously; future work should explicitly apply TALIS complex-survey weights if available in the released microdata.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are teacher AI adoption (binary) and AI integration intensity (continuous index) derived from questionnaire items, not cognitive achievement scores with TALIS plausible values. As a result, plausible-value generation/combining is not applicable to the modeled outcomes. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case exclusion or imputation), which is a reporting gap because missingness can affect both the binary adoption threshold and the constructed intensity index.
outcome_summary: The study uses OECD TALIS 2024 teacher questionnaire data pooled across ISCED 1–3 and constructs two outcomes: a binary AI adoption indicator (used AI in the past 12 months) and a continuous AI integration intensity index aggregated from AI usage items. Using an 80/20 train-test split with hyperparameters tuned via 5-fold cross-validation, the authors compare Random Forest and XGBoost against logistic and linear regression baselines. For AI adoption, Random Forest achieved AUC=0.81 (vs logistic regression AUC=0.79; DeLong p<0.001) and improved classification metrics (F1=0.69). For AI integration intensity, Random Forest reached R²=0.67 with RMSE=1.56 (vs linear regression R²=0.49; paired t-test p<0.001). SHAP interpretation highlights AI attitude, teacher collaboration, and qualification year as key predictors, but the paper relies on cross-sectional self-reports and does not document missing-data handling or survey-weight usage, limiting causal and population-representative claims.
ml_all_techniques: Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression, Linear Regression
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the OECD TALIS 2024 Teacher Questionnaire pooled dataset across ISCED 1–3 (primary, lower secondary, upper secondary). Applied theory-driven feature extraction to select variables relevant to AI integration logic and constructed two prediction targets: (1) AI adoption as a binary indicator of whether teachers used AI in the past 12 months, and (2) AI integration intensity as a continuous index aggregated from specific AI usage items. After preprocessing/normalization, the final analytic dataset comprised 89,833 high-quality and relevant cases; no further inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., missing-item handling) are explicitly reported.
effect_size: Random Forest: AUC=0.81, PR_AUC=0.74, ACC=0.75, F1=0.69; XGBoost: AUC=0.80, PR_AUC=0.73, ACC=0.73, F1=0.68; Logistic Regression: AUC=0.79, PR_AUC=0.72, ACC=0.72, F1=0.67. DeLong test p<0.001 for Random Forest vs logistic regression.
primary_finding: Using TALIS 2024 Teacher Questionnaire (pooled ISCED 1–3) the study leveraged AI attitude, teacher collaboration, year of first qualification, and enjoyment of teaching to predict AI adoption (binary), finding that Random Forest achieved the highest discrimination (AUC=0.81) and outperformed logistic regression (p<0.001). This indicates that strengthening teachers’ AI-related beliefs and providing collegial collaboration opportunities may improve adoption, though the study is cross-sectional and SHAP-based interpretation does not establish causality.
confounders: AI attitude; Teacher collaboration; Year of first qualification; Enjoyment of teaching

title: Explaining student absenteeism in Morocco using TIMSS 2023 data: a deep learning and explainable AI approach
authors: Abdelamine elouafi; Assiya Nouna; Ilyas Tammouch; Soumaya Nouna
journal: 2025 11th International Conference on Optimization and Applications (ICOA)
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the TIMSS 2023 international database for Moroccan eighth-graders, drawing on student, teacher, and school contextual questionnaire variables (BS, BT, BC). During preprocessing, the authors removed technical factors including weights, information, IDs, and duplicates, and also removed PV-related reference variables to avoid bias in prediction modeling. The manuscript does not report applying complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures, and the ML models (autoencoder + SVM/RF/XGBoost/DT) are trained on the cleaned feature set without a stated survey-weight correction. Therefore, the analysis should be interpreted as not fully accounting for TIMSS complex sampling design and clustering effects beyond any implicit effects of the original dataset structure.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a binary classification of perceived absenteeism severity based on the school principal questionnaire (BCBG15B reclassified into two classes), not a cognitive achievement score with TIMSS plausible values. Because the paper removes PV-related reference variables during preprocessing, PV handling is not applicable to the modeled outcome. The manuscript does not describe a specific missing-data strategy for the remaining variables after dropping variables with >50% missingness and variables with no data, so the exact approach for residual missingness is not fully documented.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2023 contextual questionnaire data for Moroccan eighth-graders, using the school principal variable BCBG15B reclassified into two groups (serious absenteeism vs low-to-moderate). After removing weights/IDs/duplicates and dropping PV-related reference variables, the authors train an autoencoder to compress 596 remaining features into a 10-dimensional latent representation, then fit four binary classifiers (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, Decision Tree) on the latent features. The best-performing model is SVM, with Accuracy 0.9081, F1-score 0.8883, and AUC 0.98; Random Forest and XGBoost are slightly lower (AUC 0.97 and 0.96), while Decision Tree performs worst (Accuracy 0.8174, F1 0.7890, AUC 0.84). Interpretability is provided by SHAP values mapped back to original variables via autoencoder weight matrices. Limitations include the lack of reported missing-data handling details and the absence of explicit survey-weighted estimation; SHAP explanations support prediction transparency but do not establish causal effects.
ml_all_techniques: Autoencoder, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, XGBoost, Decision Tree
sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses the TIMSS 2023 Moroccan eighth-grade sample. The authors cleaned the TIMSS dataset by removing 759 variables, including technical factors (weights, information, IDs, duplicates), eliminating 30 variables with more than 50% missing values and 70 variables with no data, removing 30 redundant numerical score variables expressed in different formats, and dropping 10 reference variables mostly related to plausible values (PVs). After this preprocessing, they retained 596 variables for modeling. For the target, they used the school principal variable BCBG15B (perceived absenteeism severity) and reclassified it into two groups: low-to-moderate absenteeism (No problem + Minor problem + Moderate problem) versus serious absenteeism (Serious problem), to enable binary classification.
effect_size: SVM (best): Accuracy 0.9081, F1-score 0.8883, AUC 0.98. Other models: Random Forest Accuracy 0.9011, F1 0.8860, AUC 0.97; XGBoost Accuracy 0.9011, F1 0.8871, AUC 0.96; Decision Tree Accuracy 0.8174, F1 0.7890, AUC 0.84.
primary_finding: Using TIMSS 2023 Grade 8 (Morocco) the study leveraged teacher- and school-level contextual factors (e.g., teacher encouragement of learning interest, class size, time for assistance, memorization-focused teaching, and teacher expectations) to predict perceived absenteeism severity as a binary outcome, finding that the SVM classifier achieved the highest discrimination (Accuracy 0.9081, F1 0.8883, AUC 0.98). This indicates that strengthening classroom climate and teacher practices—along with addressing institutional constraints such as class size and technology support—may improve attendance-related outcomes, though the study’s SHAP-based interpretability is predictive rather than causal and the paper does not report a full missing-data strategy or survey-weighted estimation.
confounders: Teacher promotes learning interest; Class size (number of students); Need more time to assist; Memorization-focused teaching; Teacher is kind; supportive; Uninterested students; High teacher expectations; presents mathematical problems; Shortage of technology support staff; allowed to use smartphones

title: Analysis of the Effects of World Bank Macroeconomic and Management Indicators on Sustainable Education Quality on PISA Scores Using the SHAP Explainable Artificial Intelligence Method
weight_fields_interpretation: The study constructs country-level datasets by combining PISA domain scores (PISAM, PISAR, PISAS) with World Bank governance/economic indicators, Economist Intelligence Unit democracy, and regional category dummies. The analytic sample is therefore an aggregate country/region-level modeling dataset rather than a student microdata file, and the manuscript does not report the use of PISA complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the models are tree-based classifiers (Random Forest and XGBoost) trained on tabular country-level predictors, the paper does not specify any survey-weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) being applied. Data preparation includes missing-value checks with trend-based interpolation for PISA scores and scaling of numerical variables, followed by two-stage feature elimination (correlation thresholding and VIF-based multicollinearity reduction) before model training.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are country-level PISA domain scale means (PISAM, PISAR, PISAS) that are used to create Low/Medium/High achievement classes via fixed score thresholds. Plausible Values are typically generated for student-level cognitive achievement scales in PISA microdata; here the study uses aggregated domain means, so PV handling is not applicable to the modeled outcome. Missing-data handling is only partially described (PISA scores imputed via trend-based interpolation), but the paper does not provide a complete, explicit missing-data strategy for all predictors and for the final analytic dataset, representing a reporting gap.
outcome_summary: The study builds three multi-class country-level classification models for PISA Mathematics (PISAM), Reading (PISAR), and Science (PISAS) by mapping each country’s domain mean into Low/Medium/High classes using fixed score thresholds. After imputing missing PISA scores via trend-based interpolation and scaling predictors, the authors apply two-stage feature selection (correlation elimination with |r|≥0.90 and VIF elimination with VIF>7.0) to reduce multicollinearity. Random Forest and XGBoost are trained separately for each target, with XGBoost selected as best-performing; class-wise Precision/Recall/F1 are mostly above 0.90, and general performance is reported as Train Accuracy=1.0, Test Accuracy=0.93–0.95, and ROC-AUC in the 0.98–1.00 range. Explanations are produced with SHAP and evaluated using Fidelity and Faithfulness (PISAM 0.95/0.85; PISAR 0.89/0.92; PISAS 0.89/0.89), supporting explanation reliability. Limitations include the use of aggregate country-level indicators (no within-country heterogeneity) and the fact that SHAP-based attributions are predictive associations, not causal effects.
sample_filtering_criteria: The manuscript describes creating three separate country-level datasets (one per target: PISAM, PISAR, PISAS) using the same explanatory features (governance, economic capacity, democracy, regional category, and a centered observation year). It reports checking missing values and imputing unavailable PISA scores using trend-based interpolation across years, scaling numerical variables, and then applying two-stage feature selection (greedy correlation elimination with |r|≥0.90 followed by iterative VIF elimination with VIF>7.0). No explicit inclusion/exclusion rules for specific countries, years, or a final country count are reported in the provided text.
effect_size: XGBoost (best model): Class-based Precision/Recall/F1 — Low: 0.97/0.97/0.97 (Support 110); Medium: 0.91/0.93/0.92 (Support 107); High: 0.96/0.94/0.95 (Support 111). General metrics reported as Train Accuracy=1.0 and Test Accuracy=0.93–0.95; ROC-AUC reported in 0.98–1.00 band; Macro Avg and Weighted Avg ≈0.93–0.95.
primary_finding: Using PISA Mathematics (PISAM) country-level domain means the study leveraged Voice and Accountability, Control of Corruption, Political Stability, Regional Category, and GDP per capita to predict PISAM achievement class (Low/Medium/High), finding that governance indicators form the most salient institutional core and that class separation is further shaped by political stability and regional location. This indicates that strengthening accountability/anti-corruption capacity and stabilizing political institutions may be key levers for moving countries toward higher mathematics achievement profiles, though the results are predictive associations rather than causal effects.
confounders: Control of Corruption; Government Effectiveness; Political Stability; Regulatory Quality; Rule of Law; Voice; Accountability; Democracy Index; Regional Category; Economic Category; GDP (total economic size); GDP per capita; Centered observation year; PISA Mathematics scale mean; PISA Reading scale mean; PISA Science scale mean

title: Disentangling Teacher and Lesson Variance and Their Relations to Supportive Learning Environments: A Machine Learning Assessment of Teacher Nonverbal Behavior
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses secondary data from the German TALIS video study (national substudy of the international TALIS video study). The analytic sample is constructed from video-recorded mathematics lessons on quadratic equations, with additional inclusion criteria for usable camera views and teacher visibility, and with a teacher-level split for training/validation of the computer-vision NVI model. The manuscript does not report applying TALIS sampling weights (e.g., student/school weights) in the multilevel modeling or in the ML-based NVI scoring, and the ML pipeline is described as using human ratings and computer-vision features rather than survey-weighted estimation. Given the absence of explicit weight-variable names and the ML-focused workflow, the analysis should be treated as unweighted with respect to complex survey design; readers should be cautious when generalizing beyond the participating German schools.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not use plausible values (PV) because the dependent variables are teacher nonverbal immediacy scores derived from computer vision and observer/teacher/student questionnaire scales, not ILSA cognitive achievement PVs. Missingness is handled via full information maximum likelihood (FIML) for the third video/lesson when four teachers lacked data; this is a model-based approach rather than PV-based imputation. Therefore, PV handling is not applicable, while missing-data handling is addressed through FIML under the multilevel path modeling framework.
outcome_summary: The study uses the German TALIS video study (Grades 8–10; mathematics lessons on quadratic equations) and develops a computer-vision model to score teacher nonverbal immediacy (NVI) from classroom video segments. Human raters provided continuous slider ratings for gesture intensity, body pose, and perceived distance; body pose was dropped due to low interrater reliability, and the final NVI scores were derived from a multimodal NVI model combining human-rated assessments with computer-vision features. The analytic design is hierarchical (situations within lessons within teachers) and uses three-level manifest modeling and path models in Mplus. Key results show that NVI variance is mostly situation-specific (≈71.7%), while NVI is positively associated with observer-rated encouragement/warmth (β = .14 at Level 1; β = .35 at Level 2) and with autonomy support (teacher- and student-rated at Level 3, both β ≈ .36–.43). NVI is not significantly related to positive student–teacher relationships. Limitations include correlational inference (no causal identification), unreported ML algorithm details in the provided text, and missing-data handling via FIML for video 3 only.
null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is dense for sampling, measures, and multilevel results, but the provided text does not specify the exact machine learning algorithm(s) used to train the computer-vision NVI model (e.g., CNN architecture, regression/classification method). As a result, ml_techniques.primary and all_techniques cannot be populated without inventing model names; the study still qualifies as predictive because it uses ML to generate NVI scores from video inputs.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the German TALIS video study data. Included 50 teachers (46% women) and their 1,140 students from Grades 8–10 across 38 schools, but for the ML NVI model development only 46 teachers were included because 4 had unavailable or low-quality video material. For the main analyses, only videos 1–2 were used for RQ2 because posttest support measures referred to the first two recorded lessons; video 3 was excluded from RQ2 due to timing of recording relative to posttest. For NVI scoring, segments were included only when they were suitable for computer vision analysis: no excessive camera movement, teacher delivered frontal presentations, teacher remained fully visible, and the teacher did not leave the frame; 30-s segments were temporally matched to 16-min observer-rated segments. For the ML model training/validation, video segments were partitioned at the teacher level (no teacher overlap between training and validation), and body-pose (relaxation) was excluded from subsequent analysis due to low interrater reliability.
effect_size: ICCteacher = 0.225 (22.5% teacher-level variance), ICClesson = 0.056 (5.6% lesson-level variance), ICCsituation = 0.717 (≈71.7% situation-level variance).
primary_finding: Using German TALIS video study the study leveraged teacher-level covariates (gender, teaching experience, school type) and observer-rated socioemotional support to analyze how machine learning-assessed NVI varied across teachers, lessons, and 30-s teaching situations, finding that 22.5% of NVI variance was between teachers while most variance (≈71.7%) was at the situation level. This indicates that teacher nonverbal immediacy is not purely trait-like and that teacher training and feedback should target situationally adaptive nonverbal behaviors rather than only stable personal characteristics.
confounders: Teacher gender; Teaching experience; School type (academic vs nonacademic); Autonomy support (teacher-rated); Autonomy support (student-rated); Positive student–teacher relationships (teacher-rated); Positive student–teacher relationships (student-rated); Socioemotional support (observer-rated)

title: Contrastive modelling of self‐regulated inquiry behaviours across nations: Evidence from TIMSS 2023 Earth Science
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2023 International Database Grade 8 Earth Science process files and the corresponding Earth Science plausible values, restricted to five countries (Chile, the United Arab Emirates, England, Korea, Turkey) and to a final analytic sample of 25,234 students after preprocessing. The manuscript lists sampling/adjustment weights (e.g., TOTWGT and WGTFAC1–WGTFAC3) in the key-variable table, but it does not explicitly state whether these complex survey weights were applied in the contrastive learning, clustering, and cross-national statistical tests. Because the core modeling is contrastive self-supervised representation learning followed by K-means clustering (and UMAP visualization), the paper does not describe a weight-aware estimation strategy; therefore, weighting usage is unclear from the text. Analysts should consult the TIMSS IDB Analyzer documentation and the authors’ analysis code (if available) to confirm whether TOTWGT/WGTFAC* were used when estimating embedding-cluster differences and country-wise tests.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2023 Grade 8 Earth Science digital process data (BSPM8) from five countries (Chile, UAE, England, Korea, Turkey), extracting 1176 standardized screen-level indicators capturing screen visit frequency (F), first-visit time (R), and total time on screen (S). Missing process indicators were handled with mean imputation and features were z-standardized; students were retained only from the top and bottom 25% of Earth Science achievement to form proxy extremes, excluding the middle 50% to maximize contrast. A SimCLR-style contrastive representation learning model (MLP encoder with a 128-dimensional projection head; NT-Xent loss) produced embeddings that were clustered with K-means (k=2), yielding strong separability (silhouette = 0.85). Cross-national tests showed no systematic differences in embedding norms across countries (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.6867) and poor country-based clustering (negative silhouette), suggesting generalizable inquiry structures. The higher-achieving cluster showed an average Earth Science mean plausible value about 150 points higher than the lower-achieving cluster, but the strategic/non-strategic profile construction used achievement quartiles as anchors, so results are correlational rather than causal.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2023 Grade 8 Earth Science digital process data (BSPM8 process files) and corresponding Earth Science plausible values. Preprocessing extracted 1176 standardized process indicators (screen visit frequency F, first-visit time R, total time on screen S) and applied mean imputation for missing process indicators, then z-standardized features. For contrastive pair construction, achievement quartiles were used only to create proxy extremes: students in the top 25% and bottom 25% of Earth Science achievement were retained as anchors, while the middle 50% were excluded to maximize behavioral contrast; the final analytic sample comprised 25,234 students across Chile, the UAE, England, Korea, and Turkey.
effect_size: Contrastive training: NT-Xent loss plateau ~0.14 by final epoch; clustering separability: K-means silhouette score = 0.85 (k=2); cross-country clustering by country labels: silhouette score = -0.2399; Kruskal-Wallis on embedding norms across countries: H = 2.2673, p = 0.6867. Additional analysis (Earth Science achievement (Plausible Values) difference between clusters): Cluster-level achievement gap: average Earth Science mean plausible value in the higher-achieving cluster is ~150 points higher than the lower-achieving cluster; distributional evidence: higher-achieving cluster shows narrower interquartile range than the lower-achieving cluster (exact PV summary statistics not numerically reported beyond the ~150-point difference).
primary_finding: Using TIMSS 2023 Grade 8 Earth Science process data, the study leveraged screen visit frequency (F), first-visit time (R), total time on screen (S), and language of assessment to derive a latent strategic vs non-strategic inquiry profile via contrastive representation learning followed by K-means clustering, finding two well-separated clusters (silhouette = 0.85) that align with SRL-interpretable monitoring-oriented vs surface/fast navigation patterns. This indicates that embedding-based process profiling can support adaptive assessment and real-time scaffolding that targets metacognitive regulation behaviors, while the negative country-label separability suggests these behavioral structures generalize across diverse education systems (though the strategic/non-strategic labels were anchored using achievement quartiles, limiting causal interpretation).
confounders: Country; Sex; Age; Language of assessment; Screen visit frequency (F); First-visit time (R); Total time on screen (S); Earth Science plausible values; Administration quality flag; Reliability/participation flag; Participation quality flag 1; Participation quality flag 2; Weight factor 1 (WGTFAC1); Weight factor 2 (WGTFAC2); Weight factor 3 (WGTFAC3)

title: Evaluating Neural Networks Architectures for Competency Prediction from Process Data Using PISA Computer-Based Mathematics Assessment
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the U.S. sample from the PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics assessment (CBMA) and constructs an analytic dataset from process logs for 10 mathematics items within CBMA units. The analytic sample is restricted to students with complete data across all ten items for the assessment-level latent proficiency model (n=376), while item-level models use item-specific samples (n=378–402) after excluding missing/invalid responses. The manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures; instead, it focuses on model comparison via stratified student-level cross-validation. Because the models are neural networks trained on process sequences, the paper does not describe any weight-aware estimation, so results should be interpreted as predictive performance on the analyzed U.S. CBMA sample rather than population-representative estimates.
outcome_summary: The study uses the U.S. sample of the PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics assessment (CBMA) process data to compare recurrent neural network architectures (RNN, GRU, LSTM) for predicting (i) item-level correctness and (ii) assessment-level latent proficiency. For assessment-level prediction, the dependent variable is PV1 (a single plausible value) derived from the full 30-item mathematics assessment; the analytic sample for this model includes students with complete data across 10 items (n=376). Across item-level models, most items achieved AUC > 0.6 and Kappa > 0.25, with CM038Q06 near chance (AUC≈0.5; Kappa≈0). At the assessment level, adding expert-engineered process features to action-sequence inputs improved accuracy (correlations up to 0.62; RMSE reductions in most configurations) but increased training time. The paper uses student-level stratified 5-fold cross-validation to reduce leakage and applies SHAP for interpretability; however, it does not report survey-weighted inference and uses only PV1, so generalization and causal interpretation are limited.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the U.S. PISA 2012 CBMA process-data sample for computer-based mathematics. Item-level models were trained on item-specific samples with missing or invalid responses excluded (item-level n ranges from 378 to 402). Assessment-level latent proficiency models used only students with complete data across all ten items (n=376, 95%). Sequential inputs were padded with zeros to equal length per item, and cross-validation splits were performed at the student level to prevent leakage.
effect_size: Neural networks (RNN/GRU/LSTM) with sequential features vs sequential+expert features. Correlation with PV1: 0.28–0.62 (Table 3). Best improvement: two-layer LSTM with 100 nodes correlation increased from 0.36 to 0.62. RMSE decreased in most configurations (e.g., one-layer RNN with 100 nodes RMSE 1.16→0.93). Training time increased when adding expert features (e.g., one-layer LSTM 50 nodes 94.3→1189.32 s).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2012 CBMA U.S. the study leveraged expert-engineered features together with action-sequence inputs (and varied RNN/GRU/LSTM architecture, layers, and nodes) to predict assessment-level latent proficiency (PV1). It found that adding expert-engineered features improved predictive accuracy (correlations up to 0.62 and lower RMSE in most configurations) but increased training time. This indicates that combining domain-informed process summaries with sequence models can improve early proficiency estimation for adaptive testing, though computational cost may rise and results are based on a single PV (PV1) rather than combined PV inference.
confounders: Gender; Grade level; Birth year; Average actions per item; Unique actions count; Predominant action proportion; Predominant score proportion; Expert-engineered features; Sequence length; Model type (RNN/GRU/LSTM); Number of layers; Number of hidden nodes

title: Artificial Intelligence, Academic Resilience, and Gender Equity in Education Systems: Ethical Challenges, Predictive Bias, and Governance Implications
authors: F.R. Trejo-Macotela; G.C. González-Flores; M.O.-E. (author name not fully specified in provided text); M.F. González-Pérez
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 student-level microdata and constructs a binary academic resilience target using country-relative ESCS and PV1MATH quartiles. The analytic sample is defined after removing incomplete observations for the selected variables, yielding 613,744 students across 80 educational systems. Although PISA provides sampling weights, the authors explicitly do not incorporate sampling weights into the modelling process, aligning with a predictive/pattern-recognition objective rather than population-level inference. As a result, the reported performance and fairness diagnostics reflect relationships within the observed sample and may not generalize perfectly to the underlying national populations represented by PISA’s complex survey design.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2022 student microdata (613,744 students across 80 educational systems) to predict a binary academic resilience indicator defined within each country as ESCS in the bottom quartile and mathematics achievement in the top quartile using PV1MATH. After median-based imputation for missing values and SMOTE applied only to the training set, six supervised classifiers were compared using hold-out evaluation (80/20) and 5-fold cross-validation for the best model. Ensemble boosting models performed best: CatBoost achieved AUC=0.941 (CV AUC=0.949) with F1=0.275 and PR-AUC=0.332. Fairness diagnostics for CatBoost showed gender disparities: males had a higher positive prediction rate (0.155 vs 0.110) and higher false positive rates (0.138 vs 0.089), with demographic parity ratio≈1.40 and equality-of-opportunity gap≈0.053. Limitations include omission of PISA sampling weights, use of a single plausible value (PV1MATH), and the fact that SHAP/feature importance support interpretability but do not establish causal effects.
ml_all_techniques: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2022 student dataset and retained students with complete information on the selected variables (gender, immigration status, grade repetition, ESCS, PV1READ, PV1SCIE, and PV1MATH). The dependent variable (academic resilience) was constructed within each country using ESCS and PV1MATH country-specific quartiles; missing values in selected variables were imputed using median-based imputation. The final analytic sample after removing incomplete observations comprised 613,744 students across 80 educational systems.
effect_size: Model comparison (hold-out 80/20 + 5-fold CV for best model): CatBoost AUC=0.941, F1=0.275, PR-AUC=0.332; XGBoost AUC=0.941, F1=0.276, PR-AUC=0.332; LightGBM AUC=0.941, F1=0.278, PR-AUC=0.334; Gradient Boosting AUC=0.940, F1=0.270, PR-AUC=0.321; Random Forest AUC=0.931, F1=0.310, PR-AUC=0.249; Logistic Regression AUC=0.930, F1=0.239, PR-AUC=0.253. Best model (CatBoost) 5-fold CV average ROC-AUC=0.949.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 the study leveraged immigration status, socioeconomic status (ESCS), grade repetition, and reading/science achievement (PV1READ/PV1SCIE) to predict academic resilience defined by ESCS bottom-quartile and PV1MATH top-quartile, finding that ensemble boosting models (especially CatBoost) achieved the highest discrimination (AUC≈0.941; CV AUC≈0.949). This indicates that non-linear ensemble models can effectively identify resilient students under socioeconomic disadvantage, but the reliance on PV1MATH (single plausible value), median imputation, and omission of PISA sampling weights means results should be treated as predictive associations rather than population-representative estimates.
confounders: Gender (FEMALE); Immigration status (IMMIG); Grade repetition (REPEAT); Socioeconomic status (ESCS); Reading achievement (PV1READ); Science achievement (PV1SCIE)

title: Using machine learning to predict student mathematics performance in six East Asian countries: evidence from PISA 2022
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for mathematics achievement among 15-year-old students in six East Asian education systems, with an analytic sample of 26,718 after outlier removal. The manuscript describes preprocessing (median imputation, RobustScaler, SelectKBest) and a train/test split with cross-validated hyperparameter tuning, but it does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights. Because the analysis is implemented in scikit-learn with standard ML models (e.g., XGBoost/LightGBM/Random Forest) and no weight-aware estimation is described, the weighting strategy is unclear from the text and should be treated as potentially unweighted. Analysts using the PISA database should apply the appropriate student sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) when producing population-representative estimates; however, the paper’s ML pipeline does not document this step.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2022 mathematics microdata for 15-year-old students from Korea, Singapore, Japan, Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, and Macao (final analytic sample N = 26,718 after outlier removal). Mathematics performance is modeled as the mean of ten plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH), with missing values imputed via median imputation and predictors standardized using RobustScaler; feature selection retains the top 50 predictors. Models are trained on an 80% training set and evaluated on a 20% held-out test set, with hyperparameter tuning via 5-fold cross-validation. Among XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest, AdaBoost, Elastic Net, and linear regression, XGBoost performs best with R2 = 0.5703 (RMSE = 65.06; MAE = 51.59) and AUC-regression = 0.8104. SHAP indicates mathematics self-efficacy is the dominant predictor, but the authors emphasize the cross-sectional, non-causal nature of the data and note that averaged PVs are a simplification relative to OECD multiple-imputation recommendations.
ml_all_techniques: XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest, AdaBoost, Elastic Net, Linear Regression
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 mathematics data for 15-year-old students from Korea, Singapore, Japan, Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, and Macao. title: Supervised Machine Learning-Based Multiclass Classification and Interpretable Feature Importance Analysis of Teacher Job Satisfaction
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the PISA 2022 optional teacher questionnaire for Morocco, with teachers sampled from the same 178 schools as the student survey and with up to 25 teachers per school. The analytic file contains 2998 complete teacher records and 254 predictor variables after excluding satisfaction outcomes and school identifiers/replication weights. Although the PISA teacher file provides final teacher weights (W_FTCHRWT*) and multiple replication weights (W_FTCHRWT77–W_FTCHRWT80), the authors state that school identifiers and replication weights were excluded from the final predictor set and do not report applying complex survey weights in the ML training/evaluation. Because the models are standard supervised ML classifiers (e.g., XGBoost, random forest, SVM, ANN) that do not natively incorporate PISA complex-survey weights, the analysis appears effectively unweighted; this may affect generalisability and uncertainty quantification under clustered sampling. Preprocessing included replacing PISA missing-value codes with NaN, dropping features with ≥300 missing entries, and applying mode imputation to remaining missing values.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are derived satisfaction indices (SATJOB and SATTEACH) recoded into three classes using explicit thresholds on standardized IRT-based scores, rather than using PV-based achievement outcomes. Missing data handling is reported: missing-value codes were converted to NaN, high-missing features were removed, and remaining missing entries were imputed using mode (SimpleImputer). Therefore, PV handling is not part of the analysis pipeline, while missing-data strategy is documented.
outcome_summary: The study applies supervised multiclass ML to the PISA 2022 optional teacher questionnaire in Morocco, using 2998 lower-secondary teachers and 254 cleaned predictor variables. Two standardized satisfaction indices (SATJOB and SATTEACH) were recoded into three balanced classes (low < −0.5, medium −0.5 to 0.5, high > 0.5) and modelled with nine classifiers using identical 80/20 stratified train–test splits and hyperparameter tuning. For SATJOB_class, XGBoost performed best with Accuracy 0.61 and Macro F1 0.61; for SATTEACH_class, Random Forest led with Accuracy 0.59 and Macro F1 0.59, both substantially above chance (~0.33). Feature importance (tree-based gain and permutation) and SHAP were used to identify workload, leadership support, and psychological perceptions/retention intentions as key predictors. Limitations include moderate predictive accuracy, cross-sectional self-report data (correlational, not causal), and an apparent lack of complex-survey weight incorporation in ML training/evaluation.
ml_all_techniques: Logistic Regression, k-NN, Naive Bayes, SVM, Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost, AdaBoost, Neural Network
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2022 Morocco teacher questionnaire optional module for lower-secondary (modal grade for 15-year-olds), yielding 2998 complete teacher records. Preprocessing replaced PISA missing-value codes (e.g., 9, 99, 95, 97, 98, 998, 999, 9999, 99,999) with NaN; features with 300 or more missing entries (≈10% of 2998) were excluded. Remaining missing values were imputed using mode (SimpleImputer). For modelling, satisfaction outcome variables (SATJOB, SATTEACH) and school identifiers/replication weights were removed from the predictor set, leaving 254 predictor variables.

This indicates that combining workload-management and leadership-support interventions with attention to teachers’ perceived meaningfulness and emotional well-being may improve job satisfaction classification in Morocco, though the results are correlational and not causal due to the cross-sectional design and the use of predictive feature importance/SHAP rather than causal identification.

title: Teachers’ team innovativeness in TALIS 2018: An empirical and simulation study using glmmLasso for multilevel data
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 microdata for Korean middle school teachers and principals, with teachers nested within schools (multilevel structure). In data cleaning, the authors explicitly removed weighting-related variables (e.g., SCHWGT) from the predictor set, but they do not state whether complex survey weights were applied in estimation. The modeling approach (glmmLasso, LASSO, elastic net) is a penalized regression framework that is not described as weight-aware, so the manuscript provides insufficient detail to confirm whether sampling weights were used for population-representative inference. Missingness was handled via k-nearest neighbors imputation using Gower distance on complete observations, after excluding variables with ≥20% missingness.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is a TALIS scale score (T3TEAM) derived from confirmatory factor analysis of Likert items, not a PV-based cognitive achievement score. Missing data handling is reported as k-nearest neighbors imputation using Gower distance, so the paper does not omit the missing-data strategy.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 Korean middle school teachers and principals (2895 teachers; 163 principals) using teachers’ team innovativeness (T3TEAM) as a continuous scale score derived from four Likert items. For prediction and variable selection, the authors compare glmmLasso (penalized GLMM) against LASSO and elastic net, using repeated train/test splitting (7:3) and RMSE as the predictive error. In the empirical analysis, RMSE distributions across methods overlap (95% CIs), but glmmLasso is more parsimonious and stable, selecting far fewer predictors on average (≈30.48 vs ≈92.41 and ≈111.01). In simulation (ICC≈0.09), glmmLasso again shows similar RMSE (≈2.154) while substantially improving variable-selection accuracy at level-2 (IC2=1 vs IC2=6–7). A key limitation is that the manuscript does not clearly report whether TALIS sampling weights were applied in estimation, and the negative association for shared responsibility is correlational rather than causal.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 Korean middle school teacher and principal responses. The analytic dataset was constructed by removing irrelevant variables (including IDs and weighting/administration variables such as SCHWGT and VERSION), excluding TALIS variables with ≥20% missingness, dummy-coding categorical items (and treating multi-category items as grouped dummy variables), merging teacher and principal datasets, and retaining 2895 teachers and 163 principals with 571 explanatory variables. Missing values in the remaining predictors were imputed using k-nearest neighbors with Gower distance (k=25) based on 644 complete observations.
effect_size: Empirical Study I: RMSE distributions for glmmLasso, LASSO, and elastic net had overlapping 95% confidence intervals (exact RMSE values not reported in the abstract; Table 2 reports RMSE mean ~1.775–1.792 with overlapping CIs). glmmLasso selected fewer variables with lower variability (mean selected ~30.48, SD=9.98) versus LASSO (~92.41, SD=133.82) and elastic net (~111.01, SD=190.61).
primary_finding: Using TALIS 2018 (KOR) the study leveraged joint activities across classes, work with other teachers, team conferences, teacher self-efficacy for motivating low-interest students, and shared beliefs about teaching to predict teachers’ team innovativeness (T3TEAM), finding that most selected predictors showed positive associations while shared responsibility for school issues (TT3G48D) showed a negative association. This indicates that school policies should prioritize structured teacher collaboration and supportive, innovation-friendly school cultures, while carefully considering how “shared responsibility” is implemented so it does not undermine teachers’ perceived ownership of innovation.

title: Evaluating Neural Networks Architectures for Competency Prediction from Process Data Using PISA Computer-Based Mathematics Assessment
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the U.S. sample from the PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics assessment (CBMA) and restricts the analytic dataset to 402 students with complete action-sequence data for the specified CBMA units/items. The paper reports item-level sample sizes (378–402) and uses complete data across all ten items for the assessment-level model (n=376), but it does not report applying PISA complex survey weights or any replicate-weight procedure. Because the analysis is based on neural-network models (RNN/GRU/LSTM) trained with TensorFlow and evaluated via student-level stratified cross-validation, the manuscript does not describe weight-aware estimation; this suggests an unweighted ML pipeline. The main preprocessing described is sequence padding with zeros to equalize sequence lengths per item and student-level fold splitting to prevent leakage.
outcome_summary: The study uses the U.S. sample from the PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics assessment (CBMA) process-data to train recurrent neural networks (RNN, GRU, LSTM) that predict (i) item-level correctness and (ii) assessment-level latent proficiency. Item-level models are evaluated with AUC and Cohen’s Kappa, showing good discrimination for most items (AUC mostly >0.6; Kappa mostly >0.25) with CM038Q06 near chance (AUC ~0.5; Kappa ~0). Assessment-level models predict PV1 (single plausible value) from action sequences of 10 CBMA items and are evaluated with Pearson correlation and RMSE; correlations range from 0.28 to 0.62, with the best result for a two-layer LSTM with 100 nodes when expert-engineered features are included. Adding expert-engineered features generally improves accuracy (and interpretability via SHAP) but increases training time, and architectural complexity beyond simple configurations yields little benefit. Limitations include an unweighted ML pipeline (no survey-weight discussion) and the use of SHAP for feature importance rather than causal inference.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the publicly available PISA 2012 CBMA process-data dataset for the U.S. sample. The study draws on 402 U.S. students for item-level models, with item-level sample sizes reduced (378–402) due to missing or invalid responses. For the assessment-level latent proficiency model, only students with complete data across all ten items were retained (n=376, 95%). Sequential inputs were constructed from action sequences for the ten CBMA items and padded with zeros to a fixed maximum sequence length per item; cross-validation splitting was performed at the student level to avoid student-level leakage.
effect_size: AUC: average >0.6 for most items; exception CM038Q06 ~0.5. Cohen’s Kappa: average >0.25 for most items; exception CM038Q06 ~0.0. Expert-engineered features: slightly higher AUC across most conditions; minor Kappa changes; training time generally reduced when adding expert-engineered features.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2012 CBMA U.S. process-the study leveraged expert-engineered process summaries (e.g., total response time, time before first attempt, total number of events) together with action-sequence inputs to predict item-level correctness, finding that adding expert-engineered features produced only small AUC/Kappa gains but generally reduced training time. This indicates that for item-level prediction in CBMA tasks, simpler sequence-only neural models may be sufficient for accuracy, while expert features mainly help computational efficiency and interpretability rather than substantially improving discrimination.
confounders: Total response time; Time on each event; Time before first attempt; Rapid response indicator; Total number of events; Event frequencies; Average number of actions; Number of unique actions; Predominant action proportion; Predominant score proportion

title: Understanding Adults’ Spatial Cognitive Processes: A Time-Embedded N-Grams Model with Machine Learning
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses restricted PIAAC Cycle 1 microdata for the U.S. and restricts the analytic sample to adults who completed the numeracy “Map” interactive item, yielding N=596 after excluding 100 unmatched cases. The manuscript does not report applying PIAAC complex survey weights or any replicate-weight procedure in the ML training/evaluation pipeline. Because the models are Random Forest and XGBoost, the authors do not describe a weight-aware estimation approach; thus weighting strategy is unclear from the text. Analysts should treat the results as conditional on the modeled sample and consider whether population-representative inference requires applying PIAAC sampling weights (and replicate weights if used) when generalizing beyond the analytic subset.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are derived from the Map item’s correctness and the PIAAC numeracy proficiency level categories (e.g., incorrect–low/high and correct–low/high), rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. As a result, plausible-value generation/combining is not part of the modeling target. The manuscript reports missing counts for some background variables (e.g., ICT familiarity) but does not describe a missing-data handling method for the ML predictors/feature set, representing a reporting gap for reproducibility.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes sequential log (process) data from the PIAAC 2012 Cycle 1 U.S. numeracy “Map” interactive item, restricting to adults who completed the item and excluding 100 unmatched cases (final N=596). It predicts a four-category outcome combining Map correctness (correct vs incorrect) and numeracy proficiency level (lower: Level 2 and below; higher: Level 3–5) using Random Forest and XGBoost on (i) standard n-grams and (ii) time-embedded n-grams that discretize elapsed pauses using local action-pair time distributions, plus nine aggregate process indicators. Across 10-fold cross-validation, both models achieved accuracy above 0.70; Random Forest with time-embedded n-grams reached Accuracy=0.718 (SD=0.028) and Precision=0.774 (SD=0.045), with XGBoost showing slightly lower accuracy but comparable F1 (0.699). The most informative predictors were time-related indicators (total response time, time to first action, time to last action) and efficient action patterns (redundancy ratio). Limitations include unclear survey-weight use and a lack of documented missing-data handling for the ML features, and the interpretation of pauses as cognitive load remains ambiguous.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the U.S. PIAAC 2012 Cycle 1 dataset and restricted to adults who completed the numeracy “Map” interactive numeracy item. From 696 respondents who completed the Map item, 100 cases were excluded because process and response files could not be matched, resulting in a final analytic sample of N=596. The study further defines outcome groups using PIAAC numeracy proficiency levels (lower: Level 2 and below; higher: Level 3–5) and Map item correctness (correct vs incorrect).
effect_size: Random Forest (time-embedded n-grams): Accuracy 0.718 (0.028), Precision 0.774 (0.045), Recall 0.612 (0.048), F1 0.682 (0.034). XGBoost (time-embedded n-grams): Accuracy 0.708 (0.042), Precision 0.720 (0.059), Recall 0.683 (0.046), F1 0.699 (0.037). Validation: 10-fold cross-validation; mean (SD) reported across folds.
primary_finding: Using PIAAC 2012 Cycle 1 (U.S.) Numeracy “Map” interactive item process data, the study leveraged total response time, time to first action, time to last action, redundancy ratio, and final-response actions count to classify respondents into incorrect–low/high and correct–low/high numeracy categories, finding that time-related and direction-related sequential features were the most predictive. This indicates that incorporating temporal spacing and efficient navigation behaviors into digital numeracy assessment analytics may improve identification of adults who need targeted spatial-numeracy support, though the study is predictive (not causal) and does not document survey-weight or missing-data handling for the ML pipeline.

title: Exploring the impact of ICT interaction on students’ creative thinking across performance levels: an explainable AI perspective
authors: Cai X; Bi Y; Feng Y
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for five East Asian economies (Singapore, Hong Kong-China, Macao-China, Chinese Taipei, and Korea) and constructs a multiclass target from the OECD creative thinking score distribution (CRT_AVG_10) aggregated into three bands. The analytic dataset is further restricted by preprocessing of ICT questionnaire features (masking values 95–100 as missing) and then applying listwise deletion for missing values, yielding 17,327 samples. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA complex survey weights or replicate weights in the ML training/evaluation pipeline, and it does not name any weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT). Because the models are tree-based classifiers (Random Forest, LightGBM, XGBoost) and the paper does not describe weight-aware estimation, the safest interpretation is that analyses were conducted without explicit survey-weight incorporation.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata from five East Asian economies (Singapore, Hong Kong-China, Macao-China, Chinese Taipei, and Korea) and predicts a three-class creative thinking level (low/medium/high) derived from the OECD creative thinking score CRT_AVG_10 using the average of plausible values. ICT interaction questionnaire items IC170–IC183 serve as predictors, after preprocessing that masks non-informative responses (95–100) as missing and applies listwise deletion, resulting in 17,327 samples. For multiclass classification, the authors compare Random Forest, LightGBM, and XGBoost under 10-fold cross-validation and internal/external validation; XGBoost is selected as best-performing, with external-validation accuracy around 0.676 (and notably improved low-class recall under ADASYN). Model interpretation relies on SHAP (TreeExplainer/TreeExplainer), but the authors explicitly treat SHAP attributions as non-causal. The manuscript does not report survey-weight usage, so results may not fully reflect population-representative estimates under PISA’s complex design.
sample_filtering_criteria: Data are drawn from the PISA 2022 database and restricted to five East Asian economies (Singapore, Hong Kong-China, Macao-China, Chinese Taipei, and Korea). The dependent variable is constructed from the OECD creative thinking score field CRT_AVG_10, which is then regrouped into three classes (bottom 21.7% = Class 0, middle 51.3% = Class 1, top 27% = Class 2) using smoothed thresholds. Predictor variables are ICT interaction questionnaire items IC170–IC183. During preprocessing, responses coded 95–100 (treated as non-informative) are masked and converted to missing (NaN), and then any sample containing missing values is removed (listwise deletion). After multistage filtering, the final modeling dataset contains 17,327 samples.
effect_size: XGBoost (ADASYN-balanced training; external validation): Accuracy 0.6763; macro F1 not reported in table; per-class precision/recall/F1 reported (Low: Precision 0.3810, Recall 0.1798, F1 0.2443; Middle: Precision 0.6477, Recall 0.6959, F1 0.7231; High: Precision 0.6709, Recall 0.7256, F1 0.7243).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 creative thinking the study leveraged ICT interaction questionnaire items (notably online information-search self-efficacy, smartphone use outside school, and sharing made-up information) to predict students’ creative thinking level (low/medium/high), finding that XGBoost achieved the best overall multiclass performance and that SHAP-identified ICT behaviors differentiate all three creativity bands. This indicates that ICT policies and classroom practices should prioritize goal-aligned, information-literate, and production-oriented digital activities (rather than frequency alone) to support students at lower creative-thinking levels, though the SHAP-based evidence is predictive/associational rather than causal.

title: A machine‐learning model of academic resilience in the times of the COVID‐19 pandemic: Evidence drawn from 79 countries/economies in the PISA 2022 mathematics study
authors: Kwok-cheung Cheung; Pou-seong Sit; Jia-qi Zheng; Chi-chio Lam; Soi-kei Mak; Man-kai Ieong
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata and constructs an analytic sample of ESCS-disadvantaged students, then labels academically resilient students (ARS) vs non-academically resilient students (NRS) using an international (across 79 countries/economies) top-quartile mathematics performance criterion. The manuscript describes extensive ML preprocessing within 10-fold cross-validation modules (kNN imputation, normalization, and SMOTETomek for class imbalance), but it does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the models are standard random-forest classifiers implemented in Python (scikit-learn) and the paper does not mention weight-aware estimation, the analysis is treated as unweighted. No BRR/jackknife/Taylor replicate design details or specific PISA weight variable names (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) are provided.
outcome_summary: The study analyzed PISA 2022 mathematics data from 79 countries/economies and defined academic resilience as ESCS bottom-quarter within-country combined with top-quarter mathematics performance across countries. Using a random-forest classifier with 10-fold cross-validation, the model distinguished academically resilient (ARS) vs non-resilient (NRS) students with Accuracy=90.54%, ROC-AUC=96.79%, Precision=93.13%, Recall=87.58%, and F-measure=90.26%. The authors selected an optimal subset of 35 features via recursive feature elimination and used SHAP to estimate each feature’s direction and magnitude of contribution. Key patterns included higher math self-efficacy and stable emotional state, lower truancy, and positive future aspirations among ARS, with additional COVID-19-related school/remote-instruction and ICT-related factors. Methodologically, the analysis used kNN imputation for missing data, PV handling via a single plausible value (PVMATH1), and did not report applying PISA sampling/replicate weights; SHAP provides predictive contributions rather than causal effects.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 mathematics study data across 79 countries/economies. Followed OECD international operational definition of academic resilience: (1) selected students whose ESCS is in the bottom quarter within their own country/economy (relative adversity); (2) among these, selected students whose mathematics performance is in the top quarter across the 79 countries/economies (fixed positive adaptation); (3) coded ARS=1 and remaining ESCS-disadvantaged students as NRS=0. For mathematics performance, used the first plausible value PVMATH1 (randomly chose PV1) from the 10 PISA plausible values. Teacher questionnaire variables were largely unavailable because only 18 countries/economies completed teacher questionnaires, constraining which contextual factors could be used.
effect_size: Random Forest (10-fold cross-validation): Accuracy=90.54%, ROC-AUC=96.79%, Precision=93.13%, Recall=87.58%, F-measure=90.26%; optimal feature subset size=35 (top 35 features).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics the study leveraged math self-efficacy, math anxiety, familiarity with math concepts, truancy, and future aspirations to classify academic resilience status (ARS vs NRS), finding that the random-forest model achieved strong discrimination (ROC-AUC=96.79%) and that the top 35 features largely validated the prior resilience framework; SHAP was used to quantify feature contributions, but the paper is cross-sectional so SHAP-based importance should not be interpreted as causal effects. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

title: Hierarchical clustering of the pre-exam anxiety levels in physically inactive and active adolescent students from 56 countries: an observational study using PISA program data
authors: SE; JT; PF; LL; AS; LB; RF; PA; PV; AM
journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 data (56 countries) but does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures in the clustering workflow. The authors state they did not have access to the raw dataset and instead relied on OECD-published chi-square outputs and country-level mean percentage anxiety values, which implies the analysis is conducted on aggregated country summaries rather than student-level weighted estimates. Because hierarchical clustering is applied to country-level anxiety percentages (and not to PV-based achievement scores), the manuscript does not specify any complex-survey variance estimation or weight variable usage. As a result, readers should treat the clustering outputs as descriptive patterns across countries rather than population-representative inference unless the authors’ weighting approach is clarified.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is country-level pre-exam anxiety percentages by physical activity status (low vs high), derived from PISA 2018 rather than modeled using PV-based cognitive achievement scores. The manuscript does not describe any missing-data strategy for the underlying student responses used to compute these country percentages, representing a reporting gap for transparency. Because the analysis is performed on aggregated country means and the authors do not provide the raw-data processing steps, the missing-data handling cannot be verified from the text.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 country-level pre-exam anxiety percentages for 15-year-old students, stratified by physical activity status (low/no regular activity vs high/moderate-vigorous regular activity). It performs hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distance and selects the number of clusters via dendrogram cut at 20% plus silhouette score and dispersion metrics. For low physical activity students, the best solution used 5 clusters with silhouette = 0.60, WCSS = 309.27, 96% variability explained (BCSS), and BCSS/WCSS = 22.10; Brazil (82%) and the Dominican Republic (81%) were among the most anxious. For high physical activity students, the best solution used 4 clusters with silhouette = 0.56, WCSS = 632.80, 92% variability explained, and BCSS/WCSS = 11.18; Malaysia (82%), Brazil (81%), and Costa Rica (81%) were most anxious. Across countries, the average anxiety difference between low vs high physical activity was −3% (p < 0.01), with Russia (+11%) and the UAE (+4%) as exceptions. Limitations include reliance on aggregated country means (no student-level PV modeling), lack of reported missing-data handling, and no explicit survey-weighted inference.
null_fields_interpretation: The paper is an observational clustering study using hierarchical clustering on country-level anxiety percentages rather than a supervised predictive ML model. As a result, no predictive algorithm is evaluated for accuracy/AUC/RMSE, and the schema’s ML technique fields are left empty (primary = null, all_techniques = []). The study still reports clustering quality metrics (silhouette, WCSS/BCSS), which are appropriate for exploratory clustering but do not map to the schema’s predictive-model algorithm list.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 country-level pre-exam anxiety percentages for 15-year-old students, restricted to countries with available anxiety and physical activity classification. Students were grouped into two physical activity statuses using PISA’s operational definition: low physical activity (no regular physical activity) vs high physical activity (moderate to vigorous regular physical activity). The clustering was performed separately for each physical activity group using country-level mean anxiety percentages; the authors also note that PISA included anxiety and physical activity only for students who reported feeling well-prepared for their exams, to reduce confounding from academic preparation.

title: Why do East Asian students do so well in mathematics? A machine learning study
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade mathematics achievement and associated student, teacher, and principal questionnaire variables for five East Asian economies (Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Japan, Korea, Singapore). The manuscript reports handling of plausible values by running separate random-forest regressions for each of the five mathematics plausible values and averaging the results, but it does not report applying TIMSS complex-sample student/school weights or any replicate-weight procedure. Because the analysis is implemented with the R randomForest package and the paper does not mention weight-aware estimation tools (e.g., IEA IDB Analyzer, bifiesurvey, WeMix, intsvy), survey weights are not documented as being incorporated. Analysts using TIMSS microdata should consider whether to apply TIMSS sampling weights and replicate weights when estimating uncertainty, especially given the nested structure (students within classes/schools within economies).
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade mathematics achievement for five East Asian economies (Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Japan, Korea, Singapore; N=21,340 students) using a random-forest regression model with 22 socio-ecological predictors drawn from student, teacher, and principal questionnaires. Mathematics achievement was modeled on the TIMSS mathematics scale (number, algebra, geometry, data/probability) and handled plausible values by running separate random-forest regressions for each of the five plausible values and averaging the results. Missing data were addressed with MCMC multiple imputation in SPSS 26.0 (missingness 0–5.7%, described as missing completely at random). Model performance showed that the top 11 predictors explained 49% of variance (R2=0.49) with RMSE=0.71, and cross-validation indicated diminishing returns after the 11th variable (mean decreased MSE=0.53 for top 11 vs 0.52 for all 22). The paper does not report applying TIMSS complex-sample weights, and the cross-sectional TIMSS design limits causal interpretation of predictor importance.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade mathematics data for five East Asian economies only (Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Japan, Korea, Singapore). The analytic sample comprises 21,340 eighth-grade students, with associated mathematics teachers (n=1242) and principals (n=802) to supply classroom and school-level predictors. Mathematics achievement was modeled using the TIMSS mathematics achievement scale (number, algebra, geometry, data/probability) and handled missing questionnaire/scale inputs via MCMC multiple imputation in SPSS 26.0; the paper reports missingness was small (0–5.7%) and described as missing completely at random.
effect_size: Random forest regression with 22 predictors; tenfold cross-validation with five repeats. Whole East Asian sample: top 11 variables explained 49% of variance (R2=0.49) with RMSE=0.71; candidate sets: mean decreased MSE (Top 1: 0.78; Top 3: 0.66; Top 6: 0.59; Top 11: 0.53; Top 22: 0.52). Variable importance via mean decrease in accuracy (MDA).
primary_finding: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics the study leveraged students’ confidence in mathematics, student SES, and school emphasis on academic success (plus teaching limitation by student needs and students’ value of mathematics) to predict mathematics achievement, finding that the top three predictors were students’ confidence in mathematics, socioeconomic status, and school emphasis on academic success. This indicates that mathematics improvement strategies in East Asian contexts may yield the largest returns by combining expectancy/engagement supports with SES-sensitive learning supports and school-level goal/expectation reforms, though the study is cross-sectional and does not establish causal effects.
