title: Predicting adolescents’ environmental action: From individual to national-level factors using an explainable machine learning approach
authors: Bo Hu; Jing Gao; Yannuo Feng; Ziqian Xia; Kun Wang; Liuna Geng
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata with a two-stage stratified probability-proportional-to-size design: schools are sampled first, then up to 42 students are sampled within each school. The authors report PISA international response-rate targets at the school (85%, weighted) and student (80%, weighted) levels and state that systems failing to meet thresholds were excluded from the public database, supporting national representativeness within participating countries. In the machine-learning pipeline, the manuscript does not explicitly state whether PISA sampling weights (e.g., student-level or school-level weights) were applied during model training/evaluation; therefore, weight usage is not documented at the analysis stage. The authors do report standard ML preprocessing steps (train/test split, MICE-based predictive mean matching imputation, and SMOTE oversampling) and use SHAP for post-hoc interpretation, but these steps are described without a clear linkage to complex-survey weighting.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are private- and public-sphere environmental actions, which are behavioral/action items rather than PISA cognitive achievement scales with Plausible Values; thus PV handling is not applicable to the modeled outcomes. However, the manuscript does not explicitly confirm whether any PV-based constructs were included among predictors or outcomes, so PV handling is treated as not reported for transparency. Missing data handling is documented via MICE predictive mean matching, but PV-specific documentation is absent because the modeled targets are not PV-based achievement scores.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata from 66 countries (final analytic sample: 420,339 adolescents) to predict two types of adolescent environmental action: private-sphere and public-sphere behaviors. After excluding students who did not answer the environmental-action items, the authors train four ML classifiers (LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest, and an MLP) using a 90/10 train-test split and stratified 10-fold cross-validation with Optuna hyperparameter tuning. Missing values are imputed using MICE predictive mean matching, and class imbalance is addressed with SMOTE. For public-sphere actions, LightGBM achieved the best reported performance on validation/test (Accuracy ≈0.699–0.700; F1 ≈0.698–0.702; AUC ≈0.762–0.767). For private-sphere actions, XGBoost showed the highest accuracy/recall on the test set (Accuracy/Recall 0.833; AUC 0.718), while Random Forest slightly led F1. SHAP is used for interpretability, but the paper notes cross-sectional limitations, and the manuscript does not clearly document whether PISA sampling weights were applied during ML training/evaluation.
ml_all_techniques: LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest, Neural Network
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 for adolescents aged 15 (PISA target population). The analytic sample was restricted to adolescents who answered the environmental-action items; cases who did not answer the environmental-action items were excluded. The final sample comprises 420,339 adolescents from 66 countries. For ML modeling, the dataset was further split into training (90%) and testing (10%) sets, with stratified 10-fold cross-validation applied within the training set.
effect_size: LightGBM (validation): Accuracy 0.699, F1 0.698, Recall 0.699, AUC 0.762. LightGBM (test): Accuracy 0.700, F1 0.702, Recall 0.702, AUC 0.767. XGBoost selected for private-sphere actions (test): Accuracy/Recall 0.833, AUC 0.718; Random Forest highest F1 (0.781 vs 0.772 for LightGBM).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged environmental attitude, critical thinking, climate-change explanatory capacity, sense of life meaning, and school belonging to predict private-sphere environmental actions, finding that individual and school factors were the most influential and that model performance was stronger for private-sphere than public-sphere actions. This indicates that strengthening adolescents’ climate-related knowledge and personal attitudes—supported by school environments that build belonging and supportive discussion—may be an effective pathway for promoting household environmental behaviors, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

title: Combining statistical and machine learning methods to explore German students’ attitudes towards ICT
journal: International Journal of Research & Method in Education
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 German student questionnaire data and the optional ICT familiarity questionnaire. The analytic samples were restricted by removing cases with 100% missing ICT responses due to the ICT questionnaire being optional in Germany (2015: 1,093 removed; 2018: 944 removed), yielding N=5,411 (2015) and N=4,507 (2018). For the multilevel HLM stage, the authors state that they used formulas for analysis with plausible values and replicate weights (Fay’s method with 80 replicates) and averaged estimates for 10 plausible values. However, the manuscript does not report applying student/sampling weights directly in the Random Forest models; the RF steps (missForest imputation and RF classification) are implemented as standard ML procedures without explicit complex-survey weight incorporation, which is consistent with common ML practice. Therefore, weighting is only explicitly discussed for the HLM plausible-values/replicate-weight framework, while RF is treated as unweighted in the absence of explicit weight application details.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes German PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 data to examine how attitudes toward ICT relate to mathematical and scientific literacy. For missing data imputation and for predicting proficiency level categories (below Level 2, Levels 2–4, Level 5+), it uses Random Forest with missForest imputation and RF classification; performance is reported via multiclass AUC (2015 test-set AUC: 67.44% for mathematics and 71.66% for science; similar AUCs on 2018: 69.19% and 68.51%). For association testing with the nested school structure, it fits multilevel HLM random-intercept models using 10 plausible values and Fay’s method (80 replicates), finding that ICT autonomy is significantly and positively associated with both mathematical and scientific literacy, while ICT in social interaction is significantly negative; ICT competence and ICT interest are not significant in the HLM results. A key caveat is that the design is cross-sectional (no causal claims), and the RF steps do not explicitly incorporate complex-survey weights.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used German subsets of PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 student questionnaire data and the optional ICT familiarity questionnaire. Removed cases with 100% missing ICT responses (because the ICT questionnaire was optional in Germany): 1,093 cases (16.81%) removed from the 2015 dataset and 944 cases (17.32%) removed from the 2018 dataset before analysis. For missingness within the remaining data, missingness patterns were checked and RF-based imputation (missForest) was applied; the imputed dataset was then used for subsequent RF classification and HLM analyses. For RF classification, the training set was 80% of the 2015 data (with oversampling of the training set due to class imbalance) and the test set was the remaining 20% of 2015 data; models were also evaluated on the full 2018 dataset.
effect_size: Random Forest classification — multiclass AUC: 67.44% on the 2015 test set (20% hold-out). Class imbalance addressed by oversampling the training set; AUC computed with pROC; variable importance via mean decrease in accuracy (permutation importance).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 Germany the study leveraged ICT autonomy, socioeconomic status (ESCS), gender, ICT interest, and ICT competence to predict mathematics proficiency level categories, finding that ICT autonomy was among the most important predictors and that higher autonomy increased the probability of Level 5+ while lower autonomy increased the probability of below Level 2. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.
confounders: Gender; Socioeconomic status (ESCS); ICT competence; ICT interest; ICT in social interaction; ICT autonomy

title: Stacking: An ensemble learning approach to predict student performance in PISA 2022
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata (student questionnaire plus achievement outcomes) and constructs separate subject-specific datasets by removing identifiers (e.g., student/school IDs), birth-month, country-specific items, non-subject variables, and variables with 100% missingness within each country. The authors then convert special missing codes (valid skip, not applicable, invalid, no response) to NaN and perform country-by-country modeling. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML training/evaluation pipeline; instead, it uses train/validation/test splits and fivefold cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning. Because the models are tree-based boosting/ensemble methods and ridge regression meta-learning, the paper does not describe any complex-survey-weighted estimation, implying an unweighted ML analysis.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that it does not impute missing observations for the level-0 learners (“without imputing any missing observations”) and that stacking/blending can handle missing values, but it does not explicitly document the exact missing-data strategy used inside each algorithm (e.g., whether missingness is treated via native split directions, surrogate splits, or explicit missing indicators). This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets contain non-trivial missingness and the handling mechanism can materially affect predictive performance and comparability across countries and PVs.
outcome_summary: The study predicts PISA 2022 mathematics, reading, and science achievement using ensemble machine learning. For each subject, the authors create subject-specific datasets from the PISA 2022 student questionnaire and achievement outcomes, remove identifiers and non-subject variables, and convert special missing codes to NaN; they then train models separately for each of 80 participating countries. The dependent variables are the ten plausible values per subject, and performance is evaluated using MAPE, MAE, MSE, and RMSE, with robust linear mixed-effects models treating countries as random effects. Across countries, stacking most often yields the lowest mean MAPE/MAE/MSE (e.g., MAPE lowest for 72/80 in mathematics, 64/80 in reading, 65/80 in science). Limitations include lack of explicit documentation of the internal missing-data handling mechanism and no reported use of PISA sampling/replicate weights, so results reflect predictive accuracy rather than population-representative causal effects.
ml_all_techniques: Stacking, XGBoost, Histogram GBR, LightGBM, Blending
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 data from all countries participating in the administration (80 countries). For each subject (mathematics, reading, science), the authors removed irrelevant variables (student/school IDs, birth-month, country-specific items, variables not subject-specific) and removed variables with 100% missing values within each country. They converted codes for valid skip, not applicable, invalid, and no response to NaN (missing) and then performed the modeling separately for each country. For stacking, they split each country dataset into 80% training and 20% testing; for blending, they used 60% training, 20% validation, and 20% testing. Hyperparameters were optimized using fivefold cross-validation.
effect_size: Stacking lowest mean error across countries: lowest mean MAPE for 72/80 countries (90.00%), lowest mean MAE for 74/80 (92.50%), lowest mean MSE for 75/80 (93.75%). Robust linear mixed-effects models: stacking reference; other algorithms significantly increased MAPE/MAE/MSE vs stacking (e.g., MAPE mathematics intercept β=0.10; XGBoost/HGB/LightGBM/Blending effects significant).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 mathematics data (with ten plausible values per student), the study leveraged an ensemble stacking meta-model (level-1 ridge regression) to predict mathematics achievement, finding that stacking produced the lowest mean MAPE, MAE, and MSE for the vast majority of countries compared with XGBoost, HGB, LightGBM, and blending. This indicates that stacking-based ensemble learning may improve the accuracy and stability of cross-country achievement prediction for identifying where students are underperforming, though the paper does not document a fully transparent missing-data mechanism and does not apply survey-weighted estimation.

title: Examining ICT attitudes, use and support in blended learning settings for students’ reading performance: Approaches of artificial intelligence and multilevel model
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 reading literacy microdata for 15-year-olds from 32 OECD countries, restricted to students in blended test language classes based on questionnaire item IC152Q01HA (including cases where teachers and/or students used ICT). For the multilevel (HLM) stage, the authors explicitly implemented student weights to account for the complex design effects of PISA. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name, but it states that student weights were used in HLM to reflect PISA’s sampling design. For the RF feature-selection stage, the paper does not describe weight application; the reported RF performance is based on 10-fold cross-validation, while the HLM stage is the one that explicitly incorporates PISA weights.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 reading literacy for 15-year-olds from 32 OECD countries, restricted to blended test language classes based on IC152Q01HA and using the 10 plausible values for reading performance (PV_1–PV_10). In Stage 1, a Random Forest regression with 10-fold cross-validation (100 trees; 27 retained ICT-related factors) achieved MSE=6319.33, MAE=63.19, and R²=0.38, and produced a relative importance ranking (Gini importance). In Stage 2, hierarchical linear modeling (HLM 8) incorporated the nested student–school–country structure and used student weights plus multiple imputation (m=10) for missing variables; the authors report ICCs and f² effect sizes to support multilevel modeling. Key results show positive associations for perceived ICT competence/autonomy and reading-format preferences, negative associations for ICT as a social-interaction topic, and curvilinear (inverted U / diminishing returns) effects for several ICT attitudes, uses, and resources. Limitations include cross-sectional inference and the fact that RF feature importance is predictive rather than causal.
sample_filtering_criteria: Students from 32 OECD countries who completed the optional ICT familiarity questionnaires in PISA 2018 were selected. The analytic sample includes students in blended test language classes, operationalized using questionnaire item IC152Q01HA: students selecting ICT use by teachers alone (1), students alone (2), or both teachers and students (3) were included; cases where neither teachers nor students used ICT (4) were excluded. The dependent variable uses the 10 plausible values for PISA 2018 reading performance, and missing questionnaire variables were imputed using multiple imputation (m=10) before modeling.
effect_size: Random Forest (10-fold cross-validation): MSE=6319.33, MAE=63.19, R²=0.38; optimal feature set retained 27 ICT-related factors; feature importance via Gini; HLM used f² effect sizes (small/medium/large thresholds).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for 15-year-olds in blended test language classes, the study leveraged ESCS, ICT use at school, interest in ICT, ICT use outside for schoolwork, and ICT use outside for entertainment to predict reading performance, finding that the combined ICT-related feature set collectively predicted reading outcomes with moderate explanatory power (RF R²=0.38) and that student-level ICT factors were most important in the feature ranking. This indicates that blended-reading improvement strategies should prioritize student ICT attitudes and appropriate ICT use patterns (not only access), while also accounting for socioeconomic differences, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

title: Understanding Filipino students’ achievement in PISA: The roles of personal characteristics, proximal processes, and social contexts
authors: Joseph Y. Haw; Ronnel B. King
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the publicly available PISA 2018 Philippine microdata, which includes weights to account for PISA’s complex two-stage sampling (schools first, then students within schools). The authors state that the published dataset includes weights and that they used these weights for classical statistical inferences (correlation/regression) to obtain unbiased estimates. For the hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) step, they additionally use the 80 replicate weights included in the dataset and compute parameter estimates separately for each of the 10 plausible values, then aggregate them following PISA procedures. In the random forest (ML) step, they explicitly did not use replicate weights because random forests do not generate parameter estimates; thus, the ML variable-selection stage is not described as weight-aware.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 Reading achievement for the Philippines (N=7233 15-year-olds) and predicts reading achievement using a two-step approach: Random Forest variable importance with cross-validation, followed by hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) for interpretable parameter estimates. For the Random Forest, the full model explained about 64–66% of variance in the unobserved sample (Model 1: R²=0.66, RMSE=47.19), while the streamlined model using the top 26 predictors achieved nearly the same performance (Model 2: R²=0.64, RMSE=47.50). The HLM using the same 26 predictors explained less variance (R²=0.53) and showed small-to-moderate effects, with grade repetition ranking highest by effect size. Key predictors included reading difficulty self-concept, socioeconomic status, grade repetition, school belonging, and fixed mindset, alongside proximal processes such as online reading time and summarizing metacognition. Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causality) and the fact that the ML step does not use replicate weights, so population-representative uncertainty is handled primarily in the HLM stage.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Philippine PISA 2018 dataset for 15-year-old students (N=7233) selected via complex two-stage sampling. Excluded predictor variables with 100% missing information and removed redundant PISA index variables used to construct other indices (e.g., occupational status index used to derive ESCS). Removed variables that did not show statistically significant correlation with reading achievement in preliminary analyses, reducing the predictor set to 53 variables; then applied an 80% missingness threshold per case for missing-value analysis and retained all 7223 observations because each case had <25% missingness. Applied multiple imputation (MICE) for missing predictor/outcome data.
effect_size: Random Forest (Model 1): R²=0.66, RMSE=47.19; Random Forest (Model 2, top 26 predictors): R²=0.64, RMSE=47.50 (aggregated across 10 plausible values). HLM (using the 26 RF predictors): R²=0.53; effect sizes small-to-moderate; grade repetition largest by effect size in HLM.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 Reading (Philippines, 15-year-olds) the study leveraged self-concept of reading difficulty, socioeconomic status, grade repetition, school belongingness, and fixed mindset to predict reading achievement (PVREAD1–PVREAD10), finding that these variables were among the most important predictors and that self-concept of reading difficulty showed the highest impact in the RF model. This indicates that Philippine reading interventions may need to combine socioeconomic/school-environment supports with proximal learning experiences that build positive reading self-beliefs and metacognitive engagement, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

title: Using machine learning to predict UK and Japanese secondary students' life satisfaction in PISA 2018
weight_fields_interpretation: The study used PISA 2018 student questionnaire and well-being questionnaire data for two countries (UK and Japan) and restricted the analytic sample to students with complete enough data after preprocessing. The authors report imputing missing values using series mean and normalizing features for KNN, but they do not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation. Because the models are implemented with scikit-learn (Random Forest regression and KNN regression), the manuscript does not describe any complex survey weighting strategy, suggesting an unweighted ML analysis. Consequently, the results should be interpreted as predictive associations within the analyzed samples rather than population-representative estimates for all PISA 2018 students in each country.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because the dependent variable is the PISA 2018 life satisfaction scale score derived from student self-reports (0–10), and the paper does not describe using PV-based achievement scaling. Instead, the analysis treats life satisfaction as a continuous response for supervised regression. Missing data handling is reported (series mean imputation), so the missing-data strategy is not a reporting gap.
outcome_summary: The study used PISA 2018 student questionnaire and well-being questionnaire data for two countries (UK: 13,818; Japan: 6,109) and predicted students’ life satisfaction (ST016Q01NA, 0–10) using supervised ML regression. Two models were compared under nested cross-validation with five outer folds and five inner folds for hyperparameter tuning: Random Forest and k-nearest neighbours (KNN). Random Forest achieved higher predictive performance than KNN in both countries, with UK test R² ≈ 0.187 vs. KNN R² ≈ 0.103 (RMSE ≈ 0.451 vs. 0.474) and Japan test R² ≈ 0.138 vs. KNN R² ≈ 0.055 (RMSE ≈ 0.464 vs. 0.486). Across both countries, feature-importance rankings highlighted meaning in life, student competition, teacher support, exposure to bullying, and ICT resources, but the models explain only a modest share of variance. The paper imputes missing values via series mean and does not report applying PISA sampling/replicate weights, so results should be treated as predictive associations rather than population-representative or causal effects.
sample_filtering_criteria: Students were selected from PISA 2018 for the United Kingdom (GBR) and Japan (JPN). The dependent variable was life satisfaction (ST016Q01NA) from the PISA 2018 student questionnaire, and the model used 26 individual-level questionnaire variables (Table 2) as predictors. Missing values were imputed using series mean (missingness <10% overall), and for KNN the features were normalized; both RF and KNN were trained and tested on the same preprocessed dataset. No additional grade/school-type restrictions are reported beyond using the PISA 2018 student sample for these two countries.
effect_size: Random Forest regression (nested CV, 5 outer folds): Test R² ≈ 0.187 (mean), RMSE ≈ 0.451 (mean). KNN regression (nested CV, 5 outer folds): Test R² ≈ 0.103 (mean), RMSE ≈ 0.474 (mean).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 UK the study leveraged meaning in life, motivation to master tasks, student competition, ICT resources, and exposure to bullying to predict students' life satisfaction, finding that Random Forest outperformed KNN on both validation and test performance (higher R² and lower RMSE). This indicates that combining multiple psychosocial and school-experience variables in non-linear models may better identify students at risk of lower life satisfaction, though the study reports predictive associations rather than causal effects and does not apply survey weights.

title: Contrasting Profiles of Low-Performing Mathematics Students in Public and Private Schools in the Philippines: Insights from Machine Learning
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Philippines sample from PISA 2018, drawn via a two-stage stratified random sampling design (187 schools selected across 17 regions, then students sampled within schools). The authors report downloading the publicly released PISA 2018 database and constructing an analytic dataset by excluding variables with 100% missingness and removing students with more than 50% missing values. Missing questionnaire variables in the reduced dataset were imputed using k-nearest neighbors (k=7), followed by normalization of variables to [0,1] (except SCHLTYPE) and correlation-based feature condensation. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML training/evaluation; given the use of standard ML classifiers (e.g., Random Forest) and the absence of any weight-variable mention, weighting is likely omitted or not discussed, which may affect population-representativeness and uncertainty estimates.
outcome_summary: The study uses the Philippines sample from PISA 2018 and constructs a binary mathematics outcome from PV1MATH (PVMATH1): students below Level 1 (PVMATH1 < 357.7) are coded as poor performers and those at Level 1 or higher as better performers. After excluding variables with 100% missingness and removing students with >50% missing values, the authors impute remaining missing questionnaire data using k-nearest neighbors (k=7), normalize predictors, and then train separate classifiers for private and public schools using SCHLTYPE. Across both school types, Random Forest is selected as the best model via exhaustive hyperparameter search with five-fold cross-validation, reporting validation Precision/Recall/F1/Accuracy; for private schools Accuracy=0.79 (F1=0.65) and for public schools Accuracy=0.79 (F1=0.79). SHAP is used to rank influential predictors, highlighting shared resource/aspiration and email-safety judgment variables, plus school-type-specific motivational/engagement factors. Limitations include the lack of reported PISA sampling-weight usage and the fact that SHAP importance supports prediction, not causal inference.
ml_all_techniques: Logistic Regression, Neural Network, SVM, Decision Tree, Random Forest
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Philippines PISA 2018 student questionnaire and school questionnaire data. Excluded three variables with 100% missingness (ICTSCH, ICTHOME, ST225Q03HA) and excluded students with more than 50% missing values, reducing the sample to 7091 students. Imputed remaining missing values in the reduced dataset using k-nearest neighbor imputation with k=7. Defined the binary target using PVMATH1 (PV1MATH): students with PVMATH1 < 357.7 (below Level 1) were coded as 1 (poor performers) and those with PVMATH1 ≥ 357.7 (Levels 1–6) were coded as 0 (better performers). Then analyzed public and private school students separately using SCHLTYPE (private: SCHLTYPE=1 or 2; public: SCHLTYPE=3).
effect_size: Random Forest (best): Precision=0.69, Recall=0.61, F1=0.65, Accuracy=0.79; ROC-AUC reported in Figure 2 (exact AUC value not provided in text).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics data for the Philippines private-school students, the study leveraged internet mobile-phone access (ST012Q05NA), expectations of completing a vocational degree (ST225Q05HA), metacognitive-like email-safety judgment (ST166Q02HA), parents’ occupational status (HISEI), and expected job at age 30 (BSMJ) to classify poor versus better mathematics performers based on PV1MATH. It found that the Random Forest achieved the highest validation accuracy (0.79) and that lower values on these resource/aspiration-related variables were associated with identifying poor performers (with SHAP indicating inverse relationships for the shared top features). This indicates that interventions for low-performing private-school students should prioritize reducing digital access and strengthening realistic postsecondary/occupational expectations, while also addressing students’ ability to handle misinformation in online contexts, though the results are predictive and not causal.

title: Using machine learning to predict student science achievement based on science curriculum type in TIMSS 2019
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science microdata and extracts variables via IEA IDB Analyzer and SPSS, then merges and cleans the dataset before analysis. The analytic sample is restricted to 44 countries and to the Grade 8 Science assessment context, yielding 309,511 remaining entries after cleaning. For weighting, the authors explicitly use the science teacher weight (SCIWGT) because the key process-dimension variables (e.g., instructional clarity, instructional strategies, homework and experiment-related items) are reported by science teachers; they argue this reduces sampling bias for curriculum-to-achievement comparisons from an instructional perspective. The manuscript does not report applying student sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures for the ML prediction stage, so the weighting approach appears to focus on teacher-level weighting rather than full complex-survey student-weighted estimation.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science data from 44 countries, classifying students as integrated or separated science using TIMSS ITCOURSE (ITCOURSE=6 vs 2/3/4/5). For the curriculum effect, it estimates propensity scores using a stacked ensemble (k-NN, Random Forest, Naive Bayes as base learners; logistic regression as meta-learner) and matches integrated to separated students using KNN; after matching, Mann–Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction show integrated curricula have significantly higher science achievement across all five plausible values, with small effect sizes (Cohen’s d around 0.2). For prediction, it compares linear regression, lasso, decision trees, Random Forest, and neural networks using RMSE and R² on a 70/30 train/test split averaged across PVs; Random Forest performs best (testing R²=0.51, RMSE=74.92). Feature importance indicates socio-economic background, confidence, instructional time, and experiment frequency dominate, while curriculum type has a small coefficient. Limitations include reliance on predictive associations (not causal identification) and limited reporting of full complex-survey weighting beyond teacher weights.
ml_all_techniques: Random Forest, LASSO, Decision Tree, Neural Network, Linear Regression, Naive Bayes, k-NN, Stacking
sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science data; extracted variables of interest with IEA IDB Analyzer and merged in SPSS. After data cleaning, 309,511 entries from 44 countries remained. Curriculum type was defined using TIMSS ITCOURSE: students with ITCOURSE=6 were classified as integrated science; students with ITCOURSE in {2,3,4,5} were classified as separated science. The dependent variable was the science achievement plausible values (BSSSCI01–BSSSCI05), with separate analyses conducted for each PV.
effect_size: Model comparison using RMSE and R² on train/test splits (70%/30%) averaged across PVs. Random Forest: Testing R²=0.51, RMSE=74.92; Linear regression: Testing R²=0.21, RMSE=94.43; Lasso: Testing R²=0.22, RMSE=94.24; Decision tree: Testing R²=0.29, RMSE=89.88; Neural networks: Testing R²=0.22, RMSE=94.34. title: Irt‑latent regression with many predictors: limits and solutions
authors: Paul A. Jewsbury; J. R. Lockwood; Matthew S. Johnson
weight_fields_interpretation: This paper does not analyze an operational ILSA micro-dataset with a complex sampling design; instead, it uses simulation data generated for N=1000 test takers per simulated assessment across 1000 replications per condition. Because there is no survey sampling, no stratification/clustering, and no ILSA sampling weights are defined or applied, student/sampling weights are not part of the estimation procedure. The PV generation and regression estimation are performed within the simulation framework using fixed item parameters and marginal-maximum likelihood (EM) for the latent regression coefficients. As a result, weighting guidance for real ILSA data is conceptual: in operational settings, PVs are typically generated under the IRT-latent regression model and then combined using multiple-imputation rules, but this paper’s instability findings are driven by the interaction of predictor dimensionality, test information (items per person), and missingness—not by survey weights.
outcome_summary: This paper is a simulation-based methodological study of the conventional large-scale assessment pipeline that models latent proficiency with IRT and then uses an IRT-latent regression to generate plausible values (PVs) for contextual inference. The authors simulate N=1000 test takers per assessment, generate item responses from 2PL or 3PL models, and vary assessment design conditions via the number of observed items per person (J) and an MCAR missingness mechanism (No missing vs Missing where 30% of test takers have only 1–3 observed items). They estimate IRT-latent regression models with increasing predictor dimensionality (P) using marginal maximum likelihood (EM) and generate M=20 PVs per test taker. Across conditions, bias in population and group moments grows with P, especially for difficult 3PL and Missing designs, while moderate 2PL designs with adequate information for all test takers remain robust even at low J. The study also shows that PV-based variance estimation depends on how PVs are generated (fixed ML vs sampled regression parameters), with operational sampling leading to additional positive variance bias that increases with P. Limitations: results are derived from controlled simulations with fixed item parameters and do not directly quantify performance on real operational ILSA datasets.
null_fields_interpretation: The paper does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models (no supervised learners such as Random Forest/XGBoost/SVM are used). Instead, it develops and tests statistical properties of IRT-latent regression and PV-based estimators via simulation and theoretical derivations. Therefore, ml_techniques are intentionally empty and the study is classified as exploratory (methodological/simulation investigation rather than predictive ML).
sample_filtering_criteria: Simulation study: for each of 1000 simulated assessments per condition, the authors generated data for N=1000 test takers. Each test taker received item responses from a pool of 40 dichotomous items (3PL or 2PL), with the number of observed item responses J determined by the assessment design condition (e.g., J=4/6/8/12) and missingness introduced under MCAR (No missing: all test takers have J observed responses; Missing: 70% have J observed responses and 10% each have 1, 2, and 3 observed responses). No real-country sampling frame or analytic filtering from an operational ILSA dataset is used.
effect_size: Bias patterns reported in Tables 1 and 3–6: as P increases, bias for population mean/skewness becomes increasingly negative in difficult 3PL; variance and kurtosis bias increases; extreme percentiles (10th/90th) show stronger outward bias than median. Example magnitude: in difficult 3PL with Missing and J=4, mean population variance estimate exceeds true variance by 52.7%; in moderate 2PL with No missing and J=4, variance overestimation is 2.4%.
primary_finding: Using simulation data for IRT-latent regression with PVs, the study leveraged number of predictors (P), items per test taker (J), item missingness condition, and IRT item model type to estimate population moments and percentiles of latent proficiency, finding that estimator bias grows with P particularly when measurement precision is low for a substantial share of test takers (e.g., difficult 3PL and Missing). This indicates that expanding the predictor set in large-scale assessments can undermine validity unless assessment designs ensure at least moderate measurement precision for all test takers, especially for low-proficiency groups.

authors: Dahman Tahri; Ji Liu; Millicent Aziku

title: Metropolitan, Urban, and Rural Regions: How Regional Differences Affect Elementary School Students in Germany
authors: Jakob Schwerter; Johannes Bleher; Philipp Doebler; Nele McElvany
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 microdata for Germany, combining student, parent, teacher, and school principal questionnaires into student-level and school-level datasets, then merging into an all-in-one dataset. The analytic sample is restricted to fourth-grade students and further reduced by a school block bootstrap (resampling schools before imputing missing values), yielding on average 3,608 observations per imputed dataset (with 3,959 students in the original sample). For inference, the authors report using school-clustered and heteroskedastic-robust standard errors including survey weights via the R survey package, but the manuscript does not name the specific PIRLS weight variable(s). Because the paper’s main predictive/selection steps are based on PCA and LASSO with multiple imputation and bootstrapping, the weighting is primarily discussed for the regression standard errors rather than being integrated into the ML feature-selection procedure.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are not PIRLS achievement PV scores; the outcomes are (i) a dichotomized academic track recommendation, (ii) enjoyment of school measured via a latent variable from Likert items, and (iii) reading interest measured via Likert items. The study instead uses multiple imputation for missing questionnaire/background data, so PV-specific handling is not part of the analysis pipeline.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2016 Germany Grade 4 data (N=3,959) to test whether regional differences (metropolitan, urban/suburban, rural based on municipality size) are associated with three elementary-school outcomes: academic track recommendation (Gymnasium vs not), enjoyment of school, and reading interest. The authors use a two-step post-double-selection approach combining multiple imputation for missing questionnaire data, school-level block bootstrapping, PCA for dimensionality reduction, and LASSO for variable selection, followed by post-LASSO OLS regressions with state fixed effects. In baseline OLS models, rural and metropolitan students show higher probabilities of Gymnasium recommendations and higher well-being indicators than urban students, but these regional coefficients largely attenuate and become statistically insignificant after controlling for LASSO-selected principal components—especially those from student-level information. The paper reports no PV-based achievement metrics because the outcomes are tracking and motivation/well-being measures rather than PIRLS achievement PVs. Limitations include reliance on a proxy tracking measure, the use of linear probability models for the binary outcome, and the fact that the study is explicitly non-causal despite using ML-driven selection and bootstrapped inference.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the representative PIRLS 2016 Germany dataset and restricted to fourth-grade students (N=3,959). Outcomes were constructed from PIRLS-provided teacher-recommended secondary track options (14 options) and then dichotomized to indicate recommendation for the academic (Gymnasium) track versus not. The analysis further applies (a) exclusion of observations with only missing information and constant variables without variation, and (b) a block bootstrap at the school level (resampling schools with replacement) followed by multiple imputation of missing values (300 imputations) using missRanger with predictive mean matching. For the post-LASSO regressions, the authors include state fixed effects and control for school size and fourth-grade class size.

primary_finding: Using PIRLS 2016 Germany Grade 4 the study leveraged regional membership (rural vs urban; metropolitan vs urban) together with student and school principal components selected via LASSO to model academic track recommendation, finding that rural and metropolitan students were initially more likely to receive Gymnasium recommendations than urban students, but these regional coefficients became statistically insignificant after controlling for selected student-level characteristics. title: Uncovering Key Factors of Student Performance in Math: An Explainable Deep Learning Approach Using TIMSS 2019 Data
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 international database data and restricts the analytic sample to Moroccan eighth-grade students. The authors describe stratified random sampling at the TIMSS design level and construct a binary target from TIMSS plausible values (PVs), but they do not report applying any student/sampling weights or replicate weights in the machine-learning training/evaluation. They explicitly remove technical variables (including identifiers, weights, and metadata) from the predictive modeling phase, which suggests weights were not used as model inputs; however, the manuscript does not state whether survey weights were used for weighted estimation or evaluation. Because the models are standard classifiers trained on latent features (autoencoder + RF/XGBoost/SVM/DT), the paper does not document a complex-survey-weighted ML procedure, so results should be interpreted as unweighted (or at least not transparently weighted) estimates for the Moroccan eighth-grade population.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper constructs a binary target by grouping TIMSS PV tiers (Low vs Intermediate/High/Very High) but does not document how the five PVs were combined into a single classification target (e.g., whether PVs were averaged, treated as multiple observations, or combined via a specific rule). It also does not report any explicit missing-data handling strategy for questionnaire variables after the described variable-exclusion steps (e.g., whether remaining missing values were imputed or cases were removed). Given that TIMSS questionnaire data typically contain item nonresponse, this omission is a reporting gap that limits reproducibility and may affect model calibration and feature importance stability.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics data restricted to Morocco (n=8458 students) and constructs a binary target by grouping PV tiers: Low vs Intermediate/High/Very High. After cleaning the questionnaire-derived feature set from 700 variables down to 400 (excluding technical variables, high-missingness items, redundant scores, and PV reference variables), the authors train an autoencoder to compress the 400 inputs into 20 latent dimensions. They then train four classifiers (Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM, Decision Tree) on the latent features and evaluate using accuracy, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. SVM performs best with Accuracy=0.74, F1=0.73, and AUC=0.79, followed by XGBoost (0.73/0.71/AUC=0.76). Interpretability is provided via SHAP on latent dimensions and projection back to original variables, but the paper does not report a transparent PV-combination rule for the binary target nor a missing-data handling method, and SHAP-based importance should not be interpreted as causal effects.
ml_all_techniques: Autoencoder, Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM, Decision Tree
sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 international database and restricted to Morocco (eighth grade / collège; ages ~13–14). Built the modeling dataset from student, teacher, and school questionnaires, starting with 700 variables and removing 41 technical variables (identifiers/weights/metadata/duplicates), excluding 61 variables with 100% missingness (not administered in Morocco), excluding 74 variables with >50% missingness (rarely implemented school policies), discarding 29 redundant variables already captured in alternative formats, and excluding 95 reference variables including plausible values (PVs) from the predictive modeling inputs. title: Predictors of reading performance of fourth-grade Turkish students
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2021 fourth-grade reading data for Türkiye and constructs an analytic dataset by merging questionnaire files into a single R-scripted dataset. The authors report a preprocessing pipeline (purging cases with >20% missingness, then imputing remaining missing values via k-nearest-neighbor mean imputation with k=10, followed by centering and variance scaling) and then manually reduce predictors from 545 to 405. The manuscript does not report applying PIRLS sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the SVM training or evaluation, and the ML workflow (SVM with caret, RFE, repeated k-fold CV, and a 70/30 train-test split) is described without any weight-aware estimation. Given that SVM does not natively incorporate complex survey weights, the analysis appears to proceed as an unweighted ML classification on the prepared sample, which may limit population-representativeness under PIRLS’s clustered sampling design.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2021 fourth-grade reading data for Türkiye, recoding the dependent variable into a binary high vs low reading performance indicator using ASRIBM01 from the first plausible value benchmark categories. After preprocessing (removing cases with >20% missingness, imputing remaining missing values with k-nearest neighbor mean imputation using k=10, and normalizing), the authors train an L2-regularized linear-kernel SVM in caret with a 70/30 train-test split (n=2513 train; n=1076 test) and use 5-times repeated 10-fold cross-validation for model evaluation and recursive feature elimination (RFE) to identify the most influential predictors. The best model reports Accuracy=0.957 (95% CI 0.943–0.968), Kappa=0.914, sensitivity=0.956, specificity=0.958, and balanced accuracy=0.9572, with P<0.001 versus the no-information rate. The top predictors emphasize school instructional emphasis on foundational literacy and teacher assessment/interactive comprehension strategies, plus parental commitment to readiness. Limitations include the lack of reported complex-survey weight usage and the cross-sectional, predictive nature of the classification (no causal identification).

The final analytic dataset for ML contained 3589 students and 405 retained independent variables.

title: Beating the odds: Identifying the top predictors of resilience among Hong Kong students
authors: Faming Wang; Ronnel B. King; Shing On Leung
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 Hong Kong microdata and restricts the analytic sample to students in the bottom 25% of ESCS (Economic, Social and Cultural Status), yielding 1,459 students, of whom 251 are classified as resilient. The dependent variable is a binary indicator of resilience based on reading achievement being in the top 25% among low-ESCS students. Although PISA is collected using a complex sampling design, the manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the random forest classification. Because the analysis is implemented with the R randomForest package and the paper does not discuss survey-weighted ML estimation, the most defensible interpretation is that the model was trained on an unweighted subset; this may affect generalizability and uncertainty quantification under the clustered/survey design.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 Hong Kong microdata and constructs a binary resilience outcome among socioeconomically disadvantaged students (bottom 25% ESCS): resilient students are those whose reading achievement falls in the top 25% (n=251) versus non-resilient (n=1,208), totaling 1,459 students. title: What are the Most Important Factors Influencing Science Performance? A Machine Learning Study of Singaporean and Finish PISA Data
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 science microdata for 15-year-olds from Singapore and Finland and models science performance using ten plausible values (PVs) as the dependent variable. The authors state that PISA-derived scales were transformed using weighted likelihood estimates (WLEs) and standardized with equal weighting for each country/economy, but they do not report applying PISA sampling weights (e.g., student/school weights) or replicate weights in the machine-learning estimation. For the subsequent multilevel binary logistic regression, the paper reports multilevel structure (students within schools) and model fit statistics, but it does not specify the exact PISA weight variable or replicate-weight method. outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of PISA 2018 Spain (n=35,943; two-stage sampling) to model grade repetition in primary and secondary education as dichotomous self-reports. For variable selection, it compares four supervised ML algorithms (CART/C5.0, random forest, and stochastic gradient boosting) using AUC with 10-fold cross-validation on a 70% training / 30% validation split; stochastic gradient boosting is selected as the most accurate and used to rank the most informative predictors. In primary education, the best global model (M4) reaches PEV≈61% with the lowest AIC/BIC and an R2≈9% variance reduction relative to model 1; in secondary education, M4 reaches PEV≈55.69% with R2≈10.298% relative to model 1. Limitations include the absence of explicit causal identification and incomplete reporting of ML weighting/complex-survey handling details; relationships are therefore correlational.
ml_all_techniques: Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting
sample_filtering_criteria: Secondary analysis of PISA 2018 Spain. The initial Spanish PISA 2018 student sample is 35,943 (two-stage sampling; 92% coverage of 15-year-olds). For the multilevel logistic regression objective, the authors removed schools with fewer than 20 subjects, excluding 1,532 students from 133 centres, yielding a final multilevel analytic sample of 34,411 students. For the ML stage, the paper reports preprocessing (multiple imputation, centring/scaling) and a random 70%/30% train/validation split, but it does not specify additional grade- or item-level exclusions beyond the multilevel school-size restriction.

title: A Machine-Learning Approach to Predicting the Achievement of Australian Students Using School Climate; Learner Characteristics; and Economic, Social, and Cultural Status
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2022 microdata for Australia (15-year-olds) and reports an analytic sample of 13,437 students in 743 schools. The manuscript describes splitting the dataset into 70% training and 30% testing using stratified random sampling, but it does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML training/evaluation. Because the models are standard ML regressors (SVM, KNN, Decision Tree, Elastic Net, XGBoost) implemented via common R/Python packages, the analysis appears to follow an unweighted ML workflow; the paper does not specify any weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or complex survey design handling. No additional sample restrictions (e.g., grade bands beyond PISA’s 15-year-old cohort, or exclusions for missingness) are explicitly documented, so the exact missing-data and cleaning rules are unclear beyond the reported final sample size.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is mathematics achievement (ACHIEVE) from PISA 2022, which in PISA is typically represented using plausible values; however, the manuscript does not describe whether plausible values were used directly, averaged, or combined via Rubin’s rules. The paper also does not report any explicit missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap given that questionnaire and background variables commonly have missingness in PISA datasets. As a result, the exact treatment of PVs and missingness cannot be verified from the methods section.
outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA 2022 microdata for Australia (15-year-olds; N=13,437 students in 743 schools) to predict mathematics achievement from school climate and learner characteristics plus ESCS. Five ML regressors were compared using a stratified 70/30 train-test split and hyperparameter tuning: SVM, KNN, Decision Tree, Elastic Net, and XGBoost. Across evaluation metrics (MSE, RMSE, MAE, MAPE, R2, adjusted R2, and correlation), XGBoost performed best, with MSE=5227.0, RMSE=72.776, MAE=57.67, MAPE=0.125, and R2=0.424 (correlation=0.6577). A Friedman test (p=0.00004922) and Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons supported statistically significant performance differences, with XGBoost notably outperforming the others. The paper uses SHAP (global and local) to interpret feature influence and reports an interaction between MATHEFF and ESCS, but it does not document how plausible values and missing data were handled, and it does not report survey-weighted estimation—so results should be treated as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
ml_all_techniques: SVM, k-NN, Decision Tree, Elastic Net, XGBoost
sample_filtering_criteria: Used OECD PISA 2022 data for Australia, focusing on the standard PISA target population of 15-year-old students. The analytic sample comprises 13,437 students in 743 schools who completed the mathematics assessment; the paper does not report additional exclusions beyond the final sample size. title: DIAGNOSTIC CLASSIFICATION ANALYSIS OF PROBLEM-SOLVING COMPETENCE USING PROCESS DATA: AN ITEM EXPANSION METHOD
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 problem-solving process-log data for a single CBA item (TICKETS task 2, CP038Q01) and constructs a formatted process-data matrix by coding whether specific action sequences (“phantom items”) appear for each respondent. The analytic sample is restricted to respondents from the USA, Singapore, Austria, and Turkey with non-missing IDs and reached item responses (final N=3,760). The manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or any replicate-weight procedure; therefore, weighting strategy is not documented for these diagnostic classification analyses. Missingness is handled at the outcome level via FIML, while the process-data matrix is reported as having no missing data after preprocessing and action-sequence filtering.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are diagnostic-classification latent classes/attribute patterns and higher-order latent ability estimates derived from a diagnostic classification model (GDINA/HO-DINA) and a partial credit model for the single item, rather than PV-based achievement scores. Missing data handling is described as full information maximum likelihood (FIML) with EM for the outcome (item response) dataset; in the provided mapping, FIML/EM corresponds to multiple_imputation in this schema. The paper does not provide a detailed missing-data mechanism or an explicit imputation model for the outcome categories, so the exact statistical assumptions behind the FIML treatment are not fully documented.
outcome_summary: This Psychometrika study proposes an item-expansion method that applies diagnostic classification modeling to action-level process data from a single PISA 2012 problem-solving CBA item (TICKETS task 2, CP038Q01). Respondents from the USA, Singapore, Austria, and Turkey were restricted to those with non-missing IDs and reached item responses (final N=3,760). The authors transformed unformatted action logs into a formatted binary matrix of 14 “phantom items” (action sequences) and estimated higher-order GDINA/HO-DINA models, selecting the best-fitting reduced model using RMSEA2/SRMSR and information criteria (AIC/BIC/CAIC/SABIC). They report that latent classes diagnose skill mastery patterns more finely than the observed 0/1/2 outcome categories, and that higher-order latent ability estimates correlate strongly with PCM estimates (r=0.826) while having significantly smaller standard errors (t(3759)=-115.58, p<0.001). Limitations include reliance on expert judgment for Q-matrix retrofitting and the use of only one item; additionally, the paper does not document survey-weight application for PISA sampling design.
sample_filtering_criteria: Selected respondents from the USA, Singapore, Austria, and Turkey from the provided PISA 2012 CBA process-log file (CBA_cp038q01_logs12_SPSS.csv). Excluded respondents with missing IDs and those with not-reached item responses, yielding an analytic sample of 3,760. For process data, unformatted action-sequence logs were preprocessed to remove irrelevant/noisy actions and to dichotomize repeated actions (nonzero counts set to 1). Phantom items (action sequences) were retained only if their appearance rate was between 5% and 95%, and further filtered using theory and DCM identifiability requirements; the final formatted process-data matrix coded 1/0 for the presence of each of 14 phantom items. For outcome data (item response categories 0/1/2), missing outcome responses were handled using FIML with EM.
effect_size: Model fit: HO-GDINA test-level RMSEA2=0.032 (90% CI [0.025, 0.041]) and SRMSR=0.033; relative fit favored HO-DINA over HO-GDINA (AIC/BIC/CAIC/SABIC; likelihood ratio test p=0.180).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2012 Problem Solving (TICKETS task 2, CP038Q01) action-level process data, the study leveraged a GDINA-based diagnostic classification framework with phantom items derived from action sequences to estimate latent attribute patterns for five problem-solving skills, finding that the estimated latent classes provided more detailed diagnoses than the observed 0/1/2 outcome score categories. This indicates that process-data-informed diagnostic classification can support more fine-grained identification of which specific skills students have mastered or missed, beyond coarse score categories, though the study is limited to one item and relies on expert-driven Q-matrix construction.

Because no respondent-level outcomes are estimated from an assessment dataset, there are no sampling weights, replicate weights, or weight variables to apply. The review’s “sample” is the set of included research articles identified through database searches and screening criteria, so weighting is not part of the statistical estimation procedure. Topic modeling was conducted on abstracts (not full papers), and the main methodological steps were text preprocessing and selecting the number of topics using semantic coherence and FREX.

The dependent information is the presence and thematic content of process-data research as extracted from abstracts and coded from full papers, not PV-based student achievement.
outcome_summary: This scoping review used structural topic modeling (STM) to identify recurring themes in 221 empirical studies that used process/log data in large-scale assessments. The review’s “inputs” were the abstracts of included papers (with citations/section headings removed and standard NLP preprocessing such as lowercasing, stopword removal, and stemming), and the “outputs” were topic assignments based on the highest posterior topic probability. The authors estimated STM models with 5–10 topics and selected a six-topic solution using semantic coherence and FREX, then manually coded subtopics and extracted theories/methods from full papers. The six recurring topics were response time models, response time-general, aberrant test-taking behavior, action sequences, complex problem-solving, and digital writing. The study does not report predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) because it is not training ML models on student outcomes; instead, it maps how process data are used and which theories are invoked, with limitations related to topic-model assignment ambiguity and the exclusion of papers without abstracts.

title: Review of Text-Based Approaches to Item Difficulty Modeling in Large-Scale Assessments
authors: Sydney Peters; Nan Zhang; Hong Jiao; Ming Li; Tianyi Zhou
journal: Proceedings of the Artificial Intelligence in Measurement and Education Conference (AIME-Con) – Volume 3: Coordinated Session Papers
weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a literature review that synthesizes 37 articles (46 studies) on automated item difficulty prediction; it does not analyze a specific ILSA micro-dataset with a defined student sampling frame. Because no student-level assessment administration, scaling, or plausible-value estimation is performed in this review, there are no survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight schemes to apply. For future empirical implementations of the reviewed approaches, analysts should use the official ILSA sampling weights provided in the international database when estimating population-representative relationships, and should apply replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) when variance estimation is required. The review also notes that model performance outcomes are not directly comparable across studies due to differences in domains and difficulty-parameter scales, which further limits any attempt to standardize weighting or scaling across the synthesized literature.
handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a review article synthesizing results from prior studies rather than estimating cognitive achievement scores from ILSA plausible values. The dependent variables in the reviewed work are item difficulty parameters (e.g., p-values or IRT b-parameters) and the review itself does not perform PV-based scoring or PV combining. Therefore, plausible-value handling is not applicable to the review’s own analysis, and missing-data handling is not reported because no original dataset is analyzed here.
outcome_summary: This paper is a systematic review of text-based approaches to automated item difficulty prediction in large-scale assessments, synthesizing 37 articles (46 studies) published through May 2025. It does not train or evaluate a single ML model on an original dataset; instead, it aggregates reported modeling choices across studies, including difficulty parameter type (continuous vs categorical), subject domain, item type, input composition, feature families (hand-crafted linguistic/metadata, LLM-generated, static embeddings, contextualized embeddings), and model families (classical ML, neural networks, transformer-based language models). Across the reviewed studies, the most common difficulty targets were IRT b-parameters and transformed/standard p-values, and the most frequent regression metrics were RMSE and Pearson correlation. Reported performance ranges are summarized descriptively (e.g., RMSE ranges by difficulty parameter type), but the authors caution that metrics are not directly comparable across studies due to different domains and difficulty scales. Limitations include overrepresentation of BEA shared-task papers and limited reporting/variability in difficulty-parameter scales, which constrains cross-study benchmarking.
null_fields_interpretation: This record is a review article rather than an empirical ML study using ILSA micro-data. As a result, there is no country-level student sample, no survey-weighted estimation, no plausible-value generation, and no single predictive model with measurable performance on a unified dataset. The absence of main_findings rows and ML technique entries reflects that the paper synthesizes existing studies rather than producing new predictive estimates.
sample_filtering_criteria: No ILSA student sample is analyzed in this review. Instead, the authors conduct a literature search and apply inclusion/exclusion criteria to select 37 articles (46 studies) where the item difficulty parameter was obtained from item responses from human test-takers and the assessment was large-scale; they excluded studies focused on text complexity/readability, non-large-scale assessments, studies not using automated prediction from item text, and other reviews.

title: Artificial Neural Network and Adaptive Neuro Fuzzy Inference System Hybridized Models in the Sustainable Integration of Language and Mathematics Skills: The Case of Singaporeand Hong Kong
weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not analyze student microdata from PISA; instead, it performs document/content analysis of national curricula for Singapore and Hong Kong and then uses those content-derived counts as inputs to ANN and ANFIS models with PISA 2018 mathematics/reading scores as outputs. Because the modeling is based on curriculum-theme frequencies and country-level PISA scores (not a student-level complex survey sample), standard PISA sampling weights and replicate weights are not applicable in the way they would be for microdata estimation. The manuscript does not report applying any PISA student/sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Therefore, the results should be interpreted as model-based associations between curriculum-theme frequencies and country-level PISA scores rather than as population-representative estimates from a weighted survey design.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables used in the ANN/ANFIS modeling are PISA 2018 mathematics/reading scores at the country level (e.g., Singapore 569/548; Hong Kong 551/524), not student-level plausible-value (PV) achievement scores. As a result, PV-specific handling (Rubin’s rules, PV averaging, etc.) is not applicable. The paper also does not describe any missing-data strategy for the curriculum-theme coding counts or the country-level score inputs, representing a reporting gap for transparency about how incomplete or missing coded elements were treated.
outcome_summary: The paper examines how language skills relate to mathematics success by combining (1) content analysis of national English-language and mathematics curricula for Singapore and Hong Kong and (2) predictive modeling using ANN and ANFIS in MATLAB (2019a). The dependent variable in both models is based on PISA 2018 country-level mathematics/reading scores, while the inputs are curriculum-derived frequencies for the four language skills and language-related themes identified within mathematics curricula. ANN (Model 1) achieved RMSE = 17.6385 and R² = 0.353954, indicating an insufficient relationship. ANFIS (Model 2) slightly outperformed ANN with RMSE = 12.42771 and R² = 0.397867, but explanatory power remained low. Limitations include the use of only two countries, the absence of student-level PV/weighting procedures, and limited reporting on missing-data handling and how curriculum coding uncertainty may affect model inputs.
sample_filtering_criteria: No student-level sampling is performed. The analytic inputs are (i) curriculum documents retrieved from official ministry sources for Singapore and Hong Kong (English language and mathematics syllabi/guides) and (ii) PISA 2018 country-level mathematics and reading scores. The study applies content analysis to identify themes related to the four language skills (listening, speaking, reading, writing) and maps mathematics-curriculum themes to language-skill themes via coding and frequency counts; these coded frequencies are then used as ANN/ANFIS inputs. The paper does not report any additional inclusion/exclusion rules for student records because no student microdata are used.

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence Models in Educational Analytics and Decision Making: A Systematic Review

Because no student-level assessment dataset (e.g., PISA/TIMSS) is pooled and re-scaled within this review, there is no defined sampling frame, no PV generation, and no survey-weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) to apply at the review level. The included primary studies may use survey weights depending on their data source, but the review does not report a unified weighting scheme or replicate-weight approach. Therefore, weighting guidance for international large-scale assessments cannot be operationalized from this manuscript alone; readers must consult each included study’s methods for weight usage and complex-survey handling.

outcome_summary: This PRISMA-based systematic review (World 2023, 4:288–313) searched multiple databases (ERIC, IEEE, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Web of Science) using PICO-defined criteria focused on AI models predicting or classifying basic-education performance (primary/secondary/high school) from 2000 to September 2021.
