title: The Application of Machine Learning to Educational Process Data Analysis: A Systematic Review
authors: J. Huang; Y. P. X.; H. H. C.
weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a systematic literature review (38 peer-reviewed studies, 2013–2024) and does not conduct a new student-level or assessment micro-data analysis. Therefore, there is no analytic dataset with a defined sampling frame, no student-level weighting variables, and no replicate-weight methodology to apply. The review follows PRISMA 2020 for study selection and manually extracts information from included publications rather than re-estimating models on pooled microdata. As a result, survey weights and replicate weights are not applicable to the review’s methodology.
handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a systematic review that synthesizes findings from previously published empirical studies; it does not analyze ILSA/PISA-style student achievement outcomes with plausible values (PVs). Because no original student-level dataset is modeled in this paper, there is no PV generation/combining procedure and no missing-data imputation strategy to report at the review level. Any missing-data handling would be specific to the individual included studies, which are not reprocessed here.
outcome_summary: This paper is a systematic review rather than an empirical ML study on a single dataset. It synthesizes 38 peer-reviewed publications (2013–2024) and reports descriptive findings about the types of educational process data used (clickstream most prevalent) and how ML is applied (procedural feature coding/representation learning vs. instrumental latent-trait/measurement estimation). The review also highlights recurring challenges such as feature extraction/selection and interpretability for practical educational use, and discusses issues like scalability and replicability. No model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) are computed by the authors in this review because they do not train or evaluate ML models on a pooled dataset.
null_fields_interpretation: The record is a systematic review without original student-level microdata analysis. Consequently, there is no total student count, no country-level sample breakdown, no PV handling or missing-data imputation performed by the authors, and no primary ML model trained/evaluated in this paper. The extracted ML-related content pertains to the included studies’ methods, not to an ML pipeline implemented by the review itself.
sample_filtering_criteria: No student-level analytic sample is constructed. The review includes 38 peer-reviewed empirical studies (English-language) that applied machine learning to educational process data, identified via Scopus searches (2013-01-01 to 2024-12-01) plus ancestry and hand searches in specified journals, following PRISMA 2020 inclusion/exclusion criteria.

title: Uncovering Student Strategies for Solving Scientific Inquiry Tasks: Insights from Student Process Data in PISA
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses publicly available PISA 2015 process-log data and a small PISA 2015 field-trial subset (Task 1 in Norway; Example 2 in Norway). The manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures, and it does not name any weight variables. Because the analyses are person-centered (latent profile analysis) and process-mining visualization on log-derived indicators rather than PV-based achievement modeling, the paper provides no explicit guidance on weight use for inference. For replication with full PISA microdata, analysts should consult the OECD PISA technical documentation for appropriate student weights and replicate weights, and then decide whether to incorporate them into profile estimation and group comparisons.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this paper are derived from process-log indicators (e.g., number of actions/trials, time-on-task, time before first action) and from task response components used to define accuracy categories/profiles, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. As a result, PISA plausible values are not the target of the modeling, so PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript mentions preprocessing steps including handling missing data, but it does not specify the missing-data rule (e.g., listwise deletion, imputation) used for the analytic datasets, which is a reporting gap for reproducibility.
outcome_summary: This paper demonstrates how PISA process-log data can be used to study scientific inquiry strategies beyond product correctness. In Example 1, process mining (Disco with the fuzzy miner algorithm) was applied to PISA 2015 field-trial Task 1 in Norway (N=81) to visualize students’ simulation interaction sequences; 63.7% used the VOTAT strategy, yet only 40.7% of those achieved full correctness, highlighting difficulties in coordinating evidence with claims. In Example 2, latent profile analysis on log-derived indicators for Task 2 in PISA 2015 Norway (N=1222) identified three profiles (strategic, emergent, disengaged), with strategic students showing the highest exploration and time-on-task and the highest likelihood of successful inquiry. MANOVA results linked inquiry-based teaching practices to profile membership, with class debate about investigations differentiating all three profiles. Limitations include the absence of reported PV handling, missing-data rules, and survey-weight application details, and the fact that the methods are profiling/visualization rather than predictive ML.
sample_filtering_criteria: Example 1 uses the PISA 2015 field trial in Norway and restricts to 10th-grade students assigned to the assessment unit Running in Hot Weather; within that unit it analyzes Task 1 (second question) and further restricts to students with log data for the task (N=81). Example 2 uses PISA 2015 data from Norway and analyzes Grade 9 and Grade 10 students (0.8% Grade 9; 99.2% Grade 10) from 221 schools, using a modified released field-trial item (Task 2) and nine student-questionnaire items capturing inquiry-based teaching and learning practices; the analytic sample for Task 2 is N=1222.
effect_size: Not reported (process-mining visualization; descriptive means and proportions). Key proportions: 63.7% used VOTAT; only 40.7% of VOTAT users solved correctly. Group sizes: correct N=33, partially correct N=30, incorrect N=17.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 Field Trial (Norway) Grade 10 Science data for Task 1, the study leveraged VOTAT navigation behavior, number of actions/trials, and response-time indicators to characterize how students’ log-derived sequences relate to correct, partially correct, and incorrect inquiry performance, finding that many students used VOTAT but only 40.7% of those achieved full correctness. This indicates that instruction should not only encourage VOTAT use but also support students in planning and executing the univariable-to-evidence coordination needed to complete the task successfully, while recognizing that process patterns alone do not guarantee correct scientific reasoning.
confounders: VOTAT navigation behavior; Interactive strategy (multivariable); Number of actions; Number of trials; Time-on-task; Time before first action; Multiple-choice response accuracy; Constructed text response accuracy; Explain inquiry ideas frequency; Laboratory practical experiments frequency; Argue about science questions frequency; Draw conclusions from experiments frequency; Opportunities to explain ideas frequency; Design own experiments frequency; Class debate about investigations frequency; Teacher explains concept relevance frequency; Investigation to test ideas frequency

title: Discovering action insights from large-scale assessment log data using machine learning
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the 2012 PIAAC log dataset for two problem sets (“Party Invitation” and “Club Membership”) and constructs analytic samples by filtering out incomplete logs or sequences with missing actions. The manuscript reports stratification by performance levels for comparisons and then builds sequence embeddings (Word2Vec/Doc2Vec) followed by supervised group classification (neural network and random forest). No complex survey weighting variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are mentioned, and the ML models are trained on behavioral action-sequence representations rather than PV-based achievement scores. Given the absence of explicit weighting discussion, the analysis should be treated as unweighted with respect to PIAAC’s complex survey design, which may limit population-representativeness of the classification results.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are performance groups derived from PIAAC problem-set scores (e.g., score0 vs score3; correct vs incorrect) based on action-sequence logs, not PV-based cognitive achievement scales. The paper states that incomplete logs/sequences with missing actions were removed during preprocessing, but it does not provide a formal missing-data handling method for other variables used in modeling (e.g., whether any additional missingness was imputed or how remaining missingness was treated). This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling beyond the explicit log-completeness filter.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes 2012 PIAAC problem-solving log data for two tasks (“Party Invitation” with 35 actions; “Club Membership” with 25 actions) and preprocesses logs by removing incomplete sequences with missing actions. It converts action sequences into embeddings using Word2Vec (action-level) and Doc2Vec (sequence-level), then validates “meaningful actions” via clustering coherence (silhouette scores) and supervised group classification using a neural network and random forest. For “Party Invitation,” focusing on mail-moving actions (case2) yields the best separation (silhouette 0.491) and the strongest NN performance (accuracy 94.6%, F1 up to 0.962). For “Club Membership,” focusing on mail-sending and environment actions (case2) improves separation (silhouette 0.333) and classification (NN F1 up to 0.917, accuracy 0.876; RF accuracy up to 0.880). Limitations include lack of explicit survey-weight handling discussion, reliance on log-derived group labels, and potential representativeness constraints.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the 2012 PIAAC log data for two specific problem sets: “Party Invitation” (35 distinct actions) and “Club Membership” (25 distinct actions). Preprocessed the dataset to remove incomplete logs or sequences with missing actions, then stratified by performance levels to compare high- vs low-performing groups. For feature verification, created three cases per problem set by using (case1) all actions, (case2) only the identified meaningful actions, and (case3) sequences with the meaningful actions excluded; sorting actions were excluded from consideration in “Club Membership” due to infrequency.
effect_size: Doc2Vec + Neural Network: F1 0.850–0.962 and accuracy 0.850–0.946 across cases; best case2 (mail-moving actions only) accuracy 94.6% with silhouette 0.491. Doc2Vec + Random Forest: F1 0.893–0.951 and accuracy 0.852–0.930 across cases; best case2 accuracy 92.3% with similar silhouette improvement.
primary_finding: Using PIAAC 2012 Problem Solving data from the “Party Invitation” problem set, the study leveraged embedded action-sequence representations (Word2Vec/Doc2Vec) and focused on mail-moving actions to predict the performance group (score0 vs score3), finding that restricting to the meaningful mail-moving actions (case2) produced the highest clustering coherence (silhouette 0.491) and the strongest classification performance (NN accuracy 94.6%, F1 up to 0.962). This indicates that identifying and validating a small set of high-impact actions can improve automated detection of low vs high problem-solving performance from log data, supporting adaptive feedback systems that target the specific action steps learners miss, though the results are based on log-derived group labels and do not establish causal effects.
confounders: Age group; Gender; Performance level (score group); Problem set type

title: Evaluating test-taking motivation based on process data and its influence on academic performance
authors: Jimei Ding; Ting Li; Yuan Liu; Jieyu Sang
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 science cognitive item process data for two science clusters (S01 and S02) and restricts the analytic sample to students who completed both clusters and had valid responses for the target items. After excluding 28 students with missing all answers to the target items or with total reaction time outside the normal range (3600 s), the authors analyze 2853 students. For the multilevel regression analyses, they explicitly incorporate the sampling weights provided by the PISA datasets into all multilevel analyses to improve population representativeness. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so replicate-weight usage cannot be confirmed; however, complex survey weighting is applied at least at the main estimation stage.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 science process data from two science clusters (S01 and S02) to develop a situational test-taking motivation construct termed “behavioral effort,” defined by four process indicators: time to last visit, time to first action, number of actions, and user missingness. After excluding 28 students with missing target-item responses or extreme total reaction time (>3600 s), the authors retain 2853 students from China and several Western-culture countries/regions. Behavioral effort is operationalized by K-means clustering into two groups (low effort: n=1013; high effort: n=1840), and its validity is checked against self-reported effort and response time effort (RTE). In multilevel regression with sampling weights, behavioral effort shows the strongest positive association with science performance (Est.=87.338, p<0.001, d=1.083), larger than RTE (d=0.773) and self-report (d=0.448). Cultural moderation is significant for behavioral effort and self-report but not for RTE (p=0.083), and the study uses the first plausible score for the outcome, with full PV results in supplemental materials.
null_fields_interpretation: The paper does not train predictive ML models; instead, it uses K-means clustering to derive behavioral effort groups and then applies multilevel regression (MLM) to test associations with science performance. Therefore, the ML technique fields are intentionally left empty (no supervised ML algorithm is evaluated), even though the study is predictive in the statistical sense (predicting PV-based achievement from motivation indicators).
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 student cognitive items in the science domain, selecting two science clusters (S01 and S02) and excluding adaptive testing items (reading literacy) to maintain consistency. Restricted to representative students from Confucian and Western cultures who completed both S01 and S02. Excluded 28 students who were missing all answers to the target items or whose total reaction time exceeded the normal range (3600 s). For the science academic performance outcome, used the first plausible score (first PV) from the PISA science scaling (with detailed results for all 10 PVs in supplemental materials).
countries_formatted: CHN (1067); GBR; USA; CAN; AUS; SGP; KOR; JPN
effect_size: Multilevel regression (MLM) with sampling weights. Behavioral effort: Est.=87.338, p<0.001, d=1.083; Self-reported effort: Est.=17.604, p<0.001, d=0.448; Response time effort: Est.=32.449, p<0.001, d=0.773. Additional analysis (Behavioral effort group membership (low vs high)): K-means clustering with Yeo-Johnson transformation; number of clusters selected using elbow rule and silhouette coefficient (final solution: 2 groups). Group sizes: low effort n=1013 (35.5%), high effort n=1840 (64.5%).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2018 Science (clusters S01 & S02) the study leveraged behavioral effort, self-reported effort, and response time effort (RTE) alongside SES and gender in multilevel regression to predict science academic performance (first PV), finding that behavioral effort had the largest positive association (d=1.083). This indicates that process-derived behavioral effort may be a more sensitive indicator of motivation-related performance differences than self-report or response-time effort alone, supporting motivation-aware feedback and interpretation in low-stakes testing.
confounders: Socioeconomic status (SES); Gender; Culture (Western vs Confucian); Competitiveness; Work mastery

title: Investigating the Predictive Performance of Process Data and Result Data in Complex Problem Solving Using the Conditional Gradient Boosting Algorithm
authors: F.N. Aydin; K.A. Korkmaz; I. Demir
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 computer-based problem-solving data for Türkiye and constructs an analytic sample by including only students who answered the first climate control unit item (CP025Q01) and then excluding those who never clicked the required “apply” button, yielding a final sample of 915 participants. For the dependent variable (CPS ability score), the authors estimate CPS-related ability using IRT models (GPCM/PCM/GRM) and explicitly state that student weights were included in all estimations. For the predictive modeling stage (conditional gradient boosting), hyperparameter tuning and model building were performed by incorporating student weights, indicating that the complex survey design is accounted for via student weighting rather than replicate-weight variance estimation. The manuscript does not report replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty estimation is likely based on the weighting approach used in the IRT estimation and the weighted ML training procedure described.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2012 Türkiye computer-based problem-solving data focused on the first climate control unit item (CP025Q01). The dependent variable is a CPS score estimated via IRT (GPCM/PCM/GRM) using expectation–maximization and full-information maximum likelihood, with student weights included; EAP ability estimates are scaled to mean 500 and SD 100. Missingness occurs in perseverance and openness-to-problem-solving (about 34% each) and is handled by imputing with missForest, with analyses repeated across mean/median/missForest and missForest selected due to better distributional properties. Predictive modeling uses conditional gradient boosting (mboost/blackboost) with a 70/30 train-test split and hyperparameter tuning via grid search with 10-fold cross-validation. Performance improves from process-only (R2=0.551) to result-only (R2=0.599) to combined data (R2=0.705), with top predictors including VOTAT strategy behaviors and mathematical/reading literacy. The findings are predictive and may not generalize beyond Türkiye or beyond a single CPS item, and the paper does not report replicate-weight variance estimation.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2012 Türkiye computer-based problem-solving data and included only individuals who answered the first climate control unit item (CP025Q01). From the initial sample of 994 participants, excluded cases during creation of the process variable “number of apply” for students who never clicked the “apply” button, because clicking “apply” is necessary for meaningful exploration in the task. For ability estimation, used data from students across forms that include CPS items (Forms 31–38), and then restricted the final ability-score dataset to Forms 31, 32, 35, and 36 that include the CP2 cluster containing the climate control unit.
effect_size: Conditional gradient boosting (mboost/blackboost) — MAE: 50.369, MAPE: 0.103, BIAS: 1.250, MSE: 3808.385, RMSE: 61.712, R: 0.742, R2: 0.551
primary_finding: Using PISA 2012 Türkiye CPS data (climate control unit item CP025Q01) with process data only, the study leveraged VOTAT strategy score, total time on task, number of reset events, non-intervention observation, and bottom VOTAT applications to predict CPS score, finding moderate predictive performance (R2 = 0.551) with higher CPS associated with greater VOTAT use and a negative nonlinear relationship with total time. This indicates that embedding strategy indicators (e.g., VOTAT-like behaviors) and time-effort signals into CPS scoring or formative feedback could improve the interpretability and responsiveness of complex-problem assessments, though the study is predictive rather than causal.

title: Human-Centered AI for Discovering Student Engagement Profiles on Large-Scale Educational Assessments
authors: Guo, H.; Johnson, M.; Saldivia, L.; Worthington, M.; Ercikan, K.
journal: Journal of Measurement and Evaluation in Education and Psychology
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses NAEP Grade 8 Mathematics digital assessment process/log data for a single NAEP item block (2022 administration; 14 items; 30 minutes). The manuscript reports a final analytic sample size after excluding students with irregular response time and abnormal completion, but it does not describe the application of NAEP complex survey weights or any replicate-weight procedure. Because the paper focuses on ML-based profile discovery and active learning with deep learning (autoencoder + LSTM) and supervised ensemble classification (random forest + SVC), it does not report a weighting variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or how weights were incorporated into model training or evaluation. As a result, readers should treat the reported profile proportions and model behavior as conditional on the analytic sample rather than explicitly population-representative estimates.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are engagement profile labels derived from process/log-derived features (navigation sequences, response-time categories, and derived test-level aggregates) rather than NAEP cognitive achievement scores with plausible values. The paper does not describe any missing-data strategy for questionnaire/background variables or for process-log features (e.g., how missing timestamps, tool-use logs, or incomplete sequences were handled beyond excluding irregular response time/abnormal completion). This is a reporting gap because process-log datasets commonly contain partial or missing events that can affect sequence modeling and clustering.
outcome_summary: The study demonstrates a human-centered AI (HAI) framework using NAEP 2022 Grade 8 Mathematics digital process/log data from one released item block (14 items; 30 minutes). After excluding students with irregular response time and abnormal completion, the analytic sample contains 14,008 students from the USA. Step 1 created interpretable process features, including item response-time categories derived from item-specific rapid-responding thresholds and test-level aggregates (total score, total response time, total visits). Step 2 used an autoencoder with LSTM layers to compress sequential navigation information into an 8-dimensional latent space, then clustered students (K-means with 30 clusters) and had human experts label representative and extreme cases, yielding 10 engagement profiles with more than half linked to low-performing students. Step 3 scaled labeling via active learning with a soft-voting ensemble (random forest + SVC), using pseudo-label confidence thresholds (e.g., >0.75), but the paper does not report numeric predictive metrics or survey-weighted estimates, limiting claims about population representativeness and classifier accuracy.
ml_all_techniques: Autoencoder, LSTM, K-means, t-SNE, Random Forest, SVM, Ensemble voting classifier, Active learning
sample_filtering_criteria: Used NAEP 2022 Grade 8 Mathematics digital assessment process/log data for one publicly released item block containing 14 items (30 minutes). Excluded students with irregular response time and abnormal completion on the selected item block; the remaining analytic sample size is N=14,008.
effect_size: Not reported (profile frequencies reported; model accuracy/confidence thresholds described but no numeric accuracy metrics provided). Additional analysis (Engagement profile membership (fully labeled profiles after active learning)): Not reported (stopping rule based on inability to improve model accuracy; pseudo-label confidence threshold >0.75 used).
primary_finding: Using NAEP 2022 Grade 8 Mathematics digital item-block the study leveraged total score, total response time, total number of visits, item response-time categories, and item navigation sequences to create engagement profiles, finding ten differentiable profiles with more than half associated with low-performing students. This indicates that combining process/log-derived timing and navigation context with performance information can produce actionable, human-interpretable engagement typologies for low-achieving learners, though the paper does not report predictive accuracy metrics for the profile classifier.
confounders: Total score (block); Total response time; Total number of visits; Item response time category; Item navigation sequence; Visits per item

title: An engagement‑aware predictive model to evaluate problem‑solving performance from the study of adult skills’ (PIAAC 2012) process data
authors: Jinnie Shin; B. W.; W. P.; M. G.
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PIAAC 2012 PS-TRE process-log data from the first round of the PIAAC Main Study (2011–2012) and restricts analyses to a single PS-TRE booklet (PS1) and to three countries (United States, South Korea, United Kingdom). The manuscript does not report applying PIAAC sampling weights or replicate weights, nor does it name any weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or describe complex-survey variance estimation. Because the models are deep-learning sequence models (LSTM with attention) trained on process-derived graph/network statistics, the paper does not document whether weights were incorporated; this omission suggests an unweighted or weight-agnostic estimation approach. Analysts using the same log dataset should verify whether PIAAC-provided weights are available for the restricted booklet/country subset and whether the authors’ training/evaluation pipeline accounted for the complex sampling design.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are engagement status (binary) and task/problem performance categories derived from PS-TRE item/task scoring, predicted from process-log-derived sequence representations. Plausible Values are typically used for cognitive achievement scales in ILSA reporting, but here the outcomes are modeled as classification targets from process data rather than PV-based achievement scores, so PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript does not describe any missing-data strategy for predictors or labels (e.g., how incomplete sequences, missing timestamps, or absent graph statistics were handled), which is a reporting gap given that log-based sequences can vary in length and completeness.
outcome_summary: The study develops an engagement-aware deep-learning framework for PIAAC 2012 PS-TRE process-log data restricted to booklet PS1 and three countries (United States, South Korea, United Kingdom). It converts each examinee’s action sequence into a directed graph, summarizes the graph with five network statistics, and feeds these into an LSTM with a global attention layer. Two model variants are compared: Attention-LSTM (performance only) and Effort-Aware Attention-LSTM (jointly predicts performance and binary engagement status labeled via T-disengagement thresholds). Across countries, the engagement-aware model improves performance prediction (overall F1 roughly 0.88–0.90 vs ~0.82–0.83; AUC ~0.82–0.84 vs ~0.70–0.75; accuracy ~0.80–0.88 vs ~0.75–0.78). Engagement prediction is also strong (F1 ~0.92–0.94; AUC ~0.86–0.88). Limitations include lack of reported survey-weight usage and no documented missing-data handling for log-derived sequences.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIAAC 2012 PS-TRE process-log data from the first round of the PIAAC Main Study (Aug 2011–Nov 2012) and restricted the analysis to the cognitive domain PS-TRE booklet PS1. The analytic dataset includes only the three countries explicitly analyzed (United States, South Korea, United Kingdom) and uses the PS1 items/tasks (14 tasks total in PS-TRE overall; the study reports experimenting with items included in booklet PS1). Engagement labels were created at the item/task level using the T-disengagement method based on item-specific response-time thresholds, and the model was trained to predict both performance and engagement for each task.
effect_size: Effort-Aware Attention-LSTM vs Attention-LSTM (3 countries; 3-fold CV averages). Overall performance: US ACC 0.802 vs 0.779, AUC 0.821 vs 0.751, F1 0.875 vs 0.824; SK ACC 0.859 vs 0.751, AUC 0.824 vs 0.700, F1 0.886 vs 0.828; GB ACC 0.883 vs 0.778, AUC 0.835 vs 0.771, F1 0.900 vs 0.816. Task-level: largest F1 improvement reported for Task 5 (+0.21 to +0.28) and accuracy improvement (+0.20 to +0.23).
primary_finding: Using PIAAC 2012 PS-TRE (Booklet PS1) process-log the study leveraged directed-graph network statistics (centralization, density, flow hierarchy, shortest path, total nodes) to predict problem-solving performance categories, finding that the Effort-Aware Attention-LSTM improved performance across all three countries and metrics relative to Attention-LSTM. This indicates that explicitly modeling test-taking engagement alongside sequential process information can yield more accurate estimates of adult problem-solving performance in low-stakes digital assessments, though the paper does not report survey-weight use or a missing-data strategy.

title: When didactics meet data science: process data analysis in large‑scale mathematics assessment in France
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses France’s national grade-9 mathematics large-scale assessment (CEDRE) interactive “Tree growth” item pilot data collected in May 2017, focusing on students’ logged interaction features for one technology-enhanced task. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights or any specific weight variable (e.g., sampling/design weights) for the pilot log-data analysis. Because the supervised model is a Random Forest classifier and the clustering uses DBSCAN/k-means, the paper does not describe any weighting strategy to correct for the clustered sampling structure (students within schools/classes) or for differential selection probabilities. Analysts should therefore treat the results as descriptive/predictive for the pilot item sample unless weights are confirmed elsewhere; the paper’s main emphasis is on didactically grounded feature engineering and model-based feature importance rather than population-representative estimation.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a binary correctness label for a single interactive item (“correct boolean”), derived from students’ responses within the log-data task. Plausible Values are generated in ILSA frameworks for cognitive achievement scales, but this study models item-level correctness rather than PV-based achievement scores, so PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe any explicit missing-data procedure for the engineered log features (e.g., deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap given that log-derived variables can be incomplete when interactions are interrupted or tools are not used.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes process log data from a pilot administration (May 2017) of France’s CEDRE grade-9 mathematics technology-enhanced “Tree growth” item, using engineered interaction features derived from students’ tool use and input-search behavior. For supervised learning, the authors train a Random Forest classifier to predict a binary correctness label and report ROC AUC = 0.78, with feature importance highlighting search breadth (month list length), concentration around the target (standard deviation), and refinement steps (distances from early inputs and alternations). In parallel, they segment students using unsupervised clustering (DBSCAN, with k-means used for stability comparison) and interpret four student profiles, distinguishing trial-and-error versus pencil-supported structural approaches. The paper’s main limitation for policy inference is that it models item-level correctness rather than PV-based achievement, does not report missing-data handling, and does not discuss whether weighting or hierarchical sampling adjustments were applied to the pilot sample.
sample_filtering_criteria: Uses the pilot test administration (May 2017) of CEDRE interactive mathematics items in grade 9, selecting one specific technology-enhanced item (“Tree growth”) and analyzing students’ recorded digital traces from that item. The manuscript states a sample of 3000 grade-9 students per item for the pilot; the analytic dataset is therefore the set of students who attempted the chosen item and for whom the engineered log features (e.g., month list length, alternations, time spent, distances to target, pencil use) were constructed. No additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., minimum completion time, tool-use thresholds, or missing-feature handling) are reported.
effect_size: Random Forest — ROC AUC: 0.78
primary_finding: Using CEDRE 2017 pilot Grade 9 Mathematics “Tree growth” process-the study leveraged month-list length, dispersion (standard deviation), and distances from the target (plus alternation behavior) to predict item success (correct boolean), finding that the Random Forest achieved ROC AUC = 0.78. This indicates that didactically grounded interaction features (how students search and refine inputs) can support actionable identification of likely success/failure on technology-enhanced mathematics tasks, though the paper does not establish causal effects and does not report missing-data handling or survey-weighted representativeness.
confounders: Month list length; First input between 200-600; Number of alternations; Time spent on item; Distance from first input; Distance from second input; Distance from last input; Std dev of month values; Target value entered; Pencil use

title: Predictive Machine Learning Approach for Complex Problem Solving Process Data Mining
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 computer-based assessment (CBA) problem-solving microdata for the Climate Control task (CP025Q01), combining scored cognitive item response data with problem-solving log-file data. The analytic dataset is constructed by extracting only entries relevant to the Climate Control task and then merging with the task success indicator; the authors also report data cleaning, downsampling to balance the TRUE/FALSE success classes, and removal of corrupted entries. The manuscript does not mention applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) and does not report any weight variable names. Because the models are standard supervised ML classifiers (e.g., deep learning, random forest, gradient boosted trees) and the paper provides no survey-weighting procedure, the analysis is treated as unweighted; this may leave residual bias from the complex sampling design.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is task success for a specific PISA 2012 CBA unit (Climate Control CP025Q01), derived from the scored cognitive item response file and treated as a binary classification target (TRUE/FALSE). Plausible Values are typically generated for cognitive achievement domains in PISA, but this paper predicts success on a single process-based problem-solving item rather than PV-based achievement scores; therefore PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript describes data cleaning, downsampling for class balance, and removal of corrupted entries, but it does not explicitly document how missing values were handled (e.g., complete-case deletion vs. imputation), which is a reporting gap for reproducibility.
outcome_summary: The study predicts success on the PISA 2012 computer-based Climate Control problem-solving task (CP025Q01, first unit item) using supervised ML on features engineered from raw log files. Two feature sets were compared: VOTAT-strategy action ratios and time-based paradata features. Across six classifiers (Naive Bayes, logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, gradient boosted trees, and deep learning), deep learning performed best overall: with VOTAT-based features it reached F-measure 94.3% (accuracy 93.9%, AUC 0.947), and with time-based features it reached F-measure 77.1% (accuracy 77.1%, AUC 0.847). After genetic-algorithm optimization of the neural network architecture, F-measure improved to 94.9% (VOTAT) and 77.9% (time). The manuscript does not report a survey-weighting strategy and does not explicitly document missing-data handling, limiting interpretability and reproducibility.
ml_all_techniques: Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, Neural Network, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2012 computer-based assessment problem-solving data and extracted only records relevant to the Climate Control task unit item CP025Q01 (first question). The initial Climate Control dataset was assembled from (i) the scored cognitive item response data file containing each student’s assessment result and (ii) the problem-solving data files containing the full log of slider positions, button clicks, and actions; sequence order numbers and timestamps were assigned per entry. The final dataset was produced after prediction preprocessing including data cleaning, downsampling to balance the TRUE/FALSE success classes, and elimination of corrupted entries, resulting in 15,194 remaining entries.
effect_size: Deep learning (VOTAT-based features) — Accuracy: 93.9%, AUC: 0.947, Recall: 99.7%, F-measure: 94.3%; Deep learning (time-based features) — Accuracy: 77.1%, AUC: 0.847, Recall: 77.1%, F-measure: 77.1%. Best overall by F-measure: deep learning with VOTAT-based features (F-measure 94.3%); random forest and gradient boosted trees also reached 94.5% F-measure with VOTAT-based features but were lower with time-based features (F-measure 69.7% and 75.6%). Optimized deep learning via genetic algorithm — F-measure: 94.9% (VOTAT-based) and 77.9% (time-based).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2012 CBA Problem Solving (Climate Control CP025Q01) the study leveraged VOTAT strategy usage ratios and time spent on task phases to predict Climate Control task success (TRUE/FALSE), finding that deep learning achieved the highest F-measure with VOTAT-based features (94.3%, optimized 94.9%), while time-based features yielded substantially lower performance (F-measure 77.1%, optimized 77.9%). The paper reports strong predictive accuracy but does not document survey-weight usage or missing-data handling, and the nested sampling structure is not explicitly addressed in the ML pipeline. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.
confounders: VOTAT strategy usage ratios; Time spent on task phases

title: Predicting science achievement scores with machine learning algorithms: a case study of OECD PISA 2015–2018 data
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2015 microdata for 13 randomly selected countries and predicts PISA 2018 science outcomes using the same set of predictors. The analytic sample is defined by (i) selecting only those 13 countries, (ii) using PV2SCIE as the science achievement target, (iii) splitting each country’s PISA-2015 data into training (75%) and testing (25%) subsets, and (iv) excluding cases with missing predictor variables during preprocessing. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so the weighting strategy is unclear; given the ML focus (XGBoost/RF/SVR), the analysis may have been conducted without complex-survey weighting. For replication, analysts should use the OECD/PISA sampling weights and PV procedures from the OECD database documentation when estimating population-representative relationships, and ensure missingness handling is consistent with the authors’ exclusion rule.
outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA 2015 science data from 13 randomly selected countries (n=67,329) and predicts PISA 2018 science achievement using four supervised models: multiple linear regression, support vector regression, random forest, and XGBoost. The target is PV2SCIE, and the authors split each country’s PISA-2015 data into training (75%) and testing (25%) sets, optimizing hyperparameters via grid search with 10-fold cross-validation. Missing cases are excluded during preprocessing, and performance is evaluated with Pearson’s r, RMSE, and MAE. Across both PISA-2015 testing and PISA-2018 estimation, XGBoost is reported as the best-performing model, with moderate correlations (0.40<r<0.69) and the highest PISA-2018 predictive correlation in Luxembourg (r=0.600; RMSE=75.06; MAE=59.97) and the lowest in Finland (r=0.467; RMSE=79.38; MAE=63.24). The study also reports very high accuracy for country-average predictions and highlights SMINS, ESCS, HOMEPOS, and TMINS as top predictors, but it does not clearly document complex-survey weighting, so generalizability and causal interpretation for policy are limited.
ml_all_techniques: Linear Regression, SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost
sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses OECD PISA 2015 science data for 13 randomly selected countries from the PISA 2015 population. It restricts the dataset to those 13 countries and uses the science achievement plausible value PV2SCIE as the target. For model training and evaluation, each country’s PISA-2015 data are randomly split into training (75%) and testing (25%) subsets. During preprocessing, missing data detected in a small number of cases are directly excluded (complete-case style) before training/testing. A second validation approach is also used where 25% (16,832 students) of the full 13-country dataset is repeatedly sampled three times, then split into 75% training and 25% testing within each sample.
effect_size: Best model: XGBoost. Country-level testing performance (r): highest Luxembourg r=0.600 (RMSE=75.06, MAE=59.97) and lowest Finland r=0.467 (RMSE=79.38, MAE=63.24). Overall reported correlation range: moderate correlations (0.40 < r < 0.69).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2015 Science data (PV2SCIE) from 13 countries to train XGBoost and predict PISA 2018 Science achievement (PV2SCIE), the study leveraged SMINS, ESCS, HOMEPOS, and TMINS (with BELONG also appearing among high-importance variables in some countries) to estimate student science outcomes. It found that XGBoost outperformed MLR, SVR, and Random Forest across all researched countries, with moderate predictive correlations and lowest errors for countries like Luxembourg. This indicates that strengthening science learning time and addressing socioeconomic disparities may improve future science achievement, though the study’s predictive (not causal) design and the lack of explicit survey-weight handling limit policy causal claims.
confounders: Computer for school work; Gender; Books at home (count); Parental support for learning; Mother education (ISCED); Father education (ISCED); Highest parental education; Class discipline in science; Science learning time (weekly); Total learning time (weekly); Sense of belonging to school; Parents emotional support; Home possessions; Family wealth; Socioeconomic status (ESCS); Teacher adaptation; Received feedback; Teacher support in science

title: Text-Based Approaches to Item Difficulty Modeling in Large-Scale Assessments: A Systematic Review
weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a systematic review that synthesizes results across 37 articles (46 difficulty-prediction studies) rather than analyzing a single ILSA micro-dataset. Because no student-level assessment dataset is pooled or re-estimated here, there is no application of ILSA sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the review’s own analyses. The review’s quantitative synthesis uses count-based aggregation and descriptive statistics of reported performance metrics, so weighting is not part of the methodological pipeline. For future empirical work using ILSA micro-data, analysts should apply the official complex-survey weights provided by the data producer when estimating population-representative relationships and when reporting uncertainty for model performance.
handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a systematic review that does not fit predictive models to student-level ILSA plausible values (PVs) or report any PV-based scaling/estimation procedure. The review aggregates published outcomes (e.g., RMSE, MAE, Pearson r, R², accuracy) across heterogeneous studies that used different item difficulty parameters (CTT p-values, transformed p-values, IRT b parameters) rather than re-estimating PV-based achievement scores. Therefore, PV handling and missing-data handling are not applicable to the review’s own analysis, and missing-data handling is not reported as a review protocol detail.
outcome_summary: This systematic review synthesizes 37 articles (46 difficulty-prediction studies) on text-based item difficulty modeling in large-scale assessment contexts, focusing on models that predict item difficulty parameters from item text and related metadata. Across the reviewed studies, item difficulty was operationalized using CTT p-values and transformed p-values as well as IRT b-parameters (with regression framed as the dominant task), and performance was summarized using common metrics such as RMSE, MAE, MSE, R², and Pearson/Spearman correlations, plus accuracy metrics for categorical difficulty. The review reports benchmark ranges including RMSE as low as 0.165 and Pearson correlation as high as 0.87, with exact accuracy up to 0.806, while emphasizing that results are not directly comparable due to heterogeneity in datasets, difficulty parameter definitions, and evaluation protocols. Methodologically, the review highlights under-reporting of preprocessing and the need for standardized benchmarking, and it notes that many studies come from the BEA shared task (USMLE items), which may bias observed trends. Because this is not an original empirical ML study, no single weighting scheme, PV handling strategy, or missing-data procedure is estimated by the authors.
null_fields_interpretation: This record is a systematic review rather than an empirical ILSA micro-data analysis. As a result, there is no student-level sample, no country-level per-country N, no PV estimation/scaling step, and no ML model training/evaluation performed by the review itself; it only aggregates reported outcomes from included studies. Consequently, fields such as total_students, countries, and ml_techniques are intentionally left empty/null, and the methodological emphasis is on the review’s screening/coding and synthesis approach.
sample_filtering_criteria: Not applicable: the study is a systematic review. It screened 93 articles, excluded 17 after abstract/keywords screening and 52 after full-text screening using criteria including (1) not large-scale, (2) focused on text complexity/readability rather than item difficulty, (3) not automated prediction from item text, (4) review articles, and (5) difficulty parameter not estimated from human test-taker responses. It then coded 37 articles and treated each dataset/assessment difficulty-prediction task as a separate study, yielding 46 studies for synthesis.

title: Identifying students’ solution strategies in digital mathematics assessment using log data
authors: de Schipper; EdS; RF; SK; RdS; BV
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses French national low-stakes CEDRE digital mathematics assessment data (2019) administered in ninth grade, with abilities estimated via a 2PL model using MML (EM) and Warm’s WLE. The analytic sample is restricted to students who interacted with the specific digital item and for whom score, estimated ability, and response time were registered (final N=802). The manuscript does not report applying complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights or replicate weights) in the clustering/mixture-model stage, and no weight variable names are provided. Because the analysis is based on log-derived behavioral variables and a finite mixture model, the paper’s weighting approach (if any) is not documented; readers should treat the ability comparisons across latent classes as descriptive/associational rather than fully population-representative unless weights are confirmed in the full technical documentation.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable used to relate solution-strategy classes to mathematical ability is an estimated ability score (theta) obtained via Warm’s WLE from a 2PL model, not a PV-based achievement score. The paper reports explicit exclusions for missing/invalid log components (no interaction, no score/ability/response time, and a technical malfunction for response times), but it does not describe any additional missing-data imputation strategy for other variables. Therefore, missing-data handling beyond the stated exclusions is not fully documented.
outcome_summary: The study analyzes log data from the French CEDRE 2019 ninth-grade digital mathematics assessment, focusing on one interactive item (“Product Equation”) and using the entire assessment to estimate students’ mathematical ability via a 2PL model (MML with EM for item parameters, then Warm’s WLE for student abilities). An exploratory finite mixture (model-based clustering) approach was used to identify five latent solution-strategy classes from constructed log-behavior variables; model selection relied on BIC/AIC across 2–6 classes with robustness checks via bootstrapping. The resulting classes differed in estimated ability: the disengaged class (class 5) showed the lowest mean theta and was significantly lower than classes 1–4 (p<0.001 after Bonferroni; large effects d≈−0.86 to −1.11). The paper does not report survey-weight usage or PV handling because the outcome is WLE theta rather than PV achievement, and it uses t-tests for class mean comparisons, so results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.
null_fields_interpretation: This paper is primarily an exploratory process-data clustering study rather than a supervised predictive ML study: it uses finite mixture models to form latent strategy groups and then compares ability across those groups. As a result, no predictive ML algorithm (e.g., Random Forest/XGBoost) is trained and no classification/regression performance metrics (accuracy/AUC/RMSE) are reported. The 'primary' ML technique field is therefore left empty because the analysis goal is strategy discovery and descriptive inference, not predictive modeling.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used CEDRE 2019 ninth-grade digital mathematics assessment log data for the single analyzed item (“Product Equation”), administered in TAO. Excluded students who did not interact with the assessment environment at all, and excluded students for whom no score, estimated ability, or response time was registered. Additionally removed five students due to a technical malfunction in the registration of their response times. Cleaned item-level log interactions by removing construction events (typing longer sequences) and deletion events (deleting previously typed input), and then constructed strategy-related variables from the remaining interactions.
effect_size: Not reported (exploratory finite mixture model; model fit via BIC/AIC across 2–6 classes; selected 5-class model).
primary_finding: Using CEDRE 2019 Grade 9 Mathematics data for the digital 'Product Equation' item, the study leveraged log-derived behavioral indicators (e.g., interaction timing and specific input/answer behaviors) to identify latent solution-strategy classes, finding five distinct groups with different in-assessment behavior patterns. This indicates that process-log data can support didactically interpretable student-strategy profiling beyond correctness alone, enabling more targeted feedback and instruction.
confounders: Latent solution-strategy class

title: Exploring the relationship between process data and contextual variables among Scandinavian students on PISA 2012 mathematics tasks
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics assessment data for Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, restricting to students with available log files for three selected CBAM items (CM015Q01, CM015Q02D, CM015Q03D). Because PISA employs a two-stage sampling design with unequal selection probabilities, the authors incorporate sampling weights to obtain unbiased estimations in the CFA/latent regression analyses. They implement this in R using lavaan.survey, which applies the complex survey design during estimation. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that sampling weights were used; replicate weights are not mentioned.
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are item-level response accuracy (binary/ordinal), response time, and frequency of actions derived from CBAM log files, and the contextual covariates are questionnaire scales/indices rather than PV-based achievement scores. Missing contextual data are handled via full-information maximum likelihood (FIML) in parameter estimation, which is treated here as multiple-imputation-style handling because it uses all available data under a likelihood-based framework rather than listwise deletion.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2012 computer-based mathematics assessment (CBAM) log files for Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, focusing on three interactive items (CM015Q01, CM015Q02D, CM015Q03D) administered to age-15 students. From log files, the authors extract response accuracy (binary/ordinal), response time (log-transformed), and frequency of actions (log-transformed) and fit a three-factor CFA model representing math proficiency, speed, and exploration behaviour. They incorporate PISA sampling weights via lavaan.survey and handle missing contextual data using full-information maximum likelihood (FIML). Measurement invariance results show weak invariance fits best (CFI≈0.968; RMSEA≈0.075; SRMR≈0.042), allowing multi-group latent regression with contextual covariates. Key substantive findings include consistent positive ESCS effects on math proficiency and country-specific associations for ICT and mathematics-experience variables; causality is not inferred because PISA is cross-sectional.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2012 CBAM mathematics data for Scandinavian countries (Denmark, Sweden, Norway) and restricted to students with available log file data for three selected interactive math items from the CD production unit (CM015Q01, CM015Q02D, CM015Q03D). From the 1614 students with available log files, 188 students were removed due to missing values in the analysis dataset, yielding a final analytic sample of 1426 students. No additional grade/school-type restrictions are reported beyond the PISA age-15 target population and the item/log availability requirement.
effect_size: Measurement invariance comparison: weak invariance preferred over configural (CFI=0.968, RMSEA=0.075, SRMR=0.042; Δχ2 p=0.18) and strong invariance (CFI=0.958, RMSEA=0.078, SRMR=0.049; Δχ2 p=0.000). Additional analysis (Latent math proficiency (response accuracy factor)): Latent regression (multi-group) — model fit: CFI=0.926, TLI=0.904, RMSEA=0.048, SRMR=0.058. Factor loadings in CFA: Accuracy 1 loading=0.507; Accuracy 2 loading=0.444; Accuracy 3 loading=0.751 (all positive and significant). Additional analysis (Latent speed (response time factor)): Latent regression (multi-group) — model fit: CFI=0.926, TLI=0.904, RMSEA=0.048, SRMR=0.058. CFA factor loadings for speed (log response time): Tm1 loading=0.513; Tm2 loading=0.787; Tm3 loading=0.773 (all positive and significant). Additional analysis (Latent exploration behaviour (frequency of actions factor)): Latent regression (multi-group) — model fit: CFI=0.926, TLI=0.904, RMSEA=0.048, SRMR=0.058. CFA factor loadings for exploration behaviour (log frequency of actions): Fq1 loading=0.697; Fq2 loading=0.656; Fq3 loading=0.881 (all positive and significant).
primary_finding: Using PISA 2012 CBAM mathematics the study leveraged contextual variables conceptually to interpret cross-country comparisons while evaluating measurement invariance for the latent process model, finding that weak measurement invariance best fit the data across Denmark, Sweden, and Norway. This indicates that factor loadings were consistent across countries, enabling meaningful comparisons of factor covariances and subsequent contextual regression effects, which supports the use of standardized latent process modeling for cross-national CBAM research.

title: A call to action: a systematic review of ethical and regulatory issues in using process data in educational assessment
weight_fields_interpretation: This study is a desk-based systematic literature review and does not analyze a student-level large-scale assessment dataset. Because no primary microdata are used, there is no sampling frame, no complex survey design, and no application of student or replicate weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT or BRR/jackknife). The review instead codes and summarizes characteristics of 22 eligible publications using an ordinal coding scheme aligned to Sclater’s (2016) code of practice. Therefore, weighting guidance for ILSA plausible values or survey inference is not applicable to the empirical unit of analysis (the included studies).
handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PV) are generated for cognitive achievement scales in ILSA assessments, but this paper does not estimate student achievement scores from ILSA microdata. Instead, it synthesizes published studies and codes whether ethical/privacy/regulatory elements are present using an ordinal rubric. Missing-data handling for PVs or student responses is therefore not part of the methodology because there is no student-level dataset being imputed or deleted.
outcome_summary: This paper is a systematic literature review (not an empirical ML study) examining how ethical, privacy, and regulatory considerations are reflected in research that uses process/log data in educational assessment. The authors searched multiple databases and hand-searched journals for 2010–2018, initially finding 1349 records after deduplication and screening down to 66 full-text candidates, then to 22 eligible studies after applying first- and second-order eligibility criteria. They coded each included study using a modified Sclater (2016) code of practice with eight categories (e.g., Responsibility, Transparency & consent, Privacy, Validity, Access, Stewardship of data, Enabling positive interventions, Minimising adverse impact) on a 0–3 ordinal scale, then summarized medians/ranges and subgroup differences. Across the 22 studies, ethics-related issues were found to feature minimally overall, with comparatively higher attention to Privacy and Transparency & consent, while responsibility and stewardship of data were rarely addressed. The review concludes that assessment standards and ethical guidance have not kept pace with the use of process data, motivating a bespoke code of ethics for educational assessment contexts.

title: Using process features to investigate scientific problem-solving in large-scale assessments
authors: Tao Gong; L. Shuai; Y. Jiang; B. Arslan
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses NAEP 2018 science pilot tasks administered via technology-enhanced items (TEIs) and analyzes process features (preparation time, execution time, mean execution time per event) alongside rubric-based item scores. The manuscript does not report the use of NAEP sampling/survey weights or any replicate-weight procedure, and it does not name any weight variables. Because the analyses are based on nonparametric tests (Kruskal–Wallis, Wilcoxon signed-rank) and omnibus ANOVA/t-tests on process-feature distributions across score groups, the paper does not provide guidance on how to incorporate complex survey design weights into these inferential comparisons. For replication or extension with NAEP microdata, analysts should consult NAEP technical documentation to determine the appropriate student weight(s) and replicate weights for variance estimation, and then re-run the group-comparison tests under a weighted/replicate framework if population-representative inference is required.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are rubric-based item scores for specific NAEP science pilot TEIs (fair and exhaustive tasks), not PV-based cognitive achievement scales. Therefore, plausible values are not applicable to the outcome construction used here. The paper states that missing values were removed prior to analysis, so missing-data handling is addressed via case deletion rather than PV-based imputation.
outcome_summary: This study analyzes NAEP 2018 science pilot TEIs using four scientific inquiry tasks (two fair tests for Grade 4 and Grade 8, and two exhaustive tests for Grade 12). Instead of training predictive ML models, the authors define three process features from event timestamps—preparation time (PT), execution time (ET), and mean execution time per answer-related event (MET)—and test whether these features differ across rubric-based score groups. Across all four tasks, Kruskal–Wallis and omnibus ANOVA results show statistically significant score-group differences for ET and MET, with PT showing stronger effects in fair tests and more mixed/marginal effects in exhaustive tasks. The paper also reports Wilcoxon signed-rank patterns: higher scores generally correspond to shorter ET in fair tests, while exhaustive tasks show longer ET for full-score students but shorter PT and MET. Limitations include the absence of survey-weight reporting and the use of group-comparison tests rather than a predictive evaluation with cross-validation, so results support relatedness rather than causal or out-of-sample predictive claims.
sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses the 2018 NAEP science pilot tasks and selects four TEI testlets: two fair tests (grade 4 and grade 8 bands) and two exhaustive tests (grade 12 band). Analyses are conducted only on students whose process and response data were available for the respective testlets; the paper notes that data were missing due to early quit or data capture glitches and that the rightmost column in Table 1 records the number of students whose process and response data were used. Before analysis, the authors remove missing values for the process features (after which winsorization is applied to each process feature). No additional school-type or country subsampling is described beyond the grade-band/testlet selection inherent to the NAEP pilot tasks.
effect_size: Kruskal–Wallis: PT χ2=12.2, df=2, p<0.005; ET χ2=89.916, df=2, p<0.001; MET χ2=64.776, df=2, p<0.001. Omnibus ANOVA: PT F(2,1604)=5.943, p<0.005; ET F(2,1604)=51.7, p<0.001; MET F(2,1604)=38.93, p<0.001. Wilcoxon signed-rank: higher-score group had shorter ET; full-score group had shorter PT and MET than lowest-score group, but differences were not statistically significant when the partial-score group was included.
primary_finding: Using NAEP 2018 science pilot TEIs (Fair test 1, Grade 8, Earth/space science) the study leveraged preparation time (PT), execution time (ET), and mean execution time (MET) to relate process features to rubric-based item score (1–3), finding that score groups differed significantly on all three temporal features (all Kruskal–Wallis p<0.005 and omnibus ANOVA p<0.005). This indicates that students’ planning and action-execution efficiency—captured by PT, ET, and MET—are strongly associated with successful control-of-variables performance, suggesting that process-informed scoring rubrics or feedback could target inefficient planning and hesitant execution stages.

title: Predicting problem-solving success in an office simulation applying N-grams and a random forest to behavioral process data
authors: Sabrina Ludwig; Andreas Rausch; Viola Deutscher; Jürgen Seifried
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a single-subject experimental/assessment setting (VET students working in the Luca office simulation) rather than an ILSA-style multi-stage sampling frame. The methods section describes voluntary participation, onboarding, and a fixed 55-minute scenario, but it does not report any sampling/survey weights or complex survey design adjustments. Because the analysis is based on ML classification using log-derived n-gram features, the manuscript does not indicate the use of any weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and no replicate-weight scheme is described. The main preprocessing steps are log export (JSON), transformation to CSV, removal of off-platform work, aggregation of subsequent events, and exclusion of low-information events; these steps define the analytic dataset used for model training/testing.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a rubric-based problem-solving success score that is dichotomized into two balanced classes using a cut score, not a PV-based cognitive achievement outcome. As a result, plausible values are not generated or required for the outcome. The manuscript also does not describe any explicit missing-data handling procedure for predictors or outcomes (e.g., imputation or case deletion rules), which is a reporting gap given that log-derived features can be affected by incomplete early windows or event aggregation.
outcome_summary: The study predicts rubric-based problem-solving success in a Luca web-based office simulation using behavioral process data represented as uni- and bi-grams derived from time-stamped log files. Success was dichotomized into two balanced classes using a cut score of 53, excluding borderline cases (n=10), and models were trained on early windows of the first 5, 10, and 20 minutes. A random forest classifier was evaluated with accuracy, F1, and ROC AUC, using a train/test split (70/30) and 10-fold cross-validation for AUC. Performance improved as the early window expanded: ROC AUC increased from 0.61 (first 5 min) to 0.63 (first 10 min) and 0.67 (first 20 min), with feature selection raising AUC to almost 0.70 for the 20-minute window. The paper does not report any explicit missing-data handling strategy and does not use survey weights; additionally, the model is trained and tested within a single simulation context, so external validity to other tasks/environments remains uncertain.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used a sample of 234 VET students who completed a single in-person Luca web-based office simulation scenario. Participants received a 15-minute onboarding scenario and then worked on a complex supplier-selection task for up to 55 minutes (with flexibility to end early). For modeling, early clickstream/keystroke data were restricted to the first 5, 10, and 20 minutes of the scenario; log preprocessing removed participants who worked outside the web-based simulation, aggregated subsequent events of the same kind into single activities, and removed events deemed uninformative due to simulation design (e.g., double clicks, tool closing). For the classification target, rubric sum scores were dichotomized using a cut at 53 points, and borderline cases (n=10) were excluded to create balanced classes.
effect_size: Random forest (M1, <5 min): accuracy = 0.53; F1 (less successful) = 0.53; F1 (more successful) = 0.53; ROC AUC = 0.61. Feature selection (robust features only) improved AUC from 0.61 to 0.65.
primary_finding: Using Luca office simulation data (VET) with early process information from the first 5 minutes, the study leveraged early-window behavioral indicators (n-gram features) to predict binary problem-solving success, finding that predictive discrimination was limited (ROC AUC = 0.61; accuracy = 0.53). This indicates that very early behavioral traces contain insufficient information for reliable success prediction, so adaptive scaffolding should be delayed until more diagnostic evidence accumulates, while still using feature selection to improve robustness.
confounders: Problem-solving success score; Age; Gender; Early window length

title: Improving math proficiency prediction in computer-based international large-scale assessments with data augmentation
authors: Aleksandar Pejić; Piroska Stanić Molcer; Dávid Fa
journal: 2022 IEEE 20th Jubilee International Symposium on Intelligent Systems and Informatics (SISY)
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the publicly released PISA 2012 computer-based assessment database and constructs a tabular dataset of 17,671 student records. The authors split the dataset into training, validation, and test sets (80/20 split with 20% for testing and an additional 20% for validation) and normalize all columns. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures, and it does not mention any weight-aware estimation tools. Because the predictive models are deep neural networks trained on augmented data, the analysis appears to be conducted without explicit incorporation of survey weights.
handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a discretized three-class “math proficiency” outcome derived from the PISA 2012 overall mathematics result, but the paper does not describe whether this outcome is based on PISA plausible values (PVs) or on an alternative scoring/aggregation approach. The manuscript also does not report any missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case deletion, imputation, or PV-based handling), which is a transparency gap because PISA datasets typically contain missing questionnaire responses and/or item nonresponse. As a result, the exact PV and missing-data procedures cannot be verified from the provided text.
outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2012 computer-based assessment data to predict a three-class math proficiency outcome (low/medium/high) from questionnaire-based background variables. A deep neural network baseline achieved weighted precision 62.99%, weighted recall 64.79%, weighted F1 63.83%, with Cohen’s kappa 0.31 and G-mean 0.58. After augmenting the minority (high proficiency) class using SMOTE, VAE, and CTGAN, the authors report improved minority-class performance, with the best minority-class recall (66.67%) and largest inverted KS distance (0.92) obtained for CTGAN (size 32). The best overall weighted F1/precision/recall among augmentation methods was reported for VAE, but the minority-class trade-off (G-mean) was highest for CTGAN (G-mean 0.63). The paper does not report a PV-based analysis or a missing-data handling strategy, and it does not discuss survey-weight usage, limiting interpretability and reproducibility.
sample_filtering_criteria: Used the publicly released PISA 2012 computer-based assessment database. The target was the overall mathematics result extracted from the PISA 2012 computer-based assessment. Background variables were taken from all three questionnaires (student, parent, school), and the final tabular dataset contained 17,671 samples. The dataset was split into training, test, and validation sets (20% test, additional 20% validation, remaining for training). All columns were normalized; no further country- or grade-specific filtering is described in the provided text.
effect_size: Neural Network (baseline): weighted Precision 62.99%, weighted Recall 64.79%, weighted F1 63.83%, Cohen kappa 0.31, G-mean 0.58. Best minority-class trade-off: Neural Network with CTGAN (size 32) achieved minority-class recall 66.67% (in augmented-class evaluation) and highest inverted KS distance 0.92; overall best G-mean reported as 0.63 for CTGAN (size 32). Best overall weighted precision/recall/F1 reported for VAE (latent dim=3/5 variants), with highest weighted recall/precision and highest F1 among VAE variants.
primary_finding: Using PISA 2012 computer-based assessment the study leveraged student math attitudes, books at home, mathematics efficacy, and out-of-school study time variables to predict three math proficiency classes, finding that training with synthetic data (especially CTGAN for minority-class recall and G-mean) improved minority-class prediction while majority-class performance deteriorated. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.
confounders: math attitudes; Books at home; Mathematics efficacy; Guided homework study time; Personal tutor study time

title: Exploring Test-Taking Disengagement in the Context of PISA 2022: Evidence from Process Data
journal: International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education
weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 process data and self-reported effort items for the Turkish sample, then constructs person-level indicators (response time, number of actions, and response-time-effort indices) and applies Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) to classify students into engagement profiles. The manuscript reports listwise deletion for missing process indicators, but it does not describe the use of PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the LPA or descriptive/correlation analyses. Because LPA and standard correlation procedures are not explicitly documented as weight-aware here, the weighting approach is unclear from the text; analysts should consult the PISA technical documentation and the authors’ data-analysis code (if available) to confirm whether complex survey design weights were applied. For replication, weighting should follow PISA’s complex sampling design guidance (student sampling weights for point estimates; replicate weights for variance estimation) and should be applied consistently across profile estimation and achievement comparisons.
handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).
outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 mathematics process data for Turkey, focusing on three engagement indicators: response time (RT), number of actions (NA), and self-reported effort (SRE) from the PISA effort thermometer. After listwise deletion of missing process indicators, the analytic sample contains 6560 students. The authors first show that engagement distributions vary substantially by thresholding approach (RTE_5sec, RTE_10p, and NA_10p), and that NA correlates most strongly with mathematics achievement (r = .43), while SRE shows the weakest association (r = .02). Using latent profile analysis, they select a three-profile solution (entropy = 0.883) and find that the Disengaged profile (10.01%) has the lowest mean mathematics achievement (421.74) compared with the Moderately-Engaged (452.689) and Highly-Engaged (536.453) profiles. A key limitation is that the manuscript does not report survey-weight handling for PISA’s complex design, and the profile-based approach is person-centered rather than a predictive ML model.
null_fields_interpretation: This paper does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models; instead, it uses Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) to uncover latent engagement subgroups and then compares mathematics achievement across profiles. Therefore, the ML technique fields are intentionally left empty (no supervised learner is reported), and the study is classified as exploratory rather than predictive.
sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is restricted to the Turkish PISA 2022 students who completed the mathematics computer-based assessment and for whom response time (RT) and number of actions (NA) could be computed; missing values on these process indicators were excluded using listwise deletion. This cleaning step reduced the sample from 7250 to 6560 students. The study focuses on mathematics performance and uses the PISA effort thermometer self-reported effort item (SRE) together with process-based indicators to estimate engagement profiles.
effect_size: LPA fit: optimal 3-profile solution; AIC 51750.54, BIC 51845.58, aBIC 51801.09; entropy 0.883; LMR test p < .05. Profile sizes: Profile 1 (Moderately-Engaged) 5431; Profile 2 (Highly-Engaged) 472; Profile 3 (Disengaged) 657. Profile differences: ANOVA p < .05; Tukey post-hoc p < .05 for RT, NA, and SRE across all profiles. primary_finding: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics (Turkey) process data, the study leveraged response time (RT), number of actions (NA), and self-reported effort (SRE) to classify students into engagement profiles, finding that a three-profile structure best captured engagement heterogeneity (Moderately-Engaged, Highly-Engaged, Disengaged).
